theory_units.summary: Space can be stretched or shortened through optical transitions, ingenious editing, imaginative storytelling, and choice of lens focal length, to manage narrative pacing for travel or distance.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting travel or journeys where showing every detail is unnecessary or when specific spatial perceptions are desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficient storytelling by removing needless travel, creating illusions of distance, or making travel appear longer or shorter as required.

theory_units.title: Handle Complex Time/Space Shifts Carefully
theory_units.summary: In complex pictures that move back and forth in time and space, handling must be careful to avoid audience confusion; viewers must never be left in doubt about the event's location and what is happening.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming stories with non-linear timelines or multiple geographical locations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience understanding and engagement despite narrative complexity.
theory_units.caution: Only suspense stories are designed to confuse the audience until the mystery is explained in the last reel.

theory_units.title: Controlled Action Filming Strategy
theory_units.summary: For controlled action (staged, rehearsed events), film from as many angles and as many times as necessary to achieve satisfactory takes, ensuring complete aesthetic and technical control.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming theatrical motion pictures or staged non-theatrical scenes where action can be directed and repeated.
theory_units.expected_effect: Optimal aesthetic and technical results; ability to refine performance and coverage.

theory_units.title: Uncontrolled Action Filming Strategy
theory_units.summary: For uncontrolled action (events that cannot be staged or repeated), adapt to prevailing conditions, follow standard filming procedures for technical excellence, and use multiple cameras for complete coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming news events, parades, engineering trials, or any one-time, unpredictable events.
theory_units.expected_effect: Best possible coverage under given conditions; technically excellent results.
theory_units.caution: Cameraman may have limited control over angle and lens choice due to lighting, space, or danger. At worst, it's a one-take affair.

theory_units.title: Plan Uncontrolled Action Camera Angles
theory_units.summary: Even when action is uncontrolled, camera angles should be carefully planned in advance, especially for events like parades, to ensure a consistent line of march and clear direction.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming events like parades where the action is not controlled but predictable.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear direction of movement; consistent visual flow for the audience.

theory_units.title: Master Scene Technique Overview
theory_units.summary: The master scene technique involves filming a continuous take of an entire event in a single setting, capturing the overall action from beginning to end, which is then intercut with closer shots.
theory_units.applies_when: General practice in dramatic narrative filmmaking to ensure comprehensive coverage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides complete footage of the sequence, allowing for flexible editing choices later.

theory_units.title: Single Camera for Staged Action with Repetition
theory_units.summary: For staged action involving professional actors that can be precisely duplicated, use a single camera to film the master scene, then repeat portions of the action for closer inter-cutting shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming theatrical films or controllable non-theatrical scenes where actors can precisely repeat performances.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for re-lighting each setup for best photographic results and actors to perform complete takes.
theory_units.caution: Action and dialogue must be precisely duplicated for closer shots.

theory_units.title: Multiple Cameras for Unrepeatable or Amateur Action
theory_units.summary: Employ multiple cameras for one-time, uncontrollable events, or when performers (amateur actors, non-professionals) cannot precisely duplicate action or dialogue, to ensure all angles are covered simultaneously.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming news events, quiz shows, engineering tests, missile launchings, or any situation where precise repetition of performance is difficult or impossible.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures complete coverage from all angles, perfect matching of action and dialogue, guarantees editorial matching.
theory_units.caution: Lighting must be a compromise, and camera set-ups are best when shooting more or less from the same angle with different focal length lenses.

theory_units.title: Editing Flexibility with Master Scene Coverage
theory_units.summary: Master scene coverage, combined with inter-cutting closer shots, provides the film editor with duplicate action and dialogue from various angles, offering wide choices in cutting the sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: During the editing phase of a production utilizing the master scene technique.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the editor to re-establish setting/actors, emphasize specific actions/dialogue/reactions, improve actor performance, shift dramatic emphasis, and re-edit if unsatisfactory.

theory_units.title: Cheating Action and Dialogue in Cut-in Shots
theory_units.summary: Precise repetition of action and dialogue in cut-in closer shots is not always strictly necessary; the 'heart' of the individual shot can be 'cheated' if player movement out of and back into the master scene matches at the cut points.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming cut-in shots after the master scene, allowing for minor adjustments or 'second-guessing' during production.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased flexibility during filming without compromising continuity at the edit points.
theory_units.caution: Action and dialogue must overlap only where scenes are inter-cut, and player movement into and out of the master shot must match-cut. Editors should be notified of any script changes.

theory_units.title: Multi-Camera Placement for Uncontrolled Action
theory_units.summary: When filming uncontrolled action with multiple cameras, all cameras must be positioned on the same side of the action axis.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming uncontrolled action (e.g., flight tests, demonstrations) with multiple cameras.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficient coverage for editorial purposes, minimizes time and effort while ensuring sufficient footage.

theory_units.title: Master Scene Blocking and Performance Requirements
theory_units.summary: Single-camera master scenes require precise blocking, repeatable performances from actors, and meticulous planning for matching closer shots to ensure continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming single-camera master scenes, especially long or complex sequences.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless intercutting between master scenes and closer shots, maintaining visual and performance continuity.
theory_units.caution: Long or complex sequences should only be attempted by professional actors capable of sustained, exact performances. Radical changes in player positions, looks, or moves will result in jarring jump-cuts. Generally, adhere to the master scene as closely as possible, allowing only limited 'cheating'.

theory_units.title: Selective Filming of Master Scenes
theory_units.summary: If editorial requirements are predetermined, it is not necessary to film an entire master scene; only the required portions need to be shot, with the rest walked through for blocking.
theory_units.applies_when: When editorial requirements for the finished film can be precisely determined in advance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Saves significant shooting time, raw film stock, and processing costs.

theory_units.title: Multi-Camera Planning for Staged Action
theory_units.summary: Staged action filmed with multiple cameras demands extensive planning and rehearsal to coordinate player and camera movements, ensuring all necessary shots are captured in one run-through.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming staged action with multiple cameras (e.g., television shows).
theory_units.expected_effect: Ability to record all necessary shots in a single run-through, ensuring synchronized performances and camera operations.
theory_units.caution: Lighting must often be a compromise due to many angles and positions, making low-key dramatic lighting rarely feasible.

theory_units.title: Multi-Camera Cut-In Lens Selection
theory_units.summary: Cut-in cameras in a multi-camera setup must use long focal-length lenses to avoid being in the line-of-sight of the wide-angle long shot camera.
theory_units.applies_when: Using cut-in cameras within a multi-camera setup that includes a wide-angle long shot camera.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures cut-in cameras and their crews remain unseen in wider shots, maintaining the illusion.

theory_units.title: Triple-Take Technique: Action Overlap for Continuity
theory_units.summary: The Triple-Take technique achieves shot-to-shot continuity by overlapping the action at the beginning and end of each consecutive shot, ensuring seamless transitions.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming without a script, or when seeking simple, robust shot-to-shot continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces a series of interlocking images, conveys an impression of uninterrupted action, assures perfect continuity, and eliminates jump-cuts.
theory_units.caution: Requires constant awareness of the action at the beginning and end of each shot. Primarily for controllable action.

theory_units.title: Seamless Continuity as Audience Goal
theory_units.summary: The ultimate goal of continuity in filmmaking is to make cuts, camera angle changes, and image size changes imperceptible to the audience, creating a continuous, natural flow of movement.
theory_units.applies_when: All stages of filmmaking, from planning to editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience remains immersed in the narrative, unaware of technical transitions, perceiving a continuous flow of action 'as in life'.
theory_units.caution: While 'cheating' time and space is permissible, it must never be apparent to the audience.

theory_units.title: Pre-Visualization for Triple-Take
theory_units.summary: Before filming with the Triple-Take technique, the cameraman should mentally pre-visualize the entire finished sequence, shot by shot, including player and camera positions.
theory_units.applies_when: Before using the Triple-Take technique, especially when filming without a script.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures proper blocking of player and camera positions, suggests necessary shots and angles, and helps identify ideal cut and overlap points.
theory_units.caution: Requires 'stream-of-consciousness' thinking to project the finished sequence in the mind's eye.

theory_units.title: Establishing and Re-establishing Long Shots
theory_units.summary: Use long shots to begin and end sequences, and to re-orient the audience whenever there are major changes in position or narrative elements.
theory_units.applies_when: Structuring sequences, especially when moving between different shot sizes or when the audience might lose spatial context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Orients the audience to the setting and spatial relationships, preventing them from becoming 'lost' when cutting to closer shots.
theory_units.caution: If the camera stays in close too long, the audience will become 'lost' and forget the location of the action.

theory_units.title: Progressive Shot Scale for Engagement
theory_units.summary: Begin a scene with a wide, high-angle shot, then progressively move the camera in, lower, and around to the side for medium shots and close-ups, mimicking natural viewing.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a scene or subject and drawing the audience into the action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Satisfies the audience's curiosity for a more intimate look, mimics natural human perception, and contributes to good continuity.

theory_units.title: Shot Scale for Narrative Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Utilize long shots for establishment, medium shots for the core action, and close-ups for emphasis on important details or emotions.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning shot coverage to effectively convey narrative and emotional weight.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves good continuity, clearly communicates the narrative, and draws audience attention to key elements.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Completed Movement with Overlap
theory_units.summary: Ideally, cuts should occur after the completion of a movement, with the entire movement repeated from a new camera angle at the beginning of the next shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning cut points and overlaps between consecutive shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the editor with choices for matching shots (before, after, or on action), creating a smoother visual effect where movement carries the splice and minimizes awareness of changes.
theory_units.caution: Certain movements should not be interrupted by cutting, as it can disturb the natural flow of action.

theory_units.title: Filming for Editing Flexibility (Overlap All)
theory_units.summary: The cameraman should overlap all complete movements between consecutive shots and avoid making editing decisions during filming, providing maximum options for the editor.
theory_units.applies_when: During filming of any sequence involving movement and multiple shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that the editor has various possibilities to study for the best screen effects, leading to match-cuts and smooth transitions.

theory_units.title: Precision in Overlapping Action
theory_units.summary: Any overlapping action from one shot to the next must be performed in precisely the same manner to ensure a perfect match-cut.
theory_units.applies_when: When actors or subjects are performing actions that need to overlap between shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves flawless match-cuts, making transitions imperceptible.
theory_units.caution: If overlapping portions are not precise duplicates, they are useless for match-cuts. Amateurs must be carefully instructed and observed.

theory_units.title: Freeze Technique for Static Subjects/Camera Moves
theory_units.summary: For static subjects or solitary tasks without perceptible movement, 'freeze' the action at intervals to allow the camera to move to a new, pre-determined angle before resuming filming.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming static individuals or solitary tasks where camera repositioning is needed during a shot without continuous subject movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for camera repositioning and new angles without appearing to interrupt continuous action, provided it's executed deftly.
theory_units.caution: Must be accomplished deftly to avoid appearing jerky when edited. Camera starts/stops and angles should be pre-determined, not impulsive.

theory_units.title: Multi-Camera for Complex Triple-Take Scenarios
theory_units.summary: While primarily single-camera, the Triple-Take technique can incorporate additional cameras for complex, time-consuming, or unrepeatable portions of a sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: When additional coverage (angles, close-ups) is required simultaneously for tricky, lengthy, or unique operations within a Triple-Take framework.
theory_units.expected_effect: Obtains necessary additional coverage without needing to repeat complex or unrepeatable actions.

theory_units.title: Triple-Take Error Correction
theory_units.summary: If a mistake occurs during Triple-Take filming, stop, switch angles, and overlap the action from just before the mistake, allowing earlier footage to be saved.
theory_units.applies_when: When an error occurs during filming using the Triple-Take technique.
theory_units.expected_effect: Minimizes retakes and film waste by only re-shooting the faulty portion of action.

theory_units.title: Triple-Take for Chronological Process Documentaries
theory_units.summary: The Triple-Take technique is well-suited for filming chronological industrial operations, tests, and training films where action can be stopped and repeated for various shots and angles.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming process-oriented documentaries or training films where the subject matter can be controlled, stopped, and personnel instructed to overlap actions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Preserves the natural flow and rhythm of an event, simplifies filming for unfamiliar personnel, and avoids repeating entire complex operations for different shots.
theory_units.caution: Requires that the work can be stopped and personnel will perform as instructed, overlapping actions accurately.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Interior Lighting Continuity
theory_units.summary: To preserve interior lighting continuity across varied shot sizes, ideally do not disturb long-shot lighting, instead use separate units for closer shots. If lights must move, mark their positions for return.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming interior scenes with varied shot sizes, especially in documentary subjects on location.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures consistent lighting for re-establishing shots and avoids visible changes in illumination between cuts.
theory_units.caution: Interior lighting continuity can be very difficult to preserve, especially if lights must be moved for each shot. Requires sufficient lighting units or meticulous marking.

theory_units.title: Director/Cameraman Expertise for Improvised Filming
theory_units.summary: When filming improvised action without a script, the director/cameraman must possess deep knowledge of filming, editing, and 'cinematic cheating' to ensure match-cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming improvised action without a detailed shooting script.
theory_units.expected_effect: Results in match-cut scenes despite improvisation, as the filmmaker instinctively knows how to manage changes in action, angles, and props.
theory_units.caution: This demanding approach requires high concentration and a comprehensive understanding of how cinematic elements affect continuity.

theory_units.title: Master Scene (Single Camera) Applicability
theory_units.summary: The single-camera master scene method is best suited for scripted productions with professional actors, controlled environments, and ample resources, where maximum editing flexibility is desired.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming from a shooting script, with professional actors, completely controlled production elements, sufficient time/film, and when the director desires the greatest range of editing choices.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the film editor with the greatest variety in assembling the sequence, resulting in a highly polished and professional product.
theory_units.caution: Demands actors capable of sustained, exact performances and precise blocking.

theory_units.title: Master Scene (Multi-Camera) Applicability
theory_units.summary: The multi-camera master scene method is ideal for uncontrolled or unrepeatable events, or when working with amateur personnel who cannot duplicate actions, requiring simultaneous coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: Action is not under cameraman's control, events cannot be interrupted, sequences are staged only once, amateur actors cannot duplicate actions, or long and closer shots must be recorded simultaneously.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures proper coverage of events that cannot be repeated or where perfect actor consistency is not possible, providing all necessary shots.
theory_units.caution: Requires extensive planning and rehearsal for staged action to coordinate multiple cameras and talent.

theory_units.title: Triple-Take (Single Camera) Applicability
theory_units.summary: The single-camera Triple-Take technique is advantageous for stop-and-go filming, working with inexperienced personnel, managing film costs, improvisational shooting, and when the filmmaker has strong editorial control 'in the camera'.
theory_units.applies_when: When it's advantageous to film in a stop-and-go pattern, inexperienced personnel perform actions best filmed individually, film costs are a factor, shooting off-the-cuff, the cameraman can control/repeat action, lighting/staging the entire event in long shot is difficult, and the filmmaker has strong editorial ability.
theory_units.expected_effect: Greater freedom during filming, minimized film waste, easier handling of difficult or long-drawn subjects, and reduced editing problems.
theory_units.caution: Limits the film editor's choices significantly as the sequence is largely 'cut in the camera'. Can lead to a 'hodge-podge' of shots if planning and concentration are lacking.

theory_units.title: Hybrid Master Scene & Triple-Take Technique
theory_units.summary: Combine techniques by filming initial and final portions of a sequence as master scenes (often single-camera), and using the triple-take method for the in-between action.
theory_units.applies_when: When a balance of control and flexibility is desired, to save film, or when different parts of a sequence lend themselves better to different techniques.
theory_units.expected_effect: Saves considerable film while allowing adaptability to prevailing conditions and narrative requirements.

theory_units.title: Flexibility in Filming Technique Choice
theory_units.summary: Do not commit to a single filming method for an entire production; analyze the event's factors and be prepared to switch between Master Scene and Triple-Take techniques as needed.
theory_units.applies_when: During pre-production analysis and throughout the filming process.
theory_units.expected_effect: Optimizes efficiency and outcome by adapting to variables like talent, action type, budget, time, and equipment availability.

theory_units.title: Providing Editorial Coverage (Cut-Ins/Cut-Aways)
theory_units.summary: Regardless of the primary filming technique, the cameraman should always provide the editor with sufficient cut-in and cut-away close-ups.
theory_units.applies_when: During any filming scenario, to support the editing process.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps shorten sequences, cover continuity lapses, and provide additional options for the editor.

theory_units.title: Screen Appearance Over Actual Reality
theory_units.summary: Action in film is judged solely by its screen appearance and how it 'should' look to the audience, even if this requires filming 'incorrectly' in reality.
theory_units.applies_when: Anytime there's a conflict between how something appears in actuality and how it needs to appear on screen for clarity and continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures correct and consistent screen appearance for the audience, preventing distraction or confusion.
theory_units.caution: An unexplained change in screen direction will disrupt continuity and confuse the audience.

theory_units.title: Constant Screen Travel for Progression
theory_units.summary: To depict continuous progression, a subject's movement across the screen should maintain a constant direction (e.g., consistently left-to-right or right-to-left) across all shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Depicting a subject (person, vehicle) moving continuously in a single direction throughout a sequence or narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly shows progression, prevents the audience from receiving the impression that the subject has turned around or is returning.
theory_units.caution: Once screen direction is established, it must be maintained, regardless of camera angles or intermingled shot sizes.

theory_units.title: Interior/Exterior Directional Match
theory_units.summary: When cutting between exterior and interior shots of a moving vehicle, the interior shot should be filmed from the same side of the vehicle as the exterior shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning from an exterior shot of a moving vehicle to an interior shot of the same vehicle.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a smoother transition and prevents the jarring impression that the vehicle has suddenly reversed direction.

theory_units.title: Establishing 'Comings and Goings' Direction
theory_units.summary: When depicting subjects traveling to and from locations, establish and consistently maintain specific screen directions for 'comings' and 'goings' (e.g., home to town L-R, town to home R-L).
theory_units.applies_when: Depicting subjects traveling between distinct locations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Orientates the audience to the geography and consistent travel paths, regardless of camera angles or shot sizes.
theory_units.caution: Travel direction for both coming and going must be consistently the same, however many times the action returns to the same locale.

theory_units.title: Contrasting Screen Travel for Opposing Subjects
theory_units.summary: Use subjects moving in opposite screen directions (e.g., L-R vs. R-L) to visually convey that they are moving towards each other, predicting a meeting or clash.
theory_units.applies_when: Depicting two subjects moving towards each other, building suspense, predicting a conflict, or adding dramatic impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience will correctly assume the subjects are approaching each other and will meet or clash, adding visual simplicity and impact.
theory_units.caution: Relies on earlier establishment of locations/directions for full effect (e.g., town toward right, ranch toward left).

theory_units.title: Shot Scale & Editing Rhythm for Climactic Build-up
theory_units.summary: Build tension towards a climax by progressively moving into closer shots and cutting them shorter and shorter, creating an accelerating editing pattern.
theory_units.applies_when: Building towards a climactic meeting, clash, or any intense moment in a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Excites viewers' emotions, increases their involvement, and leads to a frenzied, impactful finish.

theory_units.title: Neutral Shots for Directional Transition
theory_units.summary: Neutral screen movements (subject moving directly toward or away from the camera, or certain tracking/high-low shots) are non-directional and can be intercut with scenes moving in any direction.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to transition smoothly between shots with opposite screen directions, or to provide visual variety.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for switching screen direction without abruptness, can mask directional reversals, and adds visual depth and variety.
theory_units.caution: Neutral shots (head-on/tail-away) are only truly neutral if the subject remains centered in the frame. An entrance or exit implies direction.

theory_units.title: Neutral Shot Composition: Front/Rear View
theory_units.summary: To achieve an absolutely neutral screen direction, only the front or rear of the moving subject should be depicted, avoiding any side views.
theory_units.applies_when: Aiming for an absolutely non-directional shot of a moving subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents accidental indication of side-to-side travel direction.
theory_units.caution: If one side of the subject is seen, direction of travel will be indicated, making the shot non-neutral.

theory_units.title: Neutral Shots to Switch Screen Direction
theory_units.summary: A head-on or tail-away shot can begin neutrally and then exit/enter one side of the frame, or be inserted as a buffer, to deliberately switch screen direction between two otherwise opposing shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Intentionally changing the established screen direction of a subject, or needing to smoothly transition between shots with opposite directions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the editor to reverse screen movement without the abruptness of a direct cut, providing a temporary neutral condition to reset audience orientation.

theory_units.title: Neutral Shots for Visual Variety
theory_units.summary: Break up monotonous series of constant left-to-right or right-to-left shots by inserting neutral subject movements.
theory_units.applies_when: Sequences with long stretches of constant directional movement that may become visually repetitive.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides visual variety, greater depth, and a welcome change from typical side angles.

theory_units.title: Neutral Shots for Audience Impact/Involvement
theory_units.summary: Utilize head-on shots for action advancing directly toward the viewer or high-impact exits (e.g., jumping over the camera) to significantly increase audience involvement.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring to place the viewer directly in the action and maximize their emotional or physical response.
theory_units.expected_effect: Jars the audience into increased involvement with the screen action, as the moving image grows in size.

theory_units.title: Neutral Shots to Mask Directional Reversal
theory_units.summary: Insert a neutral shot between two shots moving in opposite directions to distract the audience momentarily, allowing for a complete reversal of screen movement without an abrupt cut.
theory_units.applies_when: When it's necessary to reverse the established screen movement of a subject, or to smoothly bridge two shots with conflicting directions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Distracts the audience from the directional switch, making the reversal appear less abrupt than a direct cut.

theory_units.title: 180-Degree Rule (Action Axis)
theory_units.summary: Maintain consistent screen direction throughout a series of shots by positioning all camera setups on only one side of an imaginary 'action axis' (the line of subject travel).
theory_units.applies_when: Filming any sequence where screen direction (constant or contrasting) must be maintained and respected.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that screen direction remains consistent, regardless of camera angle, and the relationship between camera and subject movement is preserved.
theory_units.caution: Crossing the action axis will disrupt screen direction and confuse the audience. For new locations, draw a new axis but remain on the same side relative to the original axis direction. Thinking of the axis as a directional movement rather than an imaginary line complicates the work.

theory_units.title: Establishing & Maintaining Screen Direction with Action Axis
theory_units.summary: Establish a subject's screen direction by their exit point (e.g., screen right for left-to-right travel). Maintain this direction by keeping the camera on one side of the action axis, an imaginary line of action or eyeline.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any moving subject (player, vehicle) to establish and maintain consistent screen direction for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents audience confusion, maintains spatial and directional continuity, makes movement clear and predictable.
theory_units.caution: Crossing the action axis inadvertently will reverse screen direction and confuse the audience. An exception occurs when two players look at each other as they walk or ride; the static action axis should then be drawn through the moving players.

theory_units.title: Safe Axis Crossing for Moving Subjects
theory_units.summary: The camera can safely cross the action axis to film opposing angles of moving subjects (walking or in a vehicle) without confusing the audience, even if screen direction appears to reverse in consecutive shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming subjects walking or riding in a vehicle, when different angles from either side of their travel path are desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for greater camera placement variety while maintaining audience understanding of directional travel.
theory_units.caution: This method specifically applies to *moving* subjects where the audience implicitly understands the physical movement. It's distinct from crossing the axis on stationary subjects which often causes confusion.

theory_units.title: Sandwich Strategy for Opposing Angle Continuity
theory_units.summary: To use opposing camera angles on a moving subject without confusing the audience, 'sandwich' shots from the opposite side of the travel axis between shots from the original established side.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to show a moving subject from opposing camera angles (crossing the action axis) while maintaining clear directional continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for visual variety with different perspectives of the moving subject while reassuring the audience of the consistent direction of travel.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the establishment and return shots clearly re-establish the original screen direction.

theory_units.title: Versatile Camera Angles for Maintaining Screen Direction of Moving Subjects
theory_units.summary: Various camera angles, including front three-quarter, side-on (static or panning), rear three-quarter, and tail-away, can all effectively maintain an established screen direction (e.g., left-to-right) for a moving subject.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming a moving player or vehicle and needing to select an appropriate camera angle that consistently maintains the established screen direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for visual variety in portraying movement while ensuring the audience clearly perceives the subject's continuous directional travel across different shot types and camera positions.
theory_units.caution: While these angles can maintain direction, careful planning of entrances and exits is still crucial for seamless cuts.

theory_units.title: Managing Screen Direction on Curves: The Long Shot Exception
theory_units.summary: When filming a subject on a curve, shooting across the action axis can inadvertently reverse screen direction in closer shots. However, a long shot or pan shot that encompasses the entire curving movement, showing the subject turn and then resume its original direction, can safely depict temporary opposite movement during the shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming subjects moving along a curved path, especially when considering camera placement that might cross the implicit action axis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains directional clarity for the audience despite the subject's path, allowing for dynamic curved movement without confusion, provided the shot is wide enough to show the full turn and the subject enters/exits correctly.
theory_units.caution: Closer shots filmed across a curve will likely depict incorrect screen travel and should be avoided for maintaining established continuity.

theory_units.title: Deliberate Screen Direction Switch via Curves or Corners
theory_units.summary: Utilize a curve or corner to deliberately switch screen direction. By shooting across the action axis, allow the subject to enter correctly but then curve/turn and exit the 'wrong' side of the frame, establishing a new screen direction for subsequent shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When a planned, abrupt change in the established screen direction of a moving subject is needed for editorial or narrative purposes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a natural-looking transition for a change in screen direction that the audience will accept, serving as a clean break between two series of shots moving in opposite established directions.
theory_units.caution: This technique works best on wide turns or curves where the subject travels enough distance to clearly establish the new direction before exiting the frame.

theory_units.title: Directional Continuity Through Doorways: The 'New Deal'
theory_units.summary: Passage through a doorway into a new setting often constitutes a 'new deal' for directional continuity, meaning established screen direction may be intentionally altered or restarted without confusing the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When a subject moves between distinct spaces through a doorway, potentially allowing for a reset or change in established screen direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides flexibility in camera placement and screen direction without disrupting the audience's spatial understanding, as the new setting justifies a new directional context.
theory_units.caution: While a switch is allowed, careful use of head-on/tail-away shots can still maintain continuity if desired. If cross-screen angles are used on consecutive shots through a door, it's smoother if the camera stays on the same side of the axis.

theory_units.title: Cheating the Action Axis for Production Factors
theory_units.summary: To accommodate production factors (e.g., light, background), the action axis can be 'cheated' by reversing both the subject's movement and the camera's position relative to the axis, thus preserving the *original intended screen direction* for the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When external factors (lighting, background, terrain) necessitate shooting a subject moving in a physically opposite direction than established, but the visual screen direction must be maintained.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for greater flexibility in shooting locations and times while still presenting consistent screen direction, avoiding continuity errors that would otherwise arise from changing physical direction.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful attention to sun angle and shadows in outdoor shots; best done around noon or in close-ups with controlled lighting. Long shots with prominent shadows are particularly prone to disclosing the cheat.

theory_units.title: Strategic Use of Entrances and Exits for Editorial Continuity
theory_units.summary: To convey continuous progression across different shots, especially when backgrounds change, subjects must enter and exit the frame 'cleanly'. Entrances and exits facilitate smooth cuts, prevent jump-cuts, and maintain the audience's spatial understanding.
theory_units.applies_when: When subjects are moving across different locations or backgrounds, or when cutting between shots to show continuous progression.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures seamless transitions between shots, avoids jarring jump-cuts, provides the editor with necessary material for smooth pacing, and maintains the audience's belief in continuous action and spatial coherence.
theory_units.caution: Failing to shoot clean entrances/exits, or mismatching exit/entrance proximity across cuts, will distract the audience and create continuity errors. For precaution, players' exits should be filmed before breaking down lighting for close-ups. When in doubt, shoot an exit immediately after filming the entrance, as it's easier to discard than reshoot.

theory_units.title: Exceptions: When Not to Force Entrances and Exits
theory_units.summary: Entrances and exits are not always necessary: when a subject remains center-screen against a consistent background, or when individual moving action shots are cross-cut with other scenes (where progression is implied by changing backgrounds).
theory_units.applies_when: When deciding whether to include entrances/exits in shots involving movement, considering the context of the editing and background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Avoids unnecessary repetitive action, streamlines editing for specific scenarios, and maintains audience engagement without artificial entrances/exits when progression is implicit or within the frame.
theory_units.caution: For same-background sequences, it's still best to 'bracket' with an entrance in the first shot and an exit in the last. For cross-cut shots, occasional entrances/exits can still add visual variety.

theory_units.title: Reaction Close-up for Explaining Directional Switches
theory_units.summary: A reaction close-up of an observer, where the observer's head movement implies they are following action in a new direction (as if behind the camera), can be used to distract the audience and justify an otherwise abrupt screen direction change.
theory_units.applies_when: When an abrupt switch in screen direction is necessary and a physical turn-around cannot be shown; used to 'explain' the change to the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience's attention is diverted to the observer, allowing them to subconsciously accept the new screen direction as logical, preventing confusion caused by a sudden directional reversal.
theory_units.caution: The observer's head movement must match the *intended new direction* of the action, as if viewing it from behind the camera (which often means the on-screen head turn appears opposite to the actual action's screen direction). Can be filmed post-production against neutral backgrounds if necessary.

theory_units.title: Methods for Explained Reversal of Screen Direction
theory_units.summary: To avoid audience confusion, established screen direction, if necessarily reversed, must be explicitly explained on screen through various visual techniques rather than abrupt cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever a change in the established screen direction of a moving subject is unavoidable due to narrative or practical reasons.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents audience disorientation and maintains the integrity of spatial continuity, even when the subject's screen direction fundamentally changes.
theory_units.caution: Abruptly cutting from one screen direction to the opposite without explanation will confuse the audience and should be avoided. Once a directional pattern is set, it should be rigidly maintained unless explained.

theory_units.title: Establishing and Maintaining Map Direction for Long Travel
theory_units.summary: For travel over great distances, align screen direction with conventional map orientation (East=right, West=left on the map). Northbound travel can ascend from lower-left to upper-right, southbound descend from upper-left to lower-right. Initial shots of passengers/crew should face this established direction.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming journeys that cover significant distances where the audience might have a pre-conceived mental map (e.g., international flights, cross-country drives).
theory_units.expected_effect: Leverages the audience's subconscious understanding of map orientation to reinforce directional clarity, preventing disorientation and distraction, and reinforcing the sense of progression.
theory_units.caution: Deviating from accepted map direction can cause a subconscious disturbance and momentary distraction for the viewer. North/South travel on a horizontal screen requires careful staging to align with compositional up/down movements.

theory_units.title: Directional Continuity in Complex Location Interiors
theory_units.summary: In multi-room, multi-floor interiors, maintain directional continuity by keeping all camera setups on the same side of the building to avoid crossing the action axis. If impossible, use head-on or tail-away shots, ensuring subjects enter/exit on the side preserving established travel direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming in complex interior locations with significant movement between rooms, floors, or stairs.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents audience disorientation in intricate spatial environments, creating a clear and consistent sense of movement and location within the building.
theory_units.caution: Physical limitations can challenge this rule; alternative strategies (head-on/tail-away) must still prioritize established screen direction.

theory_units.title: Pre-Production Planning for Screen Direction Continuity
theory_units.summary: Thoroughly plan all screen travel sequences, mapping out shots and establishing the action axis in advance to ensure constant progression and directional continuity. This prevents overlooking screen direction due to other production concerns and allows for strategic camera angles and lighting.
theory_units.applies_when: For any sequence involving significant movement or travel, especially those with many shots or complex locations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures consistent and logical screen direction throughout a sequence, minimizes continuity errors, optimizes shooting for visual quality and efficiency, and allows for creative problem-solving without sacrificing core continuity.
theory_units.caution: Failing to plan can lead to accidental reversals or overlooked action axes, particularly when prioritizing individual shots or external factors like sun angle and background.

theory_units.title: Seamless Exterior-to-Interior Transitions
theory_units.summary: To achieve a smooth match-cut between an exterior and interior vehicle shot (or vice versa), film from approximately the same camera angle, as if the camera passes through a window or side of the vehicle, maintaining the original travel axis.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning visually from the exterior of a moving vehicle to its interior, or from interior to exterior.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and immersive transition, making it feel as though the camera physically moves through the vehicle, maintaining spatial orientation for the audience.
theory_units.caution: Deviating significantly from the same camera angle will break the illusion and disrupt continuity. Vehicle mock-ups or real vehicles may impose limitations on camera angling, requiring careful planning.

theory_units.title: The Action Axis (180-Degree Rule)
theory_units.summary: Establish an imaginary line (action axis) between key players. The camera must remain on one side of this line to ensure consistent screen direction and spatial relationships between shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming consecutive matching shots involving two or more interacting players, or even a single player's consistent orientation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains consistent screen direction, prevents player transposition, and helps the audience understand the spatial layout of the scene.
theory_units.caution: Crossing the axis between cuts will transpose players on screen (e.g., left becomes right), creating a disorienting 'fake reverse' or an incorrect looking direction. The camera may not be moved 180 degrees from one setup to another.

theory_units.title: Matching The Look (Static Screen Direction)
theory_units.summary: When filming static subjects, prioritize matching the direction a player *looks* rather than just the direction they *face*, to maintain continuity across cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming consecutive shots of players who are at rest, talking, or performing in a static position, especially for match-cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures players appear to maintain their focus and spatial relationship to others, even when motionless, avoiding jarring directional shifts for the audience.
theory_units.caution: A player looking left in one shot and suddenly right in the next (without showing the shift) will break continuity. A flat-on point-of-view angle may result in a wrong look if the eyes inadvertently shift to the wrong side.

theory_units.title: Camera Crossing Axis for Rear Players (Viewpoint Preservation)
theory_units.summary: While the camera *viewpoint* must not cross the action axis, the camera *itself* can be physically moved across the axis to film players in the rear of a set, provided a new parallel axis is effectively drawn and the camera angle remains consistent with the original viewpoint.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to film players positioned deeper in the set that would require physically crossing the initial action axis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for greater camera flexibility and depth within a scene without breaking the established spatial continuity for the audience.
theory_units.caution: This technique relies on maintaining the camera *angle* (viewpoint) relative to the new, parallel axis. Mismanaging the angle can still lead to transposition. Optically achieving this with zoom/telephoto is an alternative, which keeps the lens on one side of the axis.

theory_units.title: Sweeping Gaze Past the Lens
theory_units.summary: A technique where a player turns their head and shifts their gaze from one side to the other, passing just above or below the camera lens, to relate with multiple on-screen or off-screen players.
theory_units.applies_when: A player needs to switch their attention between subjects located on either side of the camera, or from an on-screen player to an off-screen action/player.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a naturalistic shift in attention for the character without breaking the fourth wall by looking directly into the lens. A new action axis is established based on the player's final gaze direction.
theory_units.caution: The player must avoid looking directly *into* the lens. Inexperienced actors may 'sneak' a look, and inexperienced crew may hesitate to allow this shot, fearing a mismatch. Any shot that ends with a new look requires a corresponding axis for the following shot.

theory_units.title: The Neutral Look (Up/Down Gaze)
theory_units.summary: A neutral look involves a player gazing slightly above or below the camera lens, creating a non-directional look often used as a workaround or when looking at subjects at different heights.
theory_units.applies_when: A player is looking at another player/object/action significantly above or below their eye level (e.g., seated/standing, stairs). It can also be used as an emergency measure to cover an inadvertent directional mismatch or to match stock footage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can logically depict a character looking up or down at something off-screen. In emergencies, it might obscure a directional mismatch without introducing a 'wrong' direction.
theory_units.caution: Use with discretion. It can puzzle the audience by breaking normal left/right looks, may be misinterpreted as looking directly into the lens, and is rarely successful if both players are the same height. Even when used, the look should still be directed to the *side* of the camera to preserve the action axis.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Action Axis for Moving Players and Camera
theory_units.summary: When players or the camera move during a scene, the action axis is dynamic and must be redrawn at the end of each shot to maintain continuity for subsequent cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming scenes with significant player movement, camera pans, dollies, or complex master scenes where the original action axis might be altered.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for complex camera and player movement within a scene while preserving logical screen direction and preventing jump-cuts between set-ups.
theory_units.caution: While player or camera movement *during* a shot can cross the axis (as the audience observes the continuous change), they *must not cross the axis between camera set-ups* as this will cause unaccountable position changes and a mismatch in the following shot. Care must be taken to duplicate players' positions to avoid jump-cuts.

theory_units.title: Managing Interposed Objects in Opposing Close-ups
theory_units.summary: Avoid placing objects between two players if those objects will appear inconsistently transposed (e.g., left vs. right) in opposing close-ups, potentially disorienting the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming opposing close-ups of two players who have a prop or object positioned between them (e.g., on a table).
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures consistent spatial relationships and avoids confusing visual transposition of objects that are meant to be stationary between players.
theory_units.caution: Including a prop like a microphone, crystal ball, or bowl of fruit between players in opposing close-ups can lead to it appearing on the right in one shot and the left in the other, creating a visual mismatch and confusing the audience.

theory_units.title: Consistent Look for a Single Player
theory_units.summary: Even when filming a single player alone, a consistent directional look must be maintained across consecutive shots, applying the principle of the action axis to their interaction with their work or environment.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming an individual working at a desk, machine, or instrument panel, where they are the sole focus and not directly interacting with another visible player.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures visual consistency and audience understanding of the player's focus and orientation within their environment across cuts.
theory_units.caution: Do not suddenly transpose the player's apparent facing/looking direction between shots unless a turn or change is explicitly shown within a shot. Shooting over the wrong shoulder for a right-handed person (over the right shoulder) will obscure their action.

theory_units.title: Speaker and Audience Directional Continuity (Opposing Looks)
theory_units.summary: When filming a speaker addressing an audience, establish opposing looks between the speaker and audience members to simulate a direct interaction, similar to a two-shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming a master of ceremonies, instructor, or lecturer addressing a class or audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of direct engagement between the speaker and individual audience members, enhancing the feeling of a natural conversation or address.
theory_units.caution: Improper camera placement or editing can lead to mis-matched looks, making it seem like the speaker and audience are not looking at each other, especially due to the audience being spread out. A purely opposing method can become monotonous visually.

theory_units.title: Centerline Axis for Speaker-Audience (Theater)
theory_units.summary: Film a theater sequence using a centerline axis to create opposing looks between the speaker and audience, similar to a two-shot interaction.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming a theater sequence where a speaker interacts directly with the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Establishes a clear spatial relationship and 'opposing looks' for the audience, enhancing continuity and viewer orientation.

theory_units.title: Parallel Axis for Speaker-Audience (Theater)
theory_units.summary: Employ a parallel axis (running with audience rows) in theater sequences to allow the speaker to address both sides of the audience while maintaining appropriate opposing looks.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming a theater sequence where the speaker interacts with both sides of the audience, or when greater camera positioning freedom and visual variety are desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables the speaker to naturally engage a wider audience; provides visual variety when combined with the centerline axis.

theory_units.title: Audience Screen Direction Consistency
theory_units.summary: When filming audience members in medium shots or close-ups, ensure their screen direction aligns with their physical location to maintain opposing looks with the speaker and preserve spatial awareness.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming audience members in a theater or similar setting, especially in medium shots or close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear spatial relationships, ensuring audience members appear to be looking at the speaker and not confusing the viewer.

theory_units.title: Speaker-Audience Three-Shot Axis Shift
theory_units.summary: In a three-shot (speaker and two audience members on opposite sides), the speaker's shift in gaze to address one or the other creates a new action axis for subsequent two-shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Framing a speaker interacting with two distinct individuals from the audience, treated as a three-shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables fluid transitions between the speaker addressing different individuals, maintaining continuity of opposing looks.

theory_units.title: Use of Neutral Shots to Break Continuity Patterns
theory_units.summary: Insert neutral shots (without opposing looks) between shots of speaker and audience to break up repetitive back-and-forth cutting or to allow a speaker to change gaze direction without confusing continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: Wanting to vary the rhythm of opposing directional shots, or when a character needs to change their focal direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Reduces visual monotony, allows for flexible gaze changes by characters, and provides a 'reset' for screen direction.

theory_units.title: Long Shot Centerline Rule for Speaker-Audience
theory_units.summary: Long shots of the stage or audience should be filmed head-on (neutral) or from the same side of the centerline axis. Avoid filming long shots of stage and audience from opposite sides of the centerline, as it will make them appear to face the same direction.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming long shots of a stage and audience in a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures clear spatial relationships and opposing looks between speaker and audience; prevents confusing same-direction looks.
theory_units.caution: Do NOT film long shots toward the stage and toward the audience from opposite sides of the centerline, as speaker and audience will face the same direction, breaking continuity.

theory_units.title: Choosing Axis Treatment (Centerline vs. Parallel)
theory_units.summary: Use the centerline axis for simple sequences (e.g., classroom). Employ the parallel axis or a combination of both for greater camera freedom or visual variety.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding on the appropriate action axis strategy for a scene, especially one involving a speaker and an audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Optimizes for either simplicity/clarity or for dynamic visual storytelling and camera flexibility.

theory_units.title: Filming Staged Action Without Audience Interaction
theory_units.summary: When filming plays, demonstrations, or staged actions where performers do not interact with the audience, the requirement for opposing looks between performers and audience is removed.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming events where the audience is merely an observer and does not directly participate or interact with the subjects on stage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies camera setup and continuity rules by removing the requirement for opposing looks between stage and audience.

theory_units.title: Core Action Axis Rule: Camera Must Stay on One Side
theory_units.summary: When opposing looks are required, the camera must remain on one side of the centerline (action) axis. It may not cross the centerline axis in consecutive shots to avoid subjects looking in the same direction.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming any scene requiring opposing looks between subjects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains consistent screen direction and spatial relationships, preventing a confusing 'jump' in subject orientation for the viewer.
theory_units.caution: Do NOT cross the centerline axis in consecutive shots when opposing looks are required, as it will make characters look in the same direction, breaking continuity.

theory_units.title: Auditorium Camera Freedom Exception (with spaced cuts)
theory_units.summary: In long sequences set in auditoriums, the camera may move anywhere if mis-matched shots are spaced a scene or two apart during editing, due to the fixed nature of the setting preventing viewer confusion.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming lengthy sequences in fixed settings like auditoriums where the audience is static and faces one direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for greater camera flexibility and visual variety over a longer sequence without confusing the viewer about spatial orientation.
theory_units.caution: Mis-matched shots must be spaced out during editing. Still, it's pictorially more effective and easier to view when opposing looks are presented in consecutive shots.

theory_units.title: Three-Shot Staging: Dominant Player with Unit
theory_units.summary: When one player dominates and relates to two others who are close together (treated as a unit), position the dominant player on one side of the screen and the unit on the opposite side, treating them as a two-shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging a three-shot where one character has a clear focus or interaction with two other characters who are positioned closely.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies complex three-shot staging by reducing it to a two-shot principle, maintaining clear opposing looks and spatial relationships.

theory_units.title: Gaze/Action Shifts Axis in Three-Shot
theory_units.summary: In a three-shot with a dominant player, when that player shifts gaze or performs an action towards a specific supporting player, a new action axis is created between them, allowing the camera to reposition for a close-up of the dominant player.
theory_units.applies_when: A dominant character in a three-shot shifts their focus or engages with another specific character, especially when preparing for a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates smooth transitions and close-ups, maintaining directional continuity by using an intentional action or look to define the new axis.
theory_units.caution: In 'weaker situations' (less defined action/look), avoid moving the camera completely around between supporting players; stay on the original axis side.

theory_units.title: Three-Shot Staging: Equally Dominant, Spread Apart
theory_units.summary: When three spread-apart players each dominate in turn, film with a single action axis, typically positioning two players in the foreground and one in the background. Individual two-shots can be formed as players shift focus.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging a three-shot where all players are somewhat equally important and take turns being the focus, and are physically separated.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear spatial relationships and avoids disorientation as focus shifts between players.
theory_units.caution: Do NOT cross the action axis, as foreground and background players will transpose screen positions and confuse the viewer.

theory_units.title: Treating Close Players as a Single Unit
theory_units.summary: When two players are positioned close together, treat them as a single unit. Film them from the same side of the action axis so they present a consistent look towards an opposing player, effectively reducing a three-shot to a two-shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Two characters are physically close and functionally act as a single entity in relation to a third, opposing character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies the blocking and camera work, maintaining clear opposing looks and reinforcing the unit's relationship.

theory_units.title: Three-Shot as Series of Dynamic Two-Shots
theory_units.summary: In a three-shot where spread-apart players each dominate in turn, treat each interaction individually as a two-shot. Each new interaction between two players creates its own action axis as players switch their looks.
theory_units.applies_when: Three players are spread apart, and the focus of the scene shifts between different pairs of players as they speak or react.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for dynamic and fluid interactions within a three-shot, with each interaction maintaining proper directional continuity.

theory_units.title: Table Scene Establishment and Axis for Close-ups
theory_units.summary: When filming a group seated around a table, establish the scene clearly. Draw the action axis between players relating to each other to ensure opposing looks in individual close-ups, preventing audience confusion.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming a group of people seated around a table, especially for medium shots and close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents viewer confusion regarding character positions and relationships during cuts to closer shots.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Axis Creation by Off-Screen Look in Table Scenes
theory_units.summary: In table scenes, the camera can move around to film individual close-ups of players across the table because an on-screen player's look towards an off-screen player creates a new action axis.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to get close-ups of various players around a table, especially when their attention shifts to an off-screen player.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for flexible camera positioning and close-ups in complex table scenes, with the new axis guiding continuity.

theory_units.title: Sequential Gaze Shifts in Table Scenes
theory_units.summary: A player can sequentially shift their gaze to relate with different players around a table, as long as the scene is well-established and each interaction maintains opposing looks.
theory_units.applies_when: A single player interacts with multiple other players seated around a table in sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for dynamic and realistic multi-party conversations without confusing the audience, provided continuity principles are followed.
theory_units.caution: The scene must be established and opposing looks maintained for each interaction.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Mid-Player Screen Position Shift in Three-Shots
theory_units.summary: Do not follow a three-shot with two-shots that cause the middle player to appear on opposite sides of the screen in consecutive shots. Instead, break such sequences into two-shots and close-ups, or individual close-ups.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing a three-shot into closer shots, particularly when a middle player is involved.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents viewer disorientation caused by characters abruptly shifting screen position.
theory_units.caution: Avoid following a three-shot with two-shots that transpose the middle player's screen position, as this causes viewer confusion.

theory_units.title: Background Cheat for Reverse Close-ups
theory_units.summary: To achieve a reverse close-up when space or background is limited, reposition the player against a different wall. Turn both the camera and the player as if on a turntable, ensuring their relative positions, camera angle, and look match the original setup, maintaining the camera and player's look on the same side of the axis.
theory_units.applies_when: Shooting reverse close-ups on location or a limited set where physical space or suitable background prevents a direct reverse shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates the illusion of a proper reverse shot and maintains continuity of spatial relationships and screen direction, despite physical limitations.
theory_units.caution: The background may require re-dressing to avoid continuity errors if seen in other shots.

theory_units.title: Matching Stock Shots for Continuity
theory_units.summary: When integrating stock footage with newly filmed scenes, meticulously study the stock shots (projected, viewer, diagrams) beforehand to ensure that all production scenes are filmed with properly oriented opposing or matching looks and angles.
theory_units.applies_when: Incorporating stock library footage (e.g., audience, crowd shots) into a production scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves seamless integration between different sources of footage, maintaining consistent spatial relationships and screen direction.

theory_units.title: Mental Pan Technique for Matching Looks
theory_units.summary: To ensure matching looks, perform a 'mental pan' from the look of a subject in a reference shot (e.g., stock footage) to the intended subject in the next shot. This automatically suggests the correct opposing look and camera angle for the new shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to determine the correct screen direction and camera angle for a new shot that needs to match an existing shot (e.g., audience-speaker, reaction shots).
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies the process of achieving accurate opposing looks and consistent screen direction.

theory_units.title: Matching Direction of Movement and Gaze
theory_units.summary: For external movement (e.g., planes) or internal character reactions, ensure consistent direction. Reaction shots should assume the action is behind the camera. Moving subjects must travel in the same screen direction. Pilots in close-up should face the direction of travel.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming external moving objects, character reactions to off-screen action, or subjects within a moving vehicle.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear directional continuity, preventing jarring jumps in screen direction for moving objects or character gazes.

theory_units.title: Challenges of Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: Reverse shots can be confusing because they may transpose players' screen positions, introduce new backgrounds, and require viewers to re-orient players in relation to the setting.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning or executing reverse shots, highlighting potential pitfalls.
theory_units.expected_effect: Awareness of these challenges helps directors avoid common mistakes that can disorient the viewer.
theory_units.caution: Reverse shots can transpose players, introduce new backgrounds, and confuse viewers.

theory_units.title: Action Axis Ensures Reverse Shot Success
theory_units.summary: Following the action axis principle eliminates matching and editorial problems in reverse shots, ensuring consistent player looks and subject travel direction, even when filming from diametrically opposite angles.
theory_units.applies_when: Executing reverse shots, particularly over-the-shoulder, point-of-view, or travel shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guarantees proper directional continuity and spatial consistency, making reverse shots clear and effective.

theory_units.title: Reverse Shots in Fixed Seating & Distinct Settings
theory_units.summary: Camera angles can be freely reversed in settings with fixed seating (theaters, vehicles) or distinct fronts/backs (churches, courtrooms) because viewers understand the camera has moved, not the subjects. However, still aim to stay on the same side of the centerline axis for uniform directional looks, or insert neutral shots if crossing the axis.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming in locations with clear front/back distinctions or fixed seating arrangements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates camera movement flexibility without confusing the viewer, while still advising adherence to axis for optimal directional consistency.
theory_units.caution: Even in these flexible scenarios, it's still wise to stay on the same side of the axis for uniform directional looks, or insert neutral shots if crossing.

theory_units.title: Using Distinctive Features for Safe Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: Reverse shots can be safely accomplished in rooms with distinctive features (staircases, doorways, fireplaces) which help orient the viewer. Avoid reverse shots in nondescript rooms with similar backgrounds, as this confuses the viewer by presenting a new angle with a similar, unhelpful background.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning reverse shots in interior locations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Distinctive features provide visual cues that prevent viewer confusion when the camera reverses.
theory_units.caution: Avoid reverse shots in nondescript rooms, as a similar background will confuse the viewer when the angle changes due to lack of orienting visual information.

theory_units.title: Establish Overall Setting Before Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: Always establish the overall geography of a room before cutting to reverse angles, so the audience understands the spatial relationships and can comprehend the camera's change in position.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning to use reverse angles within an interior location.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents viewer confusion by providing a clear mental map of the space before altering perspective.

theory_units.title: Reverse Shot for Room Crossing: Mental Pan
theory_units.summary: When a character walks towards and exits the camera, then is picked up in a reverse shot entering and walking away to cross the room, use a mental pan to ensure directional continuity (e.g., if exiting right, they should enter left). Constant travel direction for progression requires filming from the same side of the action axis.
theory_units.applies_when: Showing a character crossing a room using a reverse shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear directional continuity of character movement, preventing confusing 'jumps' in screen direction.

theory_units.title: Reverse Shot: Fixed Group & Entering Player
theory_units.summary: When a fixed group observes a new player entering, the group's off-screen look creates a new action axis with the entering player. The camera can then be placed behind the fixed group (on the opposite side of the room but still on the same side of this new axis) to show the player entering, maintaining consistent directional looks.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a new character entering a room where a fixed group is observing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for a smooth and spatially logical introduction of a new character into an existing scene, maintaining consistent eye-lines.

theory_units.title: Framing Entering Player Between Others (Reverse Angle)
theory_units.summary: When shooting a new player entering from a reverse angle, the camera can frame them between two other players, provided the entering player walks towards the group's established look.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a character from a reverse angle and integrating them with an existing group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually integrates the entering player into the group's space and interaction, reinforcing the group's focus.
theory_units.caution: The entering player must walk towards the group's look to maintain directional consistency.

theory_units.title: Reverse Shot via Player's POV or Off-Screen Look
theory_units.summary: A reverse shot can be motivated by a player's off-screen look or point-of-view (looking past the camera). The camera is then reversed to show what the player sees. If the player is relating to another, this POV reverse should remain on the same side of the axis to maintain opposing looks.
theory_units.applies_when: Wanting to show what a character is looking at, especially when it involves reversing the camera's position.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly conveys a character's perspective and the object of their gaze, while maintaining continuity.
theory_units.caution: If the player is relating to another player, film from the same side of the axis to maintain opposing looks.

theory_units.title: Avoid Transposed Players and Confusing Backgrounds in Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: The most important rule for reverse shots is to avoid confronting the viewer with transposed players against new, confusing backgrounds. Always establish the scene type (e.g., church, bus) or a distinctive setting feature in an overall view to prevent confusion in later reverse shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning any reverse shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience maintains a clear mental map of the scene and character positions, even when the camera reverses.
theory_units.caution: Do NOT transpose players against new backgrounds. ALWAYS establish scene type or a distinctive feature beforehand.

theory_units.title: Overarching Rule: Maintain Directional Continuity
theory_units.summary: Throughout sequences depicting continuous action without time lapse, directional continuity must be maintained. This means player movements, positions, and looks must match across straight cuts, and all on/off-screen players must have properly matching looks in cut-in/cut-away shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming and editing any sequence intended to depict continuous action in real-time.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience understands the spatial relationships, movements, and interactions of characters without confusion.

theory_units.title: Redrawing the Action Axis
theory_units.summary: The action axis must be redrawn at the end of any shot if player movement or camera movement causes it to change from the original axis.
theory_units.applies_when: Player or camera movement within a shot alters the implied action axis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a new reference point for continuity in subsequent shots, preventing confusion.

theory_units.title: Action Axis as Enabler of Camera & Subject Freedom
theory_units.summary: The action axis principle enables camera and subjects to move freely and look in any direction without fear of incorrect directional looks. The key is that player movement or looks must be consistent on each side of a match-cut; therefore, note the movement/look at the beginning and end of each shot and redraw the axis if it changes.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning dynamic camera and player movements within a scene, especially across match-cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for creative freedom while ensuring continuous and logical spatial relationships for the audience.
theory_units.caution: Player movement or looks must be the same on each side of a match-cut.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Changes Within Shot, Static Between Shots (Match Cuts)
theory_units.summary: Within a single shot, players and/or the camera can change direction, cross the axis, pan, dolly, or move. However, between match-cuts (continuous action), nothing should change: players must not change movement direction, looks, or positions, and the camera must not cross the axis established at the end of the last shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning continuous action sequences involving match-cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for dynamic cinematography within a shot while ensuring seamless and logical continuity across cuts.
theory_units.caution: Between match-cuts, players must not change direction/looks/positions, and the camera must not cross the established axis at the end of the last shot.

theory_units.title: Exceptions to Match-Cut Continuity Rules
theory_units.summary: The strict match-cut continuity rules (no changes between shots) do not apply to scenes connected by dissolves or other optical effects, scenes edited into other scenes occurring elsewhere, or cases combining centerline and parallel axes. Editorial or optical interruptions imply that changes may have occurred.
theory_units.applies_when: Using transitional editing devices or combining axis treatments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides creative freedom by indicating when continuity rules can be relaxed without confusing the audience.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Directional Continuity in Intercut Sequences
theory_units.summary: Even when intercutting (e.g., chase scenes), established screen direction must be preserved. The core principle of directional continuity is remaining on the same side of moving or static players/vehicles to maintain established movement or looks in consecutive shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing sequences that involve intercutting between different subjects or locations, where a sense of continuous progression is needed.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a clear and consistent sense of direction for subjects, even when the narrative jumps between them.

theory_units.title: Opening Shots for Establishing Time and Place
theory_units.summary: Open a scene with a shot of a specific detail (e.g., place name at entry point, newspaper date) to visually establish the time and/or location.
theory_units.applies_when: Beginning a new scene or sequence that requires clear establishment of its setting in time or space.
