theory_units.expected_effect: Efficiently and visually informs the audience of the temporal and spatial context.

theory_units.title: Using Fades to Begin or End Narrative Units
theory_units.summary: Use a fade-in (black to image) to begin a story or sequence, and a fade-out (image to black) to end a story or sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: Marking the start or conclusion of a major narrative unit (story, sequence).
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly signals a narrative beginning or end, providing a sense of closure or anticipation.

theory_units.title: Fades for Time Passage or Setting Changes (with caution)
theory_units.summary: Fades can indicate a passage of time (same locale) or a switch to another setting. However, use fades sparingly to avoid a choppy, episodic effect. They are generally best at the beginning/end of a picture unless distinct time/space separations are narratively required.
theory_units.applies_when: Bridging significant gaps in time or changing locations, or at major narrative breaks.
theory_units.expected_effect: Signifies a clear break in narrative continuity, indicating a passage of time or change of place.
theory_units.caution: Use sparingly to avoid a choppy or episodic effect that disrupts narrative flow.

theory_units.title: Using Dissolves for Time/Location Shifts or Softened Cuts
theory_units.summary: Dissolves blend one scene into another, covering a time lapse, a change in location, or softening an otherwise abrupt scene change or jump-cut. Their length can vary to match dramatic tempo.
theory_units.applies_when: Bridging time or space, or when a straight cut would be too jarring due to sudden shifts in interest or composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooths transitions, signals a passage of time or location shift, and reduces abruptness.

theory_units.title: Using Matched Dissolves for Smooth Transitions
theory_units.summary: Matched dissolves connect two scenes similar in form, motion, or content (e.g., flowers/jewels, wheels/propellers, match flame/forest fire) for smoother transitions and to preserve narrative flow.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring a particularly elegant or thematic transition between two visually or thematically linked scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a very smooth, often symbolic, transition that can reinforce narrative themes or ideas.
theory_units.caution: Matched dissolves should not be overly tricky or draw attention away from the narrative. Images should stem from the story.

theory_units.title: Distorted Dissolves for Altered States of Mind/Flashbacks
theory_units.summary: Distorted dissolves (shimmying, blurry, out-of-focus) denote a sudden switch to a character's subconscious, retrospective, mentally unbalanced, drunken, or other abnormal state of mind. They are often accompanied by eerie sound and can introduce flashbacks.
theory_units.applies_when: Portraying a character's subjective, non-linear, or compromised mental state, or signaling a flashback.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually and audibly immerses the audience in the character's distorted reality or mental shift.

theory_units.title: Flashback/Flashforward Dissolve Bracketing (with exceptions)
theory_units.summary: Generally, use a pair of dissolves to bracket flashbacks, flashforwards, or other abnormal conditions. A return dissolve may be omitted if the audience clearly comprehends the change, or if startling/shocking the viewer with a straight cut (e.g., from a dream/nightmare) is desired.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing and exiting non-linear narrative segments like flashbacks or flashforwards.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly demarcates non-linear narrative, preventing confusion. Offers flexibility to create shock or simplify when context is clear.

theory_units.title: Frozen Dissolves for Time Stillness or Stylized Transitions
theory_units.summary: Frozen dissolves (where the last and first frames are frozen) denote time standing still. A stylized variation involves dissolving from a frozen photographic image to a matched painting/drawing, then to another, and back to a frozen photographic image that then moves, used for a highly pictorial effect.
theory_units.applies_when: Wanting to convey a sense of arrested time, or to create a distinct, artistic, and pictorial transition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a specific visual metaphor for time or a highly aesthetic, almost tableau-like transition.
theory_units.caution: The stylized variation requires specialized optical effects setup for matching images to paintings/drawings.

theory_units.title: News Event Transition: Freeze Frame to Still Image
theory_units.summary: For news events (e.g., a trial), freeze a frame with a simulated photographer's flash, then dissolve it to a still picture, which is then revealed as part of a newspaper story as the camera pulls back.
theory_units.applies_when: Portraying a news event and transitioning from live action to its media representation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Effectively communicates the transformation of an event into a published news item, often with a sense of formality or historical distance.

theory_units.title: Wipes for Scene Transitions
theory_units.summary: Wipes are moving optical effects where one scene pushes another off-screen. They can be vertical, horizontal, angular, or more complex shapes (circular, stars, etc.), with distinct lines or soft blends.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning between scenes, offering a stylized or energetic visual break.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear, often dynamic, visual demarcation between scenes.
theory_units.caution: Rarely used in dramatic films due to their mechanical nature.

theory_units.title: Caution on Wipes in Dramatic Films
theory_units.summary: Wipes are mechanical transitions and, aside from simple vertical/horizontal/angular types, are rarely used in dramatic films. They are more common in trailers, advertising, and TV commercials.
theory_units.applies_when: Considering the use of wipes, especially in dramatic contexts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Awareness helps avoid anachronistic or tonally inappropriate transitions in dramatic filmmaking.
theory_units.caution: Wipes are rarely employed in dramatic films (except for simple varieties); they can feel mechanical and are now mainly used in trailers, advertising, and commercials.

theory_units.title: Montage Transitions for Condensing Time or Space
theory_units.summary: A montage transition is a rapid editing technique, a series of short scenes connected by cuts, dissolves, or wipes, used to condense time or space. It depicts story portions where details are not needed but continuity or narrative progression is essential.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to show a lengthy or complex event (e.g., journey, operation) in a condensed, efficient manner without showing every detail.
theory_units.expected_effect: Accelerates narrative pace, conveys the passage of time or completion of a process, and maintains narrative continuity without slowing the story.

theory_units.title: Montage for Time & Space Compression
theory_units.summary: Employ a series of short, representative scenes to condense extensive periods of time or vast distances into a few moments.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to depict a long process, a journey, or development that spans significant duration or geographical scale efficiently.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives extensive effort, significant passage of time, or vast distances covered in a short screen duration, avoiding lengthy exposition.

theory_units.title: Montage for Cumulative Psychological Effect
theory_units.summary: Combine individual shots, even if loosely connected to specific events, to create a cumulative psychological effect of extensive effort or a thematic impression.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting complex processes like research, design, or development, where the overall impression is more important than detailed individual actions.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience feels the weight of the combined effort, leading to a psychological impact often greater than the sum of its individual parts.

theory_units.title: Montage for Stage-Setting
theory_units.summary: Use a montage sequence to quickly establish the context, atmosphere, or background for the main narrative.
theory_units.applies_when: Before the main event of a story, to introduce a new locale, historical period, or the preparatory journey of characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience is rapidly immersed in the new setting or premise, providing necessary context without slowing down the narrative.

theory_units.title: Superimposed Montage for Idea Connection
theory_units.summary: Superimpose two or more images on screen simultaneously to connect disparate ideas, show continuous change, or illustrate narrative elements.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to visually link concepts (e.g., circus posters over trains), depict ongoing progress (e.g., graph over production), or illustrate evolving narrative details (e.g., headlines over a trial).
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates thematic links, conveys progress or simultaneity, and adds layers of meaning to the visual narrative.

theory_units.title: Multi-Image Frame Composition
theory_units.summary: Divide the frame into multiple segments (e.g., four or more), displaying several images simultaneously, or surrounding a central image with others.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting various concurrent activities, summarizing events (e.g., sporting activities, industrial operations, test results), creating a title background, or showing events happening in several places simultaneously.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys simultaneity, complexity, provides an immersive background, or efficiently summarizes information.

theory_units.title: Montage Tempo Matching
theory_units.summary: Collaborate closely with the film editor to establish an overall tempo for action scenes within a montage, potentially using a metronome for precise beat matching.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming montage sequences where a specific rhythm, pace, or beat is desired for maximum impact and cohesion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves greater impact and cohesion for the montage, enhancing its psychological or dramatic effect on the audience.

theory_units.title: Consistent or Contrasting Camera/Subject Movement in Montage
theory_units.summary: Ensure subject movement or camera movement (pan, tilt, dolly) is either similar or contrasting throughout a series of montage shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When constructing a montage where visual flow, rhythm, or intentional juxtaposition are crucial for effectiveness.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves visual effectiveness, either through cohesive flow (similar movements) or intentional dynamism/tension (contrasting movements).

theory_units.title: Dissolve for Time Lapse and Transformation
theory_units.summary: Use a dissolve between a beginning shot and an end shot to visually represent a significant passage of time or a profound transformation.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to show a process from its start to its completion, growth, decay, or any complete change over an extended period.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly conveys large time gaps and the evolution or transformation of a subject, making the passage of time digestible for the audience.

theory_units.title: Dissolve for Repetitive Action Condensation
theory_units.summary: Employ dissolves between highlights of a repeated action to condense lengthy, redundant processes or operations.
theory_units.applies_when: When shortening industrial processes, machine operations, or routine, repetitive tasks where showing every detail would be boring or too time-consuming, especially if camera angle or image size remains largely consistent.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficiently conveys the completion of repetitive tasks without showing every detail, maintaining audience interest and pacing.

theory_units.title: Dissolve/Wipe for Insignificant Time/Space Skips
theory_units.summary: Use dissolves or wipes to bridge small, non-essential time intervals or short physical distances within a sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a character's short movement (e.g., exiting a building, changing floors in an elevator) or any brief, uneventful transition that doesn't require explicit depiction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains narrative flow by skipping over mundane moments without drawing undue attention to the transition.

theory_units.title: Visual Flashback via Historical Markers
theory_units.summary: Utilize explicit historical visual elements, such as newspaper headlines with significant dates or events, to instantly establish a specific past time for a flashback.
theory_units.applies_when: When initiating a flashback that requires clear chronological anchoring or immediate audience recognition of the historical period.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience immediately recognizes and understands the historical context of the flashback, creating a rapid shift in time.

theory_units.title: Visual Location Bridge
theory_units.summary: Bridge geographical space by cutting or dissolving to identifiable signs, names on doors, plaques on buildings, or city names on transportation terminals.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between different physical places, especially for journeys or rapid scene changes across locales.
theory_units.expected_effect: Quickly and efficiently informs the audience of the new locale, minimizing the need for verbal explanation.

theory_units.title: Wipes for Directional Travel
theory_units.summary: Employ wipes where one scene pushes the next in the direction of travel to enhance screen movement and illustrate a journey.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting travel by vehicles (e.g., trains, planes, ships) or a character's continuous movement across multiple settings, where the direction of travel is key.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic and continuous visual representation of movement and journey, reinforcing the sense of progress in a specific direction.

theory_units.title: Visual Travel Montage (Elements)
theory_units.summary: Depict lengthy travel by combining a montage of specific visual elements associated with movement and journey, such as spinning wheels, changing odometers, maps, passports, and road signs.
theory_units.applies_when: When illustrating extended trips or changes in location without needing to show every step of the journey in detail.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys the passage of distance and the experience of travel efficiently and evocatively, often with a sense of adventure or passage of time.

theory_units.title: Symbolic Location Identification (Visual)
theory_units.summary: Utilize widely recognized symbols or landmarks to quickly introduce and identify countries or cities.
theory_units.applies_when: When establishing a new geographical setting rapidly without needing explicit titles or lengthy exposition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Immediate audience recognition of the locale, fostering a sense of place and cultural context.

theory_units.title: Camera Tilt for Locale Transition
theory_units.summary: Transition between different geographical settings by tilting the camera up to a neutral element (like the sky), dissolving to a new sky, and then tilting down to reveal the new scene. Alternatively, tilt down to water/ocean waves and up to the new location.
theory_units.applies_when: When moving between distinct locations in a visually fluid and somewhat ethereal manner, using a common element (sky or water) as a bridge.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth, often poetic transition that connects the two locations via a unifying element, rather than an abrupt cut.

theory_units.title: Creative Transition Imperative
theory_units.summary: Actively seek fresh photographic treatments, novel production techniques, or new creative twists for transitions to avoid hackneyed devices and stimulate audience interest.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning any transition in a film, to prevent them from becoming predictable, stale, or drawing undue attention to themselves.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the overall production value, maintains audience engagement, and prevents transitions from detracting from the narrative.
theory_units.caution: Avoid hackneyed transitions, as they can interfere with audience interest and immersion.

theory_units.title: Narration as Continuity Driver (Compilation Films)
theory_units.summary: Utilize continuous narration to provide the main storyline and link visually disconnected scenes, particularly in documentaries or compilation films.
theory_units.applies_when: When the visuals are primarily illustrative and would lack coherence or narrative flow without a verbal explanation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Establishes a clear and coherent narrative, even if visuals are fragmented, guiding the audience through changes in time and space.

theory_units.title: Monologue-Driven Flashback/Time Progression
theory_units.summary: Use a character's monologue or narration to bridge time or space, with the picture dissolving to visually represent the described past or future events while the sound continues.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's internal thoughts or spoken recount need to be visualized as a flashback to a past event, or a flash-forward to a future scenario.
theory_units.expected_effect: Deepens character insight and provides a dynamic, engaging way to explore different time periods related to the narrative.

theory_units.title: Dialogue/Voice-Over Transitions
theory_units.summary: Transition between scenes or characters by dissolving the picture while a voice-over or dialogue continues, potentially shifting to a new speaker or silent reading.
theory_units.applies_when: When linking conversations across locations, showing the impact of a letter, or transitioning between multiple characters involved in the same report or communication.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a strong narrative thread through sound, connecting disparate visuals or characters and providing continuity across scene changes.

theory_units.title: Dialogue-Activated Straight Cut
theory_units.summary: Utilize an impactful line of dialogue as a sharp cue for an abrupt straight cut to a new scene or location.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a dramatic or immediate transition, often in direct response to a spoken command, exclamation, or declaration.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of urgency, impact, or immediate consequence, propelling the story forward rapidly and dramatically.

theory_units.title: Monologue Location Transition (Close-Up Method)
theory_units.summary: Facilitate a character's transition between locales during a continuous monologue by cutting or moving into a close-up at the end of the first scene, picking up with a close-up in the new locale, and then cutting back or pulling back to reveal the new setting.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character delivers a continuous monologue while physically moving or transitioning between two distinct settings, to ensure a smooth, character-focused transition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains focus on the character and their dialogue during an otherwise potentially jarring location switch, making the transition feel smoother and more impactful.
theory_units.caution: Such transitions are best made with close-ups to fill the frame during the switch.

theory_units.title: Abrupt Locale Switches (Fast-Paced Storytelling)
theory_units.summary: Employ straight picture cuts for rapid transitions between locales, foregoing opticals, aligning with modern faster-paced storytelling.
theory_units.applies_when: When the audience can easily comprehend the change of location without an elaborate optical transition, due to clear narrative context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a brisk narrative pace and creates a sense of immediacy, keeping the audience engaged in the story's momentum.
theory_units.caution: Only use if the audience comprehends what is happening; otherwise, it can be jarring.

theory_units.title: Dialogue/Narration/SFX to Condense Action
theory_units.summary: Bridge scenes with dialogue, narration, or sound effects to skip non-essential action and focus on significant highlights of an event.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to condense lengthy processes, show only the crucial moments of an event, or streamline exposition by letting sound carry the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Streamlines the narrative, maintains audience engagement by focusing on key information or events, and can create dramatic impact.

theory_units.title: Telephone/Broadcast as Locale Switch
theory_units.summary: Utilize telephone conversations, radio broadcasts, or television programs as a narrative device to transition between different locales.
theory_units.applies_when: When showing reactions to an event across multiple locations, following a conversation that spans distances, or revealing information that impacts various characters simultaneously.
theory_units.expected_effect: Connects disparate characters or locations through a shared auditory experience, broadening the scope of the story and showing widespread impact.

theory_units.title: Music for Location/Time Identification (Sound)
theory_units.summary: Employ familiar songs (folk, national airs, popular regional songs) to quickly establish geographical locations (countries, cities, regions) or specific historical time periods.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing a new setting or triggering a flashback without needing explicit titles or extensive visual exposition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Immediate emotional, cultural, or temporal identification of the locale or era, enhancing immersion and context.
theory_units.caution: Ensure all music usage is cleared with copyright owners.

theory_units.title: Sound Effects for Abstract/Thematic Transitions
theory_units.summary: Utilize creative sound effect blends, transformations, or sequences to represent abstract concepts like growth, transfer, transformation, or emotional shifts.
theory_units.applies_when: When visually expressing complex or metaphorical transitions without literal imagery, relying on the auditory experience to convey meaning.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds a unique, imaginative layer to transitions, conveying meaning through auditory metaphor and enriching the narrative experience.

theory_units.title: Sound Manipulation for Thematic Effect
theory_units.summary: Artistically manipulate sound (fading, dissolving, distorting, speeding, multiplying) independently or in conjunction with picture manipulation for special effects or transitional bridges.
theory_units.applies_when: When creating unique sensory experiences, evoking specific moods, adding thematic depth, or for special transitional effects like a distorted flashback.
theory_units.expected_effect: Evokes specific moods, adds thematic depth, or creates unique sensory experiences for the audience, enhancing the overall impact of the transition.

theory_units.title: Sound Precedes Picture (Anticipation)
theory_units.summary: Introduce a sound before its visual source appears on screen, allowing the audience's ear a 'head start' in processing the information.
theory_units.applies_when: When building anticipation, revealing an off-screen presence, establishing atmosphere, or creating a sense of gradual revelation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates suspense, immerses the audience by gradually introducing elements, and respects human perception (the ear takes longer than the eye to note what is transpiring).

theory_units.title: Sound-Triggered Flashback (Psychological)
theory_units.summary: Use a distinct sound (music, specific sound effect) to precede and psychologically trigger a flashback, often by a character 'hearing' it in their mind's ear before the image is recognized.
theory_units.applies_when: When connecting a current scene to a past memory through an auditory cue, adding depth to a character's internal experience or consciousness.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a powerful, often emotional, and organic link to the past, making the flashback feel more internal and subjective.

theory_units.title: Organic Transitions (Avoid Forced Staging)
theory_units.summary: Design transitions that naturally emerge from the story, characters, setting, or available props, avoiding forced actions or elaborate props staged purely for the transition.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning any scene change to ensure it feels integrated with the narrative and does not draw undue attention to itself.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and logical narrative flow, maintaining audience immersion and preventing transitions from distracting from the story.
theory_units.caution: Avoid props foreign to the setting or false action staged solely for transition. Any transition that attracts undue attention distracts from the story.

theory_units.title: Directional Continuity (Action Axis)
theory_units.summary: Establish and consistently maintain dynamic and static directional continuity by properly employing the action axis, even on uncontrolled action.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any action sequence, particularly those involving movement across the frame or within a defined space, to maintain clear spatial relationships.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents jarring visual shifts and maintains a clear sense of spatial relationships for the audience, ensuring they understand character and object positions.

theory_units.title: Overlap and Match Action for Seamless Cuts
theory_units.summary: Film action with overlap between shots and meticulously match movements from shot to shot to ensure continuous flow when edited.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting any sequence that will be cut together to appear continuous, especially for character movements or physical actions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates seamless, fluid action across cuts, making the edit invisible and maintaining audience immersion in the continuous narrative.
theory_units.caution: Mis-matching action will lead to jarring jump-cuts.

theory_units.title: Provide Overlapping Footage for Editor
theory_units.summary: Allow the editor sufficient overlapping footage for action sequences to facilitate precise cutting on action.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, when filming any scene that involves action that will be cut across multiple shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates smoother and more precise cutting on action, improving overall continuity and giving the editor more flexibility.

theory_units.title: Shoot with Editing in Mind
theory_units.summary: Approach filming with an understanding of editorial requirements, considering how each shot will be cut and ensuring it contributes to a coherent narrative while allowing for the removal of superfluous footage.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, especially for cameraman/directors who also edit their own films or work without a dedicated script or editor.
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces footage that is easier to edit into a coherent and engaging story, reducing post-production problems and enhancing the final product's quality.

theory_units.title: Prioritizing Theatrical Editorial Requirements
theory_units.summary: For theatrical features, prioritize screen direction, players' positions and looks, and meticulously match action and dialogue from shot to shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming for professional, high-budget productions where seamless continuity is paramount and editing focuses on dramatic values.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates smooth, high-quality editing focused on dramatic values rather than correcting technical errors due to mismatches.

theory_units.title: Planning for Match Cuts (Movement)
theory_units.summary: Recognize that certain camera and player movements will cut together smoothly, while others will not, requiring pre-visualization and careful observation during filming.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning sequences involving character or camera movement across multiple shots that need to appear continuous.
theory_units.expected_effect: Avoids visual mismatches and jarring jump-cuts, ensuring fluid and invisible transitions between shots.

theory_units.title: Utilize Cut-ins/Cut-aways as Problem Solvers
theory_units.summary: Strategically employ cut-in close-ups, cut-away close-ups, and reaction shots as a tool to cover or 'save' sequences that might otherwise contain jarring jump-cuts or need shortening.
theory_units.applies_when: When an unexpected jump-cut occurs, a sequence needs to be shortened without jarring edits, or to distract the viewer from a continuity issue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Improves visual continuity and masks imperfections, salvaging problematic footage and maintaining narrative flow.

theory_units.title: Vary Camera Angle/Lens for Coverage
theory_units.summary: Change the camera angle and/or the lens for every new shot to provide the best possible coverage and a variety of editing options.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any scene that requires multiple shots for editing into a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maximizes flexibility in the editing room, allowing for better pacing, visual variety, and the ability to solve potential continuity problems.

theory_units.title: Matched Cuts for Continuous Action Flow
theory_units.summary: Ensure precise matching of players' movements, positions, and eyelines across consecutive shots to maintain the illusion of continuous action.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing a sequence where action needs to flow seamlessly from one shot to the next to appear as a continuous series of moving images.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an invisible edit, immersing the audience in the continuous narrative without jarring interruptions or jump-cuts.
theory_units.caution: A mismatch in body position or directional look will result in a jump-cut, causing the player to appear to jerk or jump across the splice.

theory_units.title: Off-Axis Camera Movement for Closer Shots
theory_units.summary: When moving from a wider shot (long or medium) to a closer setup, always shift the camera closer and to one side of the subject, rather than straight in.
theory_units.applies_when: When changing shot size from a wider shot to a closer one of the same subject, to reduce the visibility of mismatches.
theory_units.expected_effect: Minimizes the discernibility of minor mismatches (e.g., slight head position difference), preventing jarring jump-cuts when cutting straight in.
theory_units.caution: Moving straight in makes mismatches most discernible.

theory_units.title: Exact Duplication for In-Frame Cuts
theory_units.summary: When cutting from a wider shot to a closer shot that still includes a portion of the previous scene (e.g., long shot to medium shot), meticulously duplicate players' positions, body movements, and looks.
theory_units.applies_when: Any cut that transitions from a wider frame to a closer one while still maintaining elements of the previous frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Avoids jarring differences in screen images that would distract the audience and breaks the illusion of continuous action.
theory_units.caution: An arm raised in a long shot should not appear lowered in the following medium shot; a head should not be depicted turned in a different direction.

theory_units.title: Cheating with Back Cuts (Audience Distraction)
theory_units.summary: Cut from a long shot to a close-up and then back to the long shot, exploiting audience distraction to 'cheat' or cover changes that occurred off-screen during the close-up.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to make subtle changes in the wider shot that would otherwise be problematic, using the close-up as a momentary diversion.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience, being momentarily distracted by the close-up, will accept any change in the last long shot as having occurred while the close-up was on screen, allowing considerable editorial freedom.

theory_units.title: Directional Eyeline for Established Off-Screen Cut-aways
theory_units.summary: For cut-aways of characters previously established in a main long shot (and now off-screen), ensure their eyeline correctly matches their established off-screen position relative to the principal players.
theory_units.applies_when: When using cut-aways to show reactions of characters who are implied to be interacting with the main scene from an off-screen position.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains consistent spatial relationships and audience understanding of character placement, preventing confusion about who is looking where.
theory_units.caution: A wrong look will give the impression the player is now on the side opposite that shown in the establishing long shot.

theory_units.title: Flexible Eyeline for Unestablished Cut-aways
theory_units.summary: For cut-aways of characters not previously shown or established in the main scene (e.g., random bystanders, 'man in the street' comments), the specific eyeline direction is less critical unless opposing looks are intentionally desired for stylistic effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When using cut-aways for general commentary or reactions from unestablished characters who are not part of the primary scene's spatial continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides flexibility in shooting such shots, as their exact spatial relationship to the main scene isn't established and thus less critical for continuity.

theory_units.title: Cut-away as Distraction/Cover
theory_units.summary: Use a cut-away close-up as a deliberate distraction to mask continuity errors, directional changes, time lapses, or jump-cuts, especially when the subject is an 'outsider' not included in the general scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to mask a problem in the main action, condense lengthy, repetitive footage without jump-cuts, or cover a directional change in travel continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Diverts audience attention from editing issues, smoothing over problems and efficiently shortening sequences without jarring edits.

theory_units.title: Compilation Cutting's Narrative Flexibility
theory_units.summary: In compilation cutting, the narration dictates the story, allowing visual matching rules to be broken and shots to be disconnected in time and space, as long as the narration presents a coherent story.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating documentaries, newsreels, reports, or travelogs where the audio explanation is primary, and visuals are illustrative rather than strictly continuous.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides significant creative freedom in visual selection and sequencing, allowing diverse shots to be used as long as the narration maintains coherence and meaning.
theory_units.caution: Every rule in the editing book may be broken if the narration makes sense and presents a coherent story.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting for Matching Action
theory_units.summary: Employ cross-cutting in compilation films when two or more consecutive shots require matching action.
theory_units.applies_when: In compilation films where continuous action needs to be shown across different shots or segments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity and logical flow of action across different perspectives or events.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting to Heighten Interest
theory_units.summary: Depict two or more separate segments of the story in an alternate manner to revive or maintain audience interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When audience interest in the current subject lags, or to dynamically present parallel narratives.
theory_units.expected_effect: Revives audience engagement and maintains curiosity by shifting focus between related, but distinct, story segments.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting for Conflict & Climax
theory_units.summary: Edit two opposing actions in an alternating pattern that gradually increases pace and proximity, leading to a smashing climax.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting two forces or actions moving towards an inevitable collision or confrontation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Builds intense anticipation and highlights the impending clash, making the climax more impactful.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting for Tension
theory_units.summary: Alternate editing of two events that have a direct bearing on each other to increase narrative tension.
theory_units.applies_when: When two or more parallel events are interdependent and their simultaneous progress (or lack thereof) creates suspense.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightens audience awareness of the stakes and the causal links between separate but related events, drawing them deeper into the dramatic situation.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting for Suspense (Anxiety)
theory_units.summary: Keep the audience in a state of anxiety by alternately cutting between events as they move toward a climax.
theory_units.applies_when: When building suspense towards a critical moment, often involving a ticking clock or impending danger.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates strong anxiety and anticipation by showing progress towards a resolution or disaster from multiple perspectives.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting for Comparisons
theory_units.summary: Alternately depict people, objects, or events to highlight their similarities or differences for comparative purposes.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative's purpose is to draw parallels or contrasts between subjects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables the audience to make direct comparisons, understanding the nuances of multiple subjects side-by-side.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting for Contrast
theory_units.summary: Show contrasts among people, countries, cultures, products, methods, or events by alternately depicting them.
theory_units.applies_when: When the goal is to emphasize stark differences or opposing elements within the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly illustrates the disparities between subjects, enhancing the audience's comprehension of their contrasting natures.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting Spatially Separated Simultaneous Events
theory_units.summary: Depict events occurring simultaneously but separated in space by alternately showing the progress of each.
theory_units.applies_when: For classic last-minute rescues, chase sequences, or showing interdependent events happening concurrently in different locations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of urgency, interconnection, and comprehensive understanding of multiple parallel narratives unfolding at the same time.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting Events Separated in Time
theory_units.summary: Cross-cut events separated in time to present a back-and-forth comparison or contrast of present events with similar past or future events.
theory_units.applies_when: When exploring historical context, future implications, or thematic links across different time periods.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides deeper context and thematic resonance by allowing direct visual comparison or contrast between different eras or temporal points.

theory_units.title: Establishing Shot in Cross-cutting Sequence
theory_units.summary: Treat the first shot in a series of cross-cuts as an establishing shot and allow it slightly greater screen length than subsequent cross-cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Beginning any cross-cut sequence to orient the audience to the context of the first event.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the audience with a clear frame of reference, preventing confusion as the cross-cutting begins.
theory_units.caution: Introductory cross-cut shots should not be thrust on the screen without identification, unless audience confusion is an important story factor.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Clarity in Cross-cutting
theory_units.summary: In most cases, ensure the audience is immediately aware of what is happening, who is involved, and where the cross-cut event is occurring, if pertinent to the story.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout any cross-cut sequence, unless intentional confusion is desired for storytelling.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents audience confusion and maintains engagement by keeping them oriented within the parallel narratives.

theory_units.title: Cross-cutting in Documentary Films
theory_units.summary: Cross-cutting is an advantageous device for documentary fact films, particularly when employed to connect, contrast, or compare two or more actions or events.
theory_units.applies_when: In documentaries to analyze relationships, show parallel developments, or highlight differences between subjects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightens audience interest and provides a dynamic departure from straightforward storytelling, effectively moving the story in time and/or space.

theory_units.title: Masking Cuts with Action
theory_units.summary: Film editors prefer to make cuts on movements so that the actual switch from one shot to another is masked by the action, making the cut less apparent than between two static shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever there is significant on-screen movement that can be used to hide an edit point.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smoother, less jarring transition for the audience, enhancing the illusion of continuous action.

theory_units.title: Editor's Role in Cutting on Action
theory_units.summary: The decision for cutting on action should be left to the editor, not made by the cameraman.
theory_units.applies_when: During the filming and post-production phases of a project.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the final editing decisions are made with a comprehensive view of all footage and narrative goals, optimizing for the best cut.
theory_units.caution: Cameramen should not attempt to cut on action in-camera, as this severely handicaps the editor.

theory_units.title: Filming Overlap for Editorial Action Cuts
theory_units.summary: The cameraman should film all moving action to completion and repeat the end of the action so that it overlaps at the beginning of the next shot, allowing the editor flexibility.
theory_units.applies_when: Anytime a shot involves movement that might be used for a cut on action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the film editor with maximum choice in where to place the cut, facilitating seamless action matching.
theory_units.caution: In-camera cutting on action (close overlapping) saves film but severely handicaps the editor.

theory_units.title: Maximizing Overlapped Movement for Editors
theory_units.summary: Always provide the film editor with as much overlapped movement as possible in consecutive shots to enable them to make the most effective cut.
theory_units.applies_when: During all filming that involves potential action cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Empowers the editor to achieve the most precise and seamless cuts, enhancing overall film continuity.

theory_units.title: Cut-in Close-ups for Movement Economy
theory_units.summary: Make cut-in close-ups of lengthy movements (e.g., climbing stairs, walking great distances) to allow the editor to shorten or lengthen shots by cutting to the closer shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene features prolonged physical action that could benefit from variable pacing or selective focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides editorial flexibility to control the perceived duration of movements, either speeding them up or drawing them out, without the audience noticing repetition.

theory_units.title: Player Movement into Close-ups for Action Cuts
theory_units.summary: Always move players into and out of close-ups to allow cutting on action.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing close-ups of actors who are performing continuous action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates clean match cuts, allowing the editor to transition seamlessly between wider shots and close-ups, making part of the movement invisible.
theory_units.caution: Statically positioning a player in a close-up forces the editor to use the entire length of movement in the preceding long shot.

theory_units.title: Clean Entrances and Exits
theory_units.summary: The camera should be started before a player enters the frame and stopped after he leaves, to provide 'clean' entrances and exits for editing.
theory_units.applies_when: Anytime a character enters or exits the frame, especially when planning for cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Gives the editor ample footage to make smooth cuts, ensuring that the character's appearance and disappearance are natural and continuous.

theory_units.title: Visual & Technical Matching for Continuity
theory_units.summary: The cameraman must film a series of shots that match visually (action, looks, positions) and technically (exposure, lighting, color, etc.) across cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever filming consecutive shots that will be edited together to form a continuous sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains the illusion of reality, preventing audience distraction and ensuring an effective presentation.
theory_units.caution: Unexplained gaps in continuity or technical variations will distract the audience and destroy the illusion.

theory_units.title: Pre-empting Editorial Problems During Filming
theory_units.summary: Film all scenes with due consideration given to all editorial factors, as this is the best solution to cutting problems.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the entire filming process.
theory_units.expected_effect: Minimizes post-production difficulties and ensures a smoother, more finished editing job.
theory_units.caution: There is rarely an excuse for pictorial or technical mis-matching that creates insolvable editing problems.

theory_units.title: Director's Responsibility for Action Matching
theory_units.summary: The director, with the help of the script girl, is responsible for matching action from shot to shot.
theory_units.applies_when: During filming of any sequence requiring continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures consistent action flow and reduces editing challenges related to mis-matched movements.

theory_units.title: Planning for Matching (Solo Cameraman/Director)
theory_units.summary: If working alone as a cameraman/director, carefully plan the places in the sequence where the camera will be shifted to new angles and thoughtfully analyze the action at that time.
theory_units.applies_when: When a single person is performing both camera and directing duties.
theory_units.expected_effect: Mitigates the vexing problem of matching in a solo production environment, especially without a script.

theory_units.title: Duplicating Movement for Editor's Cuts
theory_units.summary: If matching involves movement, ensure that the move is duplicated at the beginning of the next shot, so that the film editor may cut on action if desired.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming any action that will continue across a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the editor with the necessary overlap to create seamless match-on-action cuts.

theory_units.title: Duplicating Looks & Positions for Continuity
theory_units.summary: Players' looks and positions should be carefully duplicated in subsequent shots to prevent jarring jump-cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Anytime a character's gaze or physical stance needs to be consistent across a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains continuous screen direction and audience orientation, avoiding distracting jump-cuts.

theory_units.title: Staging Considerations for Non-Actors
theory_units.summary: Movement and staging should be restricted when dealing with non-actors, allowing them to concentrate on their action and dialogue delivery.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing individuals without professional acting experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps non-actors deliver more natural performances by simplifying their physical demands and reducing the need for precise matching.
theory_units.caution: It is asking too much to expect a professional performance from an amateur actor.

theory_units.title: Multiple Cameras for Difficult Matching
theory_units.summary: If motion or speech would be difficult to duplicate for the various type shots required for a matched sequence, use of multiple cameras should be considered.
theory_units.applies_when: For scenes with non-repeatable, complex, or highly synchronized actions and dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures perfect matching of performance and timing across different shot sizes and angles, reducing the need for repeated takes and ensuring continuity.

theory_units.title: Protection Close-ups for Jump-Cut Coverage
theory_units.summary: Cameraman should 'protect' a series of continuous shots by filming every possible cut-in and cut-away close-up that could be used to cover any jump-cuts which might crop up in editing.
theory_units.applies_when: During filming, especially for complex or difficult-to-duplicate actions like fights.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the editor with alternative footage to seamlessly cover continuity errors or mis-matched action, making the sequence more fluid.

theory_units.title: Tight Close-ups for Relaxed Action Matching
theory_units.summary: An extremely close cut-in close-up (little more than a face) can be useful for covering mis-matched action between uncontrollable or complex action shots, eliminating the need for exact position or body movement matching.
theory_units.applies_when: When dealing with actions that are difficult to duplicate precisely across takes, such as a fight.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies the matching process for the editor by focusing on only the critical element (e.g., facial expression, directional look) and making body inconsistencies irrelevant.
theory_units.caution: Only needs to show the correct directional look.

theory_units.title: Paired Tight Close-ups for Directional Looks
theory_units.summary: Tight close-ups may be filmed in pairs, providing both a left and a right look for the editor to insert anywhere in a sequence where players' looks vary as action progresses.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to cover varying eyelines or reactions during a complex scene with multiple cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Gives the editor maximum versatility to maintain consistent eyelines and reactions regardless of the specific action in wider shots, preventing jump-cuts in gaze.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Compositional Continuity
theory_units.summary: Compositional elements (players, furniture, props, background objects) should remain in the same relative area of the frame in a series of matching scenes to avoid viewer confusion.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between shots within the same scene, particularly with changes in camera angle or shot size.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents visual jarring or disorientation for the viewer, maintaining the illusion of a continuous space and coherent reality.
theory_units.caution: Shifting of compositional elements within the frame between shots may confuse the viewer.

theory_units.title: Tracking Relational Positions for Angle Changes
theory_units.summary: When changing angles for consecutive shots, the relative position of players, furniture, props, and background elements must be carefully noted to ensure compositional continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever the camera angle changes within a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that objects and characters maintain logical spatial relationships despite changes in camera perspective.

theory_units.title: Cheating/Removing Objects for Compositional Correctness
theory_units.summary: It may be necessary to remove or cheat an object's position to make it appear correct in a series of shots, especially in close-ups where objects might intrude or appear too close due to lens changes.
theory_units.applies_when: When an object unintentionally obstructs framing or creates an illogical spatial relationship between shots, particularly when changing lens focal length or camera position for close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clean, aesthetically pleasing composition and preserves the illusion of continuous space without distracting intrusions.
theory_units.caution: The object should be replaced if it appears in a subsequent wider angle shot; if it cannot be removed, it should be cheated deftly so it looks right.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cuts via Angle & Size Change
theory_units.summary: Changing both the camera angle and the image size will aid in obtaining smooth cuts between shots because the camera viewpoint is shifted as the image size increases or decreases.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between shots to ensure a seamless edit.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth transition, covering minor mis-matches and changes in furniture, props, or background objects, as the scene is viewed from a completely new angle.
theory_units.caution: Shifting the viewpoint is more effective than moving straight in or out.

theory_units.title: Inter-cutting Moving Shots with Maintained Tempo
theory_units.summary: A series of moving shots will generally inter-cut without difficulty if the tempo of the camera movement is properly maintained.
theory_units.applies_when: When building a sequence entirely of camera movements, or transitioning between them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves smooth and continuous flow between dynamic shots, preventing jarring transitions.

theory_units.title: Introducing Movement from Static Establishing Shots
theory_units.summary: Movement may be introduced in a static establishing shot and then filmed with a continuously moving camera, allowing static and moving shots to cut directly and effectively.
theory_units.applies_when: When initiating a sequence that will become dynamic from a static starting point, or reversing this process.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a natural and motivated transition from a static to a dynamic viewing experience, or vice-versa, making inter-cutting smoother.

theory_units.title: Continuous Player/Vehicle Movement Across Shots
theory_units.summary: Continuous player or vehicle movement may be carried across both static and moving shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever a character or vehicle is in continuous motion across multiple edits, involving both static and moving camera setups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains strong visual continuity of the subject's action, making the cuts less noticeable regardless of the camera's state.

theory_units.title: Inter-cutting a Series of Continuously Moving Shots
theory_units.summary: A series of continuously moving shots, of the same or different subjects, may also be inter-cut successfully.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a continuous action or a sequence of related dynamic events from various perspectives or distances.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a high level of dynamism and visual interest, keeping the audience engaged with the ongoing action.

theory_units.title: Duplicating Player Movement in Moving Camera Shots
theory_units.summary: When a continuously moving camera films a moving subject from various angles and distances, player movement should be precisely duplicated in various type shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When a moving camera tracks a moving subject, and multiple takes or angles are required to cover the action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures seamless match cuts between different moving shots of the same subject, maintaining the flow and continuity of the action.

theory_units.title: Difficulty Inter-cutting Static/Moving Shots of Static Subjects
theory_units.summary: Inter-cutting static and moving shots of static subject matter is generally difficult, as the switch is abrupt and jarring due to lack of subject movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When considering cuts between a static camera shot of a static subject and a moving camera shot of the same static subject (or vice versa).
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces an abrupt and jarring visual transition, disrupting the viewer's immersion.
theory_units.caution: Avoid this combination if possible, as it results in editing problems.

theory_units.title: Editing Static Close-ups into Moving Pans (Static Subjects)
theory_units.summary: To successfully edit a static close-up of a static subject (e.g., a dial) into a continuous pan shot of the entire static panel, the pan shot should pause at the insertion point, or both shots should be filmed with a static camera.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to highlight a detail within a larger static scene that is also being revealed by camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables a smooth transition to the static close-up without jarring, preserving the purpose of the close-up (e.g., reading a dial) and the flow of the pan.
theory_units.caution: A panning close-up would defeat the purpose of highlighting the detail as it would sweep past too quickly.

theory_units.title: Static Start/End for Moving Shots (Static Subjects)
theory_units.summary: A pan, tilt, or dolly shot of a static subject, preceded or followed by a static camera shot, should always be filmed with a static camera at the beginning and end of the moving shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When a moving camera shot (pan, tilt, dolly) of a static subject is intended to be inter-cut with static shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that the cut will be across static frames, effectively sandwiching the movement, and preventing a jarring transition from or to continuous motion.
theory_units.caution: It is very jarring to cut from a static shot of a static subject to a moving shot that begins moving immediately, or to go from a continuously moving shot of a static subject to a static shot.

theory_units.title: Motivated Inter-cutting of Mixed Shot Types
theory_units.summary: A combination of a static shot of static subject matter and a moving shot of a moving subject will inter-cut if properly motivated (e.g., through a cut-away shot for dramatic purpose).
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between very different types of shots (static camera/static subject vs. moving camera/moving subject) for dramatic effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a powerful and dynamic transition that is accepted by the audience due to clear narrative motivation, despite the technical difference.

theory_units.title: Editing Constraints of Moving Shots
theory_units.summary: A moving shot must be used in its entirety (or any continuous portion) because it is difficult, if not impossible, to cut during camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning or editing any shot involving continuous camera motion (pan, tilt, dolly).
theory_units.expected_effect: Leads to less editorial flexibility and potentially forces inclusion of superfluous footage.
theory_units.caution: Editors may be forced to leave in unnecessary action to preserve movement or avoid cutting mid-move.

theory_units.title: Editing Flexibility of Static Shots
theory_units.summary: A static shot may generally be trimmed shorter or cut into several shots, especially for static subject matter or actors in static positions.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning or editing static camera shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides maximum editorial control over shot length and pacing, allowing precise storytelling.
theory_units.caution: Does not apply to moving shots of travel action (vehicle/player in motion).

theory_units.title: Editing Moving Shots of Travel Action
theory_units.summary: Moving shots of travel action, such as a vehicle or player in motion, may be cut to any desired shot length.
theory_units.applies_when: When a moving subject (character, vehicle) is being filmed by a moving camera.
theory_units.expected_effect: Offers editorial flexibility similar to static shots for pacing, due to the repetitive nature of the movement.

theory_units.title: Straight Cuts are Faster and More Direct
theory_units.summary: Straight cuts are always faster than moving shots because they come to the point immediately, whereas a moving shot often contains much useless footage.
theory_units.applies_when: When deciding between camera movement and a series of static shots for storytelling.
theory_units.expected_effect: Accelerates the screen story and delivers information more directly to the audience.
theory_units.caution: Many mistakenly believe a moving shot contributes flow and speeds screen action, but it often slows the story by taking longer to come to the point.

theory_units.title: Dramatic Motivation for Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: Unless the camera move is dramatically motivated, it is much better to shoot several static shots that may be straight cut, rather than a long moving shot which drags.
theory_units.applies_when: When considering any camera movement, especially pans, tilts, or dollies.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures camera movement serves a narrative purpose, enhancing storytelling rather than slowing it down or introducing editorial difficulties.
theory_units.caution: Movement often slows the screen story because it takes longer to come to the point; it may also be difficult to insert between static shots.

theory_units.title: Camera Movement: Action En Route, Not Just Destination
theory_units.summary: The camera should record significant action en route, not just at its destination, when performing a moving shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing and executing any camera movement like a dolly or pan.
theory_units.expected_effect: Justifies the screen length of the moving shot by providing continuous relevant information, making it more efficient and engaging.
theory_units.caution: A dolly into a close-up that only delivers information at the end forces superfluous footage to be included.

theory_units.title: Timing Moving Shots with Synchronized Sound/Narration
theory_units.summary: Moving shots timed to a sync-sound or narration track will generally present no problem because the movement is justified by the length of the sound track involved.
theory_units.applies_when: When camera movement accompanies dialogue, music, or narration.
theory_units.expected_effect: The sound provides a natural justification for the duration of the movement, making it editorially acceptable and well-paced.
theory_units.caution: Silent shots are often poorly timed because cameraman may pan, tilt, or dolly too fast or too slowly.

theory_units.title: Timing Strategies for Silent Dolly Shots
theory_units.summary: Silent dolly shots, particularly of static subjects, are often too long because their screen length cannot be justified editorially. They should always be timed to narration, or if shooting without a script, several shots should be made at different speeds, or protected with a static shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming silent dolly shots, especially in documentary or unscripted contexts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the dolly shot's duration is appropriate for its editorial value, preventing it from dragging or altering the sequence's tempo.
theory_units.caution: Long, slow dollies may be worthless if they cannot justify their screen length or alter the sequence's tempo.

theory_units.title: Justified Camera Movement (Editorial Constraint)
theory_units.summary: Camera movement should be employed only where justified, providing its screen length does not restrict the film editor.
theory_units.applies_when: Prior to deciding on any camera movement, particularly silent shots of documentary subject matter filmed without a script.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that camera movement enhances storytelling and visual interest without creating insurmountable problems for the editor.
theory_units.caution: Requires considerable forethought, especially on static subject matter where movement is injected via pan/tilt/dolly.

theory_units.title: Locked Camera for Player Movement into Static Close-ups
theory_units.summary: A static shot of a player moving into the frame, such as sitting into a close-up, should be filmed with a locked camera, not one that moves nervously to correct framing.
theory_units.applies_when: When a player enters and settles into a static close-up.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a stable shot for clean match-cutting on action, allowing the editor to cut precisely as the player moves into position.
theory_units.caution: Camera movement at the beginning of such a close-up may prevent the editor from cutting on action, forcing a cut to the player already in position after the camera settles down.

theory_units.title: Prioritizing Camera Stillness over Minor Framing Adjustments
theory_units.summary: It is much better to be slightly off center in framing than to move the camera, as sneak framing is particularly disturbing in a close-up.
theory_units.applies_when: When making minor adjustments to framing, especially in close-ups where a player enters the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Avoids jerky, distracting camera movements that complicate editing and disrupt audience immersion.
theory_units.caution: Sneak framing (panning/tilting to correct frame as player enters) may force the editor to discard the entrance and cut to the player in position after camera settles.

theory_units.title: Rehearsal for Eliminating Sneak Framing
theory_units.summary: Proper rehearsal, enabling actors to hit their marks, can eliminate sneak framing and allow the cameraman to lock the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: During pre-production and on-set before filming takes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures actors' movements are precise, allowing for static, locked camera shots that simplify editing and improve visual quality.

theory_units.title: Avoid Newsreel Camera Technique in Production
theory_units.summary: The newsreel technique of shooting with an unlocked pan and tilt head to allow for contingencies cannot be tolerated in production filming, as such loose camera operation may complicate cutting on action and result in a less fluid film.
theory_units.applies_when: In any controlled film production environment (non-news/documentary).
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures precise camera work that supports seamless editing and a fluid cinematic experience.
theory_units.caution: Complicates cutting on action and results in a less fluid film.

theory_units.title: Purpose of Protection Shots
theory_units.summary: 'Protection' or 'cover' shots are extra scenes filmed to cover any unforeseen editing problems or to replace doubtful scenes that may present editorial difficulties.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever there is any doubt about the editorial viability of a scene during filming.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides safeguards against potential editing issues, saving time and money in post-production by having alternative footage available.

theory_units.title: When to Shoot Protection Shots
theory_units.summary: Shoot protection shots if the director or cameraman feels a scene is too short/long, camera movement is too slow/fast, a mis-match may exist, angles are cheated too much, background doesn't match, player elements are wrong, or technical reasons.
theory_units.applies_when: Any time a potential issue is identified during filming that could impact continuity, pacing, or overall quality.
theory_units.expected_effect: Proactively addresses potential editorial problems, ensuring there are options to fix issues in post-production without reshoots.
theory_units.caution: Editorial decisions are often difficult to make during shooting, so it's wise to over-protect if in doubt.

theory_units.title: Varying Moving Shot Takes for Editor's Choice
theory_units.summary: Film pan, tilt, or dolly shots several times at various speeds, and in both directions, to give the editor choices.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any camera movement, especially when editorial needs for pacing or direction are uncertain.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maximizes editorial control over the pacing and direction of camera movements, allowing the best fit for the sequence.

theory_units.title: Protecting Lengthy Moving Shots with Static Endpoints
theory_units.summary: Lengthy pan or dolly shots may be protected with a pair of static shots of each end of the scene, in case the editor must cut the footage short and cannot cut in the midst of camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any long-duration camera movement, particularly of static subjects, that might need to be shortened in editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clean, stable cut-in/cut-out points, allowing the editor to trim the moving shot's length without visible jarring cuts during movement.

theory_units.title: Dutch Angle Protection Shots
theory_units.summary: Dutch angle shots may be tilted both left and right, especially if several are filmed, so that the editor may use them in an opposing pattern or in any contrasting combination.
theory_units.applies_when: When using Dutch angles for dramatic effect, and needing versatility in post-production.
theory_units.expected_effect: Offers editorial options to create contrasting visual dynamics or balance visual flow, enhancing the expressive potential of Dutch angles.

theory_units.title: Reaction Close-ups for Lengthy Scenes
theory_units.summary: Reaction close-ups should be filmed for insertion in lengthy scenes, particularly if filmed entirely from one angle (e.g., an industrial operation), to remove unnecessary footage without a jump-cut.
theory_units.applies_when: In scenes with prolonged, potentially monotonous action or dialogue, especially when covered by a single camera angle.
theory_units.expected_effect: Breaks up long takes, allows shortening of scenes, and redirects audience focus, all while avoiding jarring jump-cuts.

theory_units.title: All-Purpose Reaction Close-ups
theory_units.summary: It is wise, particularly if filming off-the-cuff, to shoot 'all-purpose' reaction close-ups in which the player looks in all possible directions. These may be cut in anywhere they are needed.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming without a script or with limited control, and needing versatile coverage for reactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides highly flexible editorial options to cover unforeseen needs or continuity gaps, adaptable to various eyeline requirements.
theory_units.caution: Particularly useful if filmed to eliminate or use a neutral background.

theory_units.title: Reshooting Scenes for Matching Doubt
theory_units.summary: If there is the least doubt of matching scenes filmed after long intervals, or with insufficient notes, it is wise to shoot the scene both ways, despite being time-consuming and expensive.
theory_units.applies_when: When there's uncertainty about matching continuity (e.g., player's looks, travel, clothing) due to time gaps or poor documentation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents costly re-takes later by providing alternative footage that ensures matching continuity.
theory_units.caution: Discouraged when no doubts exist; however, film and a few moments for re-shooting are cheaper than later re-takes.

theory_units.title: Resolving Cheating Disputes with Dual Takes
theory_units.summary: Differences among production personnel concerning cheating of players' positions, camera angles, furniture, or props can best be settled by filming the scene both ways: in a straightforward manner, and with the desired cheat.
theory_units.applies_when: When there are disagreements on set about how to handle continuity or visual composition compromises.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that both artistic and practical concerns are addressed, providing the editor with options to satisfy different viewpoints and ensure the best final product.

theory_units.title: Background Selection for Later Protection Shots
theory_units.summary: If doubts exist about the later need for additional shots, protect the original sequence by shooting against easily-duplicated backgrounds (sky, trees, neutral walls/drapes) or low-keyed backgrounds.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming original footage that might require later cut-ins or reaction shots, especially if shot on distant locations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies the process of matching backgrounds for later-filmed protection shots, avoiding continuity problems.
theory_units.caution: Matching original backgrounds can be problematic if footage was shot on a distant location.

theory_units.title: Tight Close-ups for Difficult Background Matches
theory_units.summary: A difficult background match may be attained by filming the added close-up as tight as possible (even a choker close-up) to eliminate most or all of the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When a precise background match for an added close-up is impossible or extremely difficult.
theory_units.expected_effect: Solves background continuity problems by minimizing or removing the background entirely, focusing attention solely on the subject.

theory_units.title: Cameraman's Vigilance for Unscripted Protection Shots
theory_units.summary: The cameraman should always be on the lookout for useful protection shots not called for in the script (e.g., long shots of buildings, close-ups of signs, general activity inserts) and be aware of their possible editorial use.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the entire filming process, especially on location or in documentary contexts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides invaluable generic footage that can introduce, establish, bridge sequences, or cover unforeseen editorial problems, enhancing the editor's options.
theory_units.caution: A simple protection shot, filmed on impulse, may prove of value in solving an editorial problem.

theory_units.title: Appropriate Uses of Dissolves
theory_units.summary: Dissolves should be used to blend credit titles, provide time or space transitions, denote a flashback, or to blend a series of short scenes in a montage or TV commercial for smoother visual continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: When a distinct temporal, spatial, or emotional shift is intended, or for creative blending effects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly signals a transition or thematic connection, creating a smooth visual bridge between disparate elements.
theory_units.caution: Most often, poorly-filmed scenes cause the editor to say: 'If you can't solve it, dissolve it!'

theory_units.title: Avoiding Dissolves as a Crutch
theory_units.summary: Dissolves should not be used indiscriminately or as a 'cinematic crutch' to cover jump-cuts, insufficient coverage, directional changes, missing scenes, sloppy editing, or badly-staged material.
theory_units.applies_when: During editing, especially when tempted to use a dissolve to mask underlying production issues.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents masking deeper problems in staging, camera work, or initial editing, leading to a more professionally constructed film.
theory_units.caution: Can become a cinematic 'crutch' if used to hide poor quality.

theory_units.title: Dissolves Prohibited in Continuous Action
theory_units.summary: Dissolves should not be used in continuity sequences where continuous action flows across consecutive shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Within any sequence intended to depict continuous, unbroken action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains the illusion of real-time, uninterrupted action, preventing a jarring or unnatural visual break.
theory_units.caution: There is no good reason for using a dissolve in a continuity-type picture simply because the sequence was badly staged and cannot be edited satisfactorily with straight cuts.

theory_units.title: Motivational Use of Dissolves
theory_units.summary: Dissolves should be used only where properly motivated.
theory_units.applies_when: Every time a dissolve is considered, the filmmaker should ask for its narrative justification.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that every dissolve serves a clear storytelling purpose, contributing meaningfully to the film's structure and audience experience.

theory_units.title: Editing Flexibility in Silent Scenes
theory_units.summary: In silent scenes, only action needs to be matched, giving the editor much latitude to switch shots, condense/expand sequences, and insert reactions, as long as the depicted action conveys the original event's meaning.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing footage without synchronized dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the editor considerable creative freedom to shape the visual narrative, prioritizing conveyed meaning over strict temporal or spatial reproduction.

theory_units.title: Editing Flexibility in Narrated Sound Pictures
theory_units.summary: Narrated sound pictures offer considerable leeway in their editing, as they are basically silent pictures supplemented by descriptive narration, music, and effects.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing films that rely on voice-over, music, and sound effects rather than synchronized dialogue to tell the story.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the editor with flexibility to manipulate visual images, as the audio elements often provide continuous context, reducing the need for strict visual matching.

theory_units.title: Editing Constraints in Lip-Sync Dialogue Scenes
theory_units.summary: Lip-sync-sound pictures, where dialogue tells the story, must be cut to the sound track, severely limiting the editor's ability to juggle visual images without altering or ruining dialogue meaning.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing scenes that feature synchronized dialogue as the primary narrative driver.
theory_units.expected_effect: Restricts editorial flexibility, compelling the editor to accept available footage for a particular sound segment, with the only choice being to use or discard the shot.
theory_units.caution: Juggling the visual images may alter or completely ruin the meaning of the dialogue.

theory_units.title: Precise Matching for Dialogue Scenes
theory_units.summary: Match-cutting sync-sound scenes requires that player action or movement across straight cuts match precisely.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing any scene containing synchronized dialogue, especially with actor movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains seamless visual continuity that aligns with the audio, preventing distracting jump-cuts or mis-matches in performance.
theory_units.caution: Unlike silent shots, editors cannot choose any point in a shot for match-cutting; they must cut to the sound track and accept the portrayed action.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Strict Visual & Audio Continuity in Dialogue Filming
theory_units.summary: Strict visual and audio continuity must be maintained during filming of dialogue scenes so that both dialogue and action are matched across straight cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Crucial during on-set production of dialogue-heavy scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that the filmed footage provides the editor with the necessary material to create perfectly matched cuts, preserving the integrity of both sound and picture.
