theory_units.caution: For most effectiveness, the center of interest should be located near the hub.

theory_units.title: Form Interpretation: L-Shaped Forms
theory_units.summary: L-shaped forms suggest informality and are flexible, providing a base and an upright in combination. They are useful for landscapes and establishing long shots, creating a broad base horizontally with a strong vertical element.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director desires to convey informality, or structure a landscape/establishing shot with strong horizontal and vertical elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: A composition that feels relaxed yet grounded, with dignity from the upright element and repose from the base.

theory_units.title: Masses: Capturing Attention
theory_units.summary: Pictured masses capture and hold attention through their heavy pictorial weight and can dominate a composition by isolation, unity, contrast, size, stability, cohesion, lighting, or color.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing a shot to ensure a specific subject or area commands primary attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: The viewer's eye is drawn powerfully to the intended dominant mass.

theory_units.title: Masses: Unity and Grouping
theory_units.summary: A unified mass is strengthened when several figures or objects are tied together into a dominant group. Wildly scattered groupings should be avoided.
theory_units.applies_when: When arranging multiple subjects to act as a single compositional unit and enhance their visual strength.
theory_units.expected_effect: A clear, cohesive, and powerful visual statement from the grouped elements, avoiding visual clutter.
theory_units.caution: Avoid scattered groupings.

theory_units.title: Masses: Dominance by Size Contrast
theory_units.summary: A large mass will dominate the scene if contrasted with one or more small masses.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants a particular large element to be the undisputed focal point amidst smaller elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: The large mass commands immediate and strong attention.

theory_units.title: Masses: Dominance by Stability
theory_units.summary: A finely-composed mass with a heavy base presents an immovable appearance and will dominate through stability, especially when in a pyramid form with a dark foreground.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to convey steadfastness, permanence, or an unyielding presence through a compositional mass.
theory_units.expected_effect: The mass becomes a strong, grounded, and dominant visual element.

theory_units.title: Masses: Dominance by Compactness
theory_units.summary: A compact mass, without projections, jagged edges, or other protuberances, will dominate the scene because of its cohesiveness.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for a strong, unified, and dominant visual mass, free from distracting elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: The mass appears singular and powerful, commanding attention through its focused form.

theory_units.title: Movements: Matching Mood and Tempo
theory_units.summary: Compositional movements within a shot or sequence should change to match the changing character, mood, or tempo of the action.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning camera or subject movement to align with the evolving emotional and narrative needs of a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced emotional resonance and narrative consistency through synchronized visual dynamics.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Horizontal Movement
theory_units.summary: Horizontal movements suggest travel, momentum, and displacement. Left-to-right movement is easier to follow and smoother, while right-to-left is stronger and 'against the grain', depicting dramatic opposition.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing subject or camera movement to convey ease of travel, or dramatic conflict.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys either a natural, easy progression (L-R) or a forceful, challenging opposition (R-L).

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Ascending Vertical Movement
theory_units.summary: Ascending vertical movements suggest aspiration, exaltation, growth, freedom from weight, lightness, happiness, and elevation, useful for religious subjects.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting subjects rising or wishing to evoke feelings of hope, spirituality, or liberation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys an uplifting and positive emotional experience, suggesting progress or transcendence.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Descending Vertical Movement
theory_units.summary: Descending vertical movements suggest heaviness, danger, crushing power, doom, imminent death, or destruction.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting subjects falling or wishing to evoke feelings of dread, impending disaster, or overwhelming force.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a sense of foreboding, gravity, or unavoidable demise.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Diagonal Movement
theory_units.summary: Diagonal movement is the strongest and most dramatic, suggesting opposing forces, stresses, strains, power, and overcoming obstacles by force. It can be created even in static scenes with a Dutch tilt.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for high dramatic impact, conflict, or dynamic tension, either through actual movement or camera angling.
theory_units.expected_effect: A highly energetic and forceful visual, creating tension and a sense of struggle or power.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Zig-zag & Crossed Diagonals
theory_units.summary: Zig-zag diagonal movements suggest swiftness and menace. Crossed diagonals suggest opposing forces, such as in battle scenes.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting rapid, dangerous action, or direct confrontation and struggle.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a sense of immediate threat, unpredictable speed, or intense, direct opposition.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Curved Movement
theory_units.summary: Curved movements suggest fear or fascination through fear. Circular or revolving movements suggest cheerfulness and mechanical energy. Pendulum motion suggests monotony and relentlessness. Cascading motion suggests sprightliness, lightness, or elasticity.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing movement to evoke specific emotions like fear, joy, boredom, or liveliness.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a range of emotional states and visual paces, from unsettling to cheerful, or monotonous to lively.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Spreading/Radiating Motion
theory_units.summary: Spreading or radiating motions suggest centrifugal movement, growth from the center outward, panic (in mobs), or any activity emanating outward from a center of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to depict expansion, chaos, emanation, or a powerful central source affecting its surroundings.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a sense of dynamism, impact, or uncontrolled dispersion.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Interrupted Movement
theory_units.summary: Interrupted movement, or movement that changes direction, attracts greater viewer interest than continuous movement or movement in a constant direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to capture and sustain audience attention through dynamic visual changes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased viewer engagement and a more dynamic, less predictable visual experience.

theory_units.title: Movement Interpretation: Movement Toward/Away
theory_units.summary: Movement toward the viewer is more interesting because it increases in size, while receding movement decreases in size and loses viewer interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing subject movement to maximize or minimize viewer engagement and sense of proximity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Movement towards creates immediacy and impact; movement away reduces it.
theory_units.caution: Use receding movement sparingly if maintaining viewer interest is crucial.

theory_units.title: Balance: Viewer Psychology
theory_units.summary: Unbalanced compositions upset the viewer, disturbing their sensibilities and creating unrest in the brain, making pictures 'not look right.' Ordinarily, balance should be observed for a subconsciously agreeable picture.
theory_units.applies_when: In most scenes where the intention is to create a harmonious and aesthetically pleasing visual experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: A subconsciously agreeable and stable viewing experience for the audience.
theory_units.caution: Purposeful unbalance may be used to disturb the viewer on special occasions.

theory_units.title: Balance: Static vs. Moving Scenes
theory_units.summary: Static scenes require better compositional balance than moving scenes, where the action itself will attract the viewer's eye regardless of compositional inadequacies.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning composition for scenes with varying degrees of movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures effective visual communication; balance is critical for static shots, less so for inherently dynamic ones.

theory_units.title: Balance: Psychological Weight of Elements
theory_units.summary: Pictorial balance is concerned with the psychological weight of compositional elements, influenced by their size, shape, tonal value, color, movement, direction, contrast, and placement.
theory_units.applies_when: When evaluating and adjusting the visual equilibrium of a shot by considering the 'weight' of all its components.
theory_units.expected_effect: A harmonious and stable composition that feels subconsciously 'right' to the viewer.

theory_units.title: Balance: Center vs. Side Placement
theory_units.summary: A figure or object placed close to the center of the frame has less compositional weight than one nearer the side, as it exerts less influence on the visual balance.
theory_units.applies_when: When deciding the placement of subjects within the frame to control their visual impact and contribution to balance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Elements off-center create a more dynamic balance, engaging the viewer's eye more actively.
theory_units.caution: Placing a heavy element too far to either side will unbalance the composition.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Movement
theory_units.summary: A moving object possesses more pictorial weight than a stationary object, regardless of size, especially if light in tone, brightly colored, or contrasted against the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing a scene with both moving and static elements, and determining their relative importance.
theory_units.expected_effect: The moving element will naturally attract and hold more attention, contributing significantly to the scene's dynamic balance.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Movement Direction
theory_units.summary: An object moving toward the camera carries greater pictorial weight than a diminishing object moving away, as it appears to progressively increase in size.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing subject movement to influence its visual prominence and contribution to balance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Movement toward the camera creates a strong, commanding presence that dominates the frame and viewer attention.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Vertical Placement
theory_units.summary: The upper part of a picture is pictorially heavier than the lower part, as a higher object appears heavier than a lower one.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing vertically to ensure appropriate distribution of visual weight.
theory_units.expected_effect: Elements placed higher in the frame will naturally carry more visual gravitas.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Horizontal Placement & Eye Flow
theory_units.summary: Since viewers' eyes automatically move toward the right, the right side of the frame attracts more attention. Consequently, the left side of a picture can support greater pictorial weight than the right side.
theory_units.applies_when: When strategically placing elements horizontally to achieve balance, considering natural eye movement patterns.
theory_units.expected_effect: Compensates for the natural rightward eye movement, allowing for more impactful elements on the left while maintaining balance.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Isolation
theory_units.summary: An isolated object possesses more pictorial weight than an object crowded, merged, or stacked with others, regardless of how isolation is achieved (positioning, lighting, contrast, color).
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants a specific object to stand out and carry significant visual importance.
theory_units.expected_effect: The isolated object gains prominence and commands greater attention.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Side Placement (Weak Center)
theory_units.summary: An object will appear heavier if placed at the side of the frame, as the center of the picture is compositionally weakest in terms of exerting visual influence.
theory_units.applies_when: When intentionally giving more visual weight to an element by positioning it away from the frame's center.
theory_units.expected_effect: The off-center element becomes more impactful and contributes more to the overall balance.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Object Size (Static Scene)
theory_units.summary: In a static scene, a large object will carry more pictorial weight and tend to dominate the picture regardless of position or other factors.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing a static scene and intending a large object to be the primary focal point.
theory_units.expected_effect: The large object inherently dominates and attracts significant attention.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Shape and Form
theory_units.summary: Regularly-shaped objects carry more weight than irregularly-shaped objects. Peculiar, complex, or intricate objects may appear heavier due to the additional interest they generate. Compact objects with mass concentrated at their center carry more weight than loosely-joined objects. Vertically-formed objects appear heavier than oblique objects.
theory_units.applies_when: When selecting or arranging objects to contribute specific amounts of visual weight based on their inherent form.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shapes and forms are leveraged to achieve specific visual prominence and balance.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Brightness and Tone
theory_units.summary: A bright object possesses more weight than a darker one. High-key, light-toned objects appear to advance toward the viewer, while darker objects recede. A bright surface appears larger than a dark one due to irradiation.
theory_units.applies_when: When using lighting and color to manipulate the perceived weight and depth of objects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Brighter elements command more attention and appear closer; darker elements recede.
theory_units.caution: A black area must be larger than a white area to counter-balance it.

theory_units.title: Balance Factor: Color Temperature and Saturation
theory_units.summary: Warm colors (e.g., red) are heavier than cold colors (e.g., blue). Bright colors convey more weight than dark colors.
theory_units.applies_when: When using color to influence the visual weight and dominance of elements in a composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Warm and bright colors will draw more attention and appear more prominent.

theory_units.title: Formal Balance: Characteristics and Use
theory_units.summary: Formal (symmetrical) balance results when both sides of a composition are symmetrical or nearly equal in attraction. It suggests peace, quiet, and equality, and is usually static and less dynamic.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative requires conveying peace, quiet, equality, or a sense of formality (e.g., a cross, courthouse, pastoral scene).
theory_units.expected_effect: A calm, stable, and harmonious visual, creating a sense of order and serenity.
theory_units.caution: It is usually static and can lack force, conflict, and contrast.

theory_units.title: Formal Balance: Filming for Symmetrical Scenes
theory_units.summary: Formally balanced scenes should be filmed almost square-on with little or no camera angling, ensuring pictorial elements on each side are similar in image size. Handling (lighting, tonal values, colors, contrast) should be subtle.
theory_units.applies_when: When creating a formally balanced composition, particularly for subjects intended to convey peace or equality.
theory_units.expected_effect: A sense of order, calmness, and visual equality, aligning with the mood of the scene.
theory_units.caution: Avoid garish treatment; lighting and colors should be subtle.

theory_units.title: Formal Balance: Profile Two-Shot Dynamics
theory_units.summary: In a formally balanced profile two-shot, dominance shifts between players based on dialogue, facial expression, or action. It can be 'unbalanced' to create conflict by favoring one player with brighter lighting, better angling, brighter costume, or better background separation.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming a two-shot where initial equality is desired, or later, a shift in power/focus is needed.
theory_units.expected_effect: Initially balanced attention, then dynamic shift in viewer focus and psychological weight, potentially introducing conflict.

theory_units.title: Informal Balance: Characteristics and Use
theory_units.summary: Informal (asymmetrical) balance results when both sides of a composition are asymmetrical and different in attraction, creating a dynamic and forceful arrangement with a dominant center of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative requires a dynamic composition with a clear dominant focal point, suggesting force or conflict.
theory_units.expected_effect: A visually energetic and engaging composition that clearly directs attention to the most important element.

theory_units.title: Informal Balance: Close-ups and Lead Room
theory_units.summary: Asymmetrical balance is subtly employed in close-ups by placing the subject's head slightly off-center, providing more space in the direction they are looking. This 'look' carries sufficient psychological weight to balance the off-center position.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing close-ups of a character looking off-screen to another character, object, or action.
theory_units.expected_effect: A balanced composition that acknowledges off-screen space and directs viewer attention to the character's gaze.

theory_units.title: Informal Balance: Dominant Element and Opposing Weight
theory_units.summary: The dominant compositional element (center of interest) in an asymmetrical composition must have an opposing element on the other side of the frame to balance the scene. A smaller opposing element can compensate for its size by additional weight from its location, shape, brightness, movement, or color.
theory_units.applies_when: When structuring any asymmetrical composition to ensure visual equilibrium despite differing elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic yet balanced composition where the dominant element is clearly established but not visually overwhelming.

theory_units.title: Informal Balance: Dominant Player Positioning (Vertical)
theory_units.summary: A dominant subject should be positioned slightly higher or lower (preferably higher) than a lesser-weight opposing element to attract attention, rather than in the same horizontal line.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing a scene with multiple players to clearly establish the dominance of one character.
theory_units.expected_effect: The dominant player visually commands attention and authority over supporting characters.
theory_units.caution: Placing the dominant player at equal compositional height with a less important player may weaken the scene.

theory_units.title: Informal Balance: Dominance Through Various Means
theory_units.summary: If a dominant player is positioned lower or seated, they can still dominate the scene through better lighting, strategic positioning (e.g., on a strong compositional point), or by other players' eye-lines directed toward them. Dominance can also be achieved by depth positioning (forward appears higher, back appears lower).
theory_units.applies_when: When physical height isn't an option for dominance, or to add layers of emphasis to a seated/lower character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the intended dominant character maintains visual authority and draws primary audience attention.

theory_units.title: Informal Balance: Odd Numbers & Dynamic Dominance
theory_units.summary: Using an odd number of players or objects (especially three) facilitates informal balance, allowing a single element to dominate and create triangular compositions. Dominance can be switched dynamically within a scene through changes in position, movement, or camera action.
theory_units.applies_when: When arranging groups of subjects and needing flexible ways to establish or shift focus and power dynamics.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic and engaging composition that can adapt to narrative shifts, always highlighting the current focal point.
theory_units.caution: Avoid over-applying the odd number/triangular rule; variations are key.

theory_units.title: Gravity: Low Center for Tall Elements
theory_units.summary: Heavy compositional elements reaching skyward should possess a low center of gravity, otherwise, they will appear unstable and about to topple, which human senses rebel against.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing shots with tall or seemingly heavy objects that extend upwards.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of stability and natural order, preventing viewer discomfort caused by visual imbalance.

theory_units.title: Gravity: Counter-Balancing with Foreground
theory_units.summary: A tall structure should be supported by a broad, preferably dark-toned, base. A large foreground area should be dark-shadowed or filtered to counter-balance buildings or other strong compositional elements.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing tall or dominant elements to ensure they appear grounded and stable.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides visual support and stability to tall elements, enhancing their perceived weight and preventing top-heavy effects.
theory_units.caution: Avoid large areas of sunlighted pavements in such instances.

theory_units.title: Gravity: Movement Direction
theory_units.summary: Movement should align with natural gravitational pull (e.g., balloons ascend, objects fall, water flows downhill upper-left-to-lower-right, men climb uphill lower-left-to-upper-right).
theory_units.applies_when: When directing movement to align with natural physics, creating a sense of realism and ease.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys natural and believable movement, avoiding visual resistance for the audience.

theory_units.title: Purposeful Defiance of Gravity for Unbalance
theory_units.summary: Unbalanced compositions that defy gravity (e.g., baseless pictures, Dutch tilts, slanting diagonals) can be used to express violence, fear, panic, or impressionistic effects.
theory_units.applies_when: When the script specifically calls for disturbing, unsettling, or highly dynamic and chaotic visuals.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of unease, disorientation, and heightened emotional intensity in the viewer.
theory_units.caution: Use only when the narrative demands such an effect, as it upsets the viewer.

theory_units.title: Unity: Integrated Cinematic Elements
theory_units.summary: A picture possesses unity when all cinematic elements (line, form, mass, movement, lighting, camera/player movement, tonal values, color, editing) are perfectly integrated to convey a desired mood and atmosphere.
theory_units.applies_when: During all stages of filmmaking, from pre-production to editing, to ensure a cohesive visual and emotional experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: A unified emotional feeling and a coherent storytelling experience, avoiding discordant clashes of effects.
theory_units.caution: Mixture of cinematic effects results in a discordant clash, which will weaken the story-telling.

theory_units.title: Informal Balance with Odd Numbers
theory_units.summary: Achieve informal balance, especially with three subjects, by creating a single center of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing scenes with an odd number of subjects or pictorial elements, especially three.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention to the intended center of interest, creating a visually balanced yet dynamic shot.

theory_units.title: Creating a Quiet, Peaceful Mood
theory_units.summary: Combine specific visual and editorial elements to evoke a quiet, peaceful, and restful atmosphere.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative requires a quiet, peaceful, or restful mood.
theory_units.expected_effect: Inspires a quiet, peaceful, restful mood in the audience.
theory_units.caution: Avoid upward camera tilts, fast player movement, and short, choppy scenes as they destroy the effect.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Strategic Positioning, Angling, and Lighting
theory_units.summary: A subject can dominate a scene by being positioned lower, on the right side of the frame, and angled toward the camera, in combination with favorable lighting.
theory_units.applies_when: When a specific subject needs to be compositionally stronger and dominate the scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience attention is drawn to and held by the dominant subject.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Ascending Motion with Diagonal Formations
theory_units.summary: Strengthen the effect of ascending motion by staging subjects in a diagonal formation.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting ascending motion, such as jet fighters or mountain climbers, to enhance the visual impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually reinforces and amplifies the sense of upward movement.

theory_units.title: Composing Dignity with Symmetrical Verticality
theory_units.summary: Achieve a dignified manner by using a symmetrical, static composition for tall vertical elements.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing scenes with tall vertical elements (e.g., columns) and aiming for a dignified effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys dignity and stability.
theory_units.caution: Do not pan horizontally across vertical columns, as it destroys the dignified effect.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Action with Diagonal Movement
theory_units.summary: Increase the visual impact of action by staging movement so the viewer's eye follows a diagonal pattern.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting dynamic actions like climbing, racing, or marching, to make the action more dramatic.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases the action effect and engages the viewer's eye more actively.

theory_units.title: Recording Graceful Movement with Curving Camera
theory_units.summary: Capture graceful, twisting, and turning movements by following the subject with a complementary curving camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When recording subjects with graceful, fluid movements (e.g., a skier downhill).
theory_units.expected_effect: Accentuates the graceful effect of the subject's movement.

theory_units.title: Creating Unbalanced, Tilted, Unstable, Weird, or Violent Effects
theory_units.summary: Employ specific camera angles, composition, lighting, and editing techniques to evoke feelings of imbalance, instability, weirdness, or violence.
theory_units.applies_when: When the subject matter is weird, violent, or calls for an unbalanced, tilted, or unstable feeling.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates a sense of unease, disorientation, or heightened drama corresponding to weird or violent themes.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Visual Distraction During Important Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Refrain from using unusual camera angles, distracting background movement, or off-beat lighting in scenes focused on important dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene features important dialogue requiring primary audio attention from the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures audience attention remains on the dialogue without visual interference.
theory_units.caution: Unusual camera angles, distracting background movement, or off-beat lighting will divert attention from crucial dialogue.

theory_units.title: Preserving Unity of Style
theory_units.summary: Maintain a consistent stylistic approach throughout an entire sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, as a fundamental principle of filmmaking.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a cohesive and professional viewing experience, preventing jarring shifts in aesthetic.
theory_units.caution: Lack of stylistic unity can be jarring for the audience.

theory_units.title: Single Center of Interest
theory_units.summary: Each shot should clearly feature one primary center of interest to focus viewer attention and maintain effectiveness.
theory_units.applies_when: In most compositional situations, to ensure clear communication of the scene's focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strengthens the picture's effectiveness by directing viewer attention, preventing competition between elements.
theory_units.caution: Two or more equally dominant figures, objects, or actions will compete for attention and weaken the picture's effectiveness.

theory_units.title: Dominance in a Two-Shot
theory_units.summary: Even in a two-shot, ensure one player dominates at a time, often through speech, action, compositional treatment, lighting, or camera treatment.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing two subjects in a single shot, especially during dialogue or interaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs the viewer's eye to the currently most significant player, maintaining a clear center of interest.
theory_units.caution: Avoid having two equally dominant figures simultaneously, as it dilutes focus.

theory_units.title: Directing Attention to Significance
theory_units.summary: Always guide the viewer's attention to the most significant portion of the scene, allowing background action to complement rather than compete.
theory_units.applies_when: In every scene, to ensure narrative clarity and impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience understands what is most important in the scene, facilitating story comprehension and emotional engagement.
theory_units.caution: Background action should complement foreground action, not compete with it.

theory_units.title: Unified Group as Center of Interest
theory_units.summary: A dominant compositional element can be a closely-knit combination of several figures or objects, merged into a unified grouping.
theory_units.applies_when: When multiple subjects need to function as a single focal point, such as groups of players, trees, or machines.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for complex scenes with multiple elements to still maintain a singular, clear center of interest.

theory_units.title: Multiple Scattered Centers of Interest for Chaos
theory_units.summary: Employ several scattered centers of interest in scenes depicting violent, unbalanced, or disturbing events.
theory_units.applies_when: In scenes of battle, riot, panic, catastrophe, or other actions involving violent, unbalanced, or disturbing happenings.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys the chaos, disorder, and frantic nature of the events, immersing the audience in the disarray.
theory_units.caution: Avoid in scenes requiring a clear, singular focus.

theory_units.title: Balancing Compositional Weight
theory_units.summary: The left side of the frame can support greater compositional weight; thus, balance can be achieved by placing a smaller or less weighty center of interest on the right if a larger mass is on the left.
theory_units.applies_when: When balancing asymmetrical compositions, particularly when there is a significant element on the left.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a balanced composition despite asymmetrical elements.

theory_units.title: Off-Center Positioning for Dominance (Rule of Thirds)
theory_units.summary: Seldom center the center of interest. Preferably place it on the right dominant side of the frame, utilizing the compositional strength of the Rule of Thirds intersection points.
theory_units.applies_when: When positioning the main subject to create a dynamic and engaging composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Avoids visual monotony and creates a more interesting and dominant focus for the subject.
theory_units.caution: Centering subjects can lead to visual monotony. However, rigid adherence to off-center positioning can also lead to mechanical compositions.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Frame Bisection for Dynamic Compositions
theory_units.summary: Avoid bisecting the picture vertically, horizontally, or diagonally with prominent lines or subjects.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing any shot with strong lines or distinct halves.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents visually dull and static compositions, enhancing dynamism.
theory_units.caution: Bisecting the frame results in visually dull compositions.

theory_units.title: Strategic Horizon Placement
theory_units.summary: Do not center the horizon; instead, position it at one-third or two-thirds of the frame to avoid dividing the picture equally. In some cases, omit the horizon entirely.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing shots that include a horizon line or a distinct sky/ground division.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates more dynamic compositions and emphasizes either the sky or the ground, preventing visual dullness.
theory_units.caution: Centering the horizon divides the picture into two equal, dull parts.

theory_units.title: Subject Facing Inward with Lead Room
theory_units.summary: Position dominant subject matter to face inward toward the center of the picture, and provide a slight lead (negative space) in the direction the subject is facing.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing subjects that are looking or moving in a particular direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs the viewer's eye into the frame and makes the composition feel balanced and natural, preventing the subject from appearing to look 'out' of the frame awkwardly.

theory_units.title: Using Prominent Lines for Eye Attraction & Odd Divisions
theory_units.summary: Divide the frame with prominent lines (e.g., horizon, buildings, trees) to attract the eye to strong compositional points, favoring odd-numbered divisions, preferably thirds.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing scenes with natural or architectural lines that can guide viewer attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides the viewer's eye to the intended focal points and creates a visually appealing composition.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Compositional Monotony
theory_units.summary: Vary the positions of the center of interest, horizon placement, and player/camera movement across different scenes to prevent visual repetition.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout a sequence or film to maintain viewer engagement and avoid predictable compositions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps the visual experience fresh and engaging, preventing compositional similarity from shot to shot.
theory_units.caution: Sticking to one satisfactory compositional arrangement for all shots can lead to monotony.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Strategic Positioning/Movement
theory_units.summary: Capture audience attention by positioning a significant player or object in the most dominant portion of the composition, or by having them move into that position.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to highlight a specific subject within a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience's eye is drawn to and follows the primary subject.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Isolation
theory_units.summary: Attract attention to a player by isolating them from other subjects or having them move away from a group.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character needs to stand out, emotionally or narratively, from their surroundings or other characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the isolated character, highlighting their individuality or narrative significance.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Background Contrast
theory_units.summary: A player can attract attention by moving to achieve better contrast with the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When a player needs to be highlighted and the background offers contrasting elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases the visibility and prominence of the player.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Increased Height/Size
theory_units.summary: A player can increase their dominance by standing up or moving forward, which increases their height or relative size in the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character needs to assert authority, command attention, or appear more powerful.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually conveys increased status, power, or importance for the player.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Sudden Movement (Shock/Surprise)
theory_units.summary: A sudden move by a previously inactive player can shock or surprise the audience, making that player the center of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene requires an abrupt shift in focus or a startling revelation of a character's importance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shocks or surprises the audience, abruptly shifting their attention to the now-active player.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Forceful Action
theory_units.summary: A player can attract attention and assert dominance through forceful actions such as pounding a fist, striking another, or drawing a weapon.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character needs to express strong emotions, aggression, or a decisive moment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Immediately draws audience attention to the action and the player performing it, conveying power or intensity.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Contrasting Movement
theory_units.summary: A player can gain dominance by reversing their direction of movement, creating a contrast with other players.
theory_units.applies_when: When one player needs to stand out from a group or signify a change in intention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights the player's individual action and draws attention to them amidst others.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Obscuring Other Players
theory_units.summary: A player can assume dominance by moving in front of and obscuring other players.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character needs to assert themselves physically or narratively over others, or to visually diminish other characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually emphasizes the dominant player and demotes the obscured players.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Sound
theory_units.summary: A principal player can gain dominance through effective use of sound, such as speaking louder, shouting, silencing others, or delivering the most dramatic lines.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character needs to command verbal attention or assert themselves audibly.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience audio attention to the principal player, emphasizing their speech or presence.

theory_units.title: Eye Attraction to Brightest/Lightest/Most Colorful
theory_units.summary: Viewers' eyes are instinctively drawn to the most brightly illuminated, lightest toned, or most colorful area of a picture.
theory_units.applies_when: A fundamental principle of visual perception, used to guide audience attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Natural redirection of viewer attention to the prominent visual elements.
theory_units.caution: Be aware that subordinate elements with these qualities might unintentionally steal the scene.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Light, Color, or Illumination
theory_units.summary: Exploit the eye's attraction to brightness/color to make a leading player the center of interest by using lighter or more colorful clothing, or superior illumination.
theory_units.applies_when: When a leading player needs to be visually highlighted as the center of interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention to the leading player, making them stand out visually.
theory_units.caution: Ensure subordinate elements do not unintentionally steal the scene by having these advantages.

theory_units.title: Brightness/Contrast Creates Advance
theory_units.summary: A brighter object tends to visually 'advance' from a darker background toward the viewer.
theory_units.applies_when: A fundamental principle of visual depth perception, used to create visual separation and prominence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of depth and makes the brighter object appear closer or more prominent.
theory_units.caution: A subordinate player or object might unintentionally steal the scene if it is brighter or lighter than the intended main subject.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Movement into Light
theory_units.summary: Utilize player or camera movement to have a principal player move into a more brightly lit area, increasing dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's importance or dramatic significance needs to be heightened during a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases dramatic emphasis and makes the player the focal point. Can represent a shift from subdued to prominent.
theory_units.caution: Movement into light should be timed to coincide with action significant to the audience.

theory_units.title: Using Light/Dark Planes for Player Movement
theory_units.summary: Design sets or utilize natural environments with light and dark areas (planes) to allow players to move between them, controlling their visibility and emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning character movement and dynamic lighting within a scene, both indoors and outdoors.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables dynamic visual emphasis on players as they move, enhancing dramatic flow and visual interest.

theory_units.title: Dominance through Selective Focusing
theory_units.summary: Attract viewer attention to the center of interest by presenting significant subject matter sharply in focus while the rest of the picture is slightly soft.
theory_units.applies_when: To clearly identify and emphasize the main subject in a scene, especially in dramatic films.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the human eye directly to the sharpest image, making it the undeniable center of interest.

theory_units.title: Progressive Softening of Background with Closer Shots
theory_units.summary: In dramatic films, allow the background to become progressively softer in focus as the camera moves in for closer shots (medium shots and close-ups).
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning from wider to closer shots within a dramatic sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Naturally directs attention to the foreground subject in closer shots and maintains a sense of dramatic focus without needing unlimited depth of field.
theory_units.caution: This gradual fall-off in sharpness should be subtle if foreground action is interesting enough to hold attention.

theory_units.title: Considering Viewer Eye Scan
theory_units.summary: Carefully consider the scanning movement of viewers' eyes both within a single frame and, more importantly, across cuts between frames.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the entire filmmaking process, from composition to editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smoother, more engaging, and less distracting viewing experience, maintaining audience focus and comprehension.
theory_units.caution: Ignoring eye scan can jar viewers and distract them momentarily.

theory_units.title: Guiding Eye Scan in Two-Shots/Close-ups
theory_units.summary: In two-shots and subsequent close-ups, use correct framing, lead room, and relative heights to guide viewers' eyes in a predictable back-and-forth pattern.
theory_units.applies_when: When cutting between two interacting subjects, especially in dialogue sequences.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps viewers' eyes on a comfortable, directed path, maintaining continuity and engagement across cuts.
theory_units.caution: Improper positioning of players in the frame can jar viewers in scanning, causing momentary distraction.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Center of Interest Position Across Cuts
theory_units.summary: When cutting from a long shot to a closer shot, ensure the center of interest appears in approximately the same portion of the frame in both shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning between different shot sizes focusing on the same subject or area.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth transition for the viewer's eye, avoiding jarring jumps and maintaining focus on the center of interest.
theory_units.caution: Failure to maintain the center of interest's position will cause viewers' eyes to make a decided jump to re-find it, causing distraction.

theory_units.title: Deliberate Abrupt Eye Scan for Shock/Surprise
theory_units.summary: Intentionally make the center of attraction jump to a new area of the frame with a sudden cut, usually in conjunction with a sudden burst of activity or a new story development.
theory_units.applies_when: When the script calls for shocking the viewer, introducing a sudden element (e.g., murderer, vehicle), or a story twist.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shocks, startles, or surprises the viewer, abruptly shifting their attention to the new action or subject.
theory_units.caution: Should be employed deliberately and sparingly for maximum impact; overuse can be disorienting.

theory_units.title: Eye Scan Effectiveness by Screen Size
theory_units.summary: Eye scanning is most effective on a large screen and less important on television and small-screen projection.
theory_units.applies_when: When considering the impact of eye-scanning strategies across different exhibition platforms.
theory_units.expected_effect: Awareness of this allows for adaptation of compositional and editing choices based on intended viewing medium.
theory_units.caution: Strategies highly dependent on eye scan may have reduced impact on smaller screens.

theory_units.title: Angling Printed Matter for Eye Scan
theory_units.summary: Angle printed matter uphill (from lower left to upper right) to facilitate natural eye movement, allowing viewers' eyes to drop down for the next line.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any on-screen text or printed documents that the audience needs to read.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances readability and creates a comfortable, natural eye flow for the viewer.
theory_units.caution: Downhill angling forces the eye to move up to read the next line, which is unaccustomed and hinders readability.

theory_units.title: Introducing Threat from Screen Left for Shock
theory_units.summary: Suddenly introduce a threatening element or murderer from screen left to shock viewers who are focused on a victim or scene on the right side of the picture.
theory_units.applies_when: When a script calls for a sudden, startling introduction of danger or a villain.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a startling effect due to the abrupt right-to-left eye scan, surprising the audience.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Jump-Cut Effect with Close-ups
theory_units.summary: Avoid slight, erratic changes in image size or angle between close-ups, as this creates a distracting jump-cut effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing a sequence of close-ups, especially in dialogue or reaction shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures smooth transitions and prevents viewer disorientation, maintaining a professional and immersive viewing experience.
theory_units.caution: Slightly smaller or larger close-up images, or slightly different angles, create disconcerting expanding/contracting effects and erratic eye scanning.

theory_units.title: Deliberate Erratic Eye Scan for Unbalanced/Weird Effects
theory_units.summary: Employ scattered, oddly-sized, oddly-angled images, or Dutch tilts to force erratic eye scanning, enhancing unbalanced or weird effects.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting scenes of panic, catastrophe, or violence, or when a script calls for an unbalanced or weird aesthetic.
theory_units.expected_effect: Forces abrupt, non-linear eye movements (back-and-forth, up-and-down, diagonal), involving the audience more closely with the screen action and enhancing the chaotic mood.
theory_units.caution: Should be used deliberately for specific effects; can be disorienting if misused.

theory_units.title: Lead Room for Moving Subjects
theory_units.summary: Provide slightly more space in the direction a moving player is traveling.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing a subject in motion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the viewer's eye to anticipate the subject's movement, creating a natural and balanced composition.
theory_units.caution: Insufficient lead room can make the subject feel trapped or create an awkward visual.

theory_units.title: Lead Room for Static Subjects
theory_units.summary: Provide slightly more space in the direction a statically-positioned player is looking.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing a stationary subject who is looking off-screen or in a specific direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs the viewer's attention and implies interaction or continuation beyond the frame, creating a balanced and natural composition.

theory_units.title: Contextual Head Room Adjustment
theory_units.summary: Vary the amount of head room (distance between head and top frame line) based on background elements and compositional masses.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing any shot with subjects, particularly varying backgrounds or framing devices.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves a balanced and aesthetically pleasing composition, preventing the picture from looking bottom-heavy or crowded.
theory_units.caution: Excessive head room makes the picture look bottom-heavy; insufficient head room makes it look crowded.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Frame Contact
theory_units.summary: Players should not touch the frame edges by standing or sitting precisely on the bottom frame line, or leaning/lining up with the sides.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing subjects within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a cleaner and more professional composition, avoiding awkward visual tangents.
theory_units.caution: Contacting frame edges can create visual awkwardness or tension unless intended.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Cutting at Joints
theory_units.summary: When framing a player, especially in close-ups, ensure the frame line cuts between body joints (knees, waist, elbows, shoulders) rather than directly across them.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing subjects, particularly in medium shots and close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more natural and aesthetically pleasing cut, avoiding awkward dismemberment of the body.
theory_units.caution: Cutting across joints can make a player appear dismembered or create an unnatural visual break.

theory_units.title: Consistent Framing for Moving Subjects at Key Positions
theory_units.summary: In moving shots, ensure players arrive at key positions with framing similar to that used for static shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When staging and filming sequences involving player movement to predefined key positions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual consistency and a sense of composed order even within dynamic scenes.
theory_units.caution: Inconsistent framing at key positions can be jarring.

theory_units.title: Dominant Subject on Right
theory_units.summary: Generally position the most important player, object, or action on the right side of the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When deciding initial placement of the primary focus within a frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Often perceived as a compositionally stronger position, naturally drawing the viewer's eye.
theory_units.caution: Large masses on the right can overbalance the picture. This is a general guideline, not a rigid rule.

theory_units.title: Favoring Left-Positioned Dominant Player
theory_units.summary: If a dominant player must be on the left, compensate by giving them preferential compositional treatment such as better lighting, favorable body angling, stronger contrast, or separation from the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When narrative or blocking necessitates placing the dominant subject on the left side of the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the left-positioned player still maintains dominance and visual importance despite being on the 'weaker' side.

theory_units.title: Leading Lines Diminishing Rightward
theory_units.summary: Arrange leading lines in the composition so they diminish toward the right side of the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When using natural or constructed lines to guide viewer attention within a frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Attracts the viewer's eye to the center of interest more effectively.

theory_units.title: Strategic Frame Positions for Dramatic Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Be aware of the merits of various frame positions to strategically place subjects for best dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing any shot where dramatic impact is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Optimizes visual storytelling by using frame positions to enhance emotional or narrative significance.

theory_units.title: Cheating Player Height for Dominance
theory_units.summary: In theatrical films, subtly cheat a leading player's height to make them appear taller and more dominant, especially in medium or close shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When a leading player needs to appear taller or more commanding than others, particularly in theatrical films.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visual hierarchy, making the 'taller' player appear more powerful or significant.
theory_units.caution: Must be done subtly to avoid detection, especially in medium or close shots.

theory_units.title: Using Forced Perspective Sets
theory_units.summary: Design converging sets with built-in forced perspective where normal-sized players are in the foreground and under-sized or midget players are in the distance.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to manipulate perceived size and distance within a theatrical film, creating illusions of scale.
theory_units.expected_effect: Deceives the eye regarding the apparent size of objects and figures, allowing for dramatic scale changes.

theory_units.title: True Size Representation (Non-Theatrical Films)
theory_units.summary: In non-theatrical films, avoid falsification and strive to show the true size of objects, often by including operators, objects of known size, or familiar backgrounds for scale.
theory_units.applies_when: In documentary, instructional, or scientific films where factual accuracy of scale is paramount.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains credibility and provides accurate information about the size of objects.
theory_units.caution: Falsification of size must usually be avoided; otherwise, the true size of objects must be shown.

theory_units.title: Perceived Size through Framing
theory_units.summary: Images that crowd the frame are perceived as larger than images with more space around them, regardless of actual physical size.
theory_units.applies_when: When manipulating the perceived size or dominance of a subject within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can make a tiny object appear huge by crowding the frame, or a large object appear small by providing ample space.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Loftiness through High Framing
theory_units.summary: Make an object appear loftier by positioning it high in the frame with little sky visible above it.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the height or grandeur of a tall object like a mountain.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a sense of immense height and scale.

theory_units.title: Suggesting Larger Quantity through Overlapping/Framing
theory_units.summary: Make a relatively small number of subjects appear greater by crowding them to overlap the frame, suggesting more are outside the picture.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to imply a larger crowd, organization, or quantity than is actually present or fully visible.
theory_units.expected_effect: Relays the impression that the entire picture is vast or complicated, suggesting a large scale beyond the frame.

theory_units.title: Conveying Vastness/Complexity through Partial View
theory_units.summary: Show less than the whole of a group or object (e.g., partial crowds, electronic circuits) to convey an impression of vastness or complexity.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to make a scene feel expansive, intricate, or overwhelming.
theory_units.expected_effect: Relays the impression that the entire picture is too vast or complicated to capture in its entirety.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Height with Upward Camera Angle
theory_units.summary: Make a figure or object appear taller by angling the camera upward, especially if the image contains converging vertical parallel lines.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the height, power, or dominance of a subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually elongates the subject, making it appear taller and potentially more imposing.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Height with Low Angle & Wide-Angle Lens
theory_units.summary: Use a low angle and a wide-angle lens to make a tall building appear even taller.
theory_units.applies_when: Specifically for architectural subjects like tall buildings, to exaggerate their height.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dramatic exaggeration of height and scale.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Subjective Height with Low Angle & Crowded Frame
theory_units.summary: For a subjective height effect (e.g., from a child's viewpoint), use a low-angle shot with the subject crowding the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When attempting to convey a character's (e.g., child's) perception of height and scale from their perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a similar height effect, making the viewed subject appear larger and more imposing from the subjective viewpoint.

theory_units.title: Emotional Impact of Extreme Shots
theory_units.summary: Employ extreme long shots (especially high angle, looking down on tiny subjects) or extreme close-ups to provoke greater emotional response and audience involvement.
theory_units.applies_when: To portray hardships, vastness, isolation, or intense intimacy and evoke strong emotions in the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provokes the audience into greater involvement in the story by arousing emotions, provides visual variety.

theory_units.title: Composing for Multiple Viewpoints
theory_units.summary: Compose shots with definite viewpoints in mind, recognizing that a composition perfect for one angle may be poor from another, especially in sequences with multiple angles.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning any scene that will be covered from several different camera angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that all shots within a sequence are visually effective and cohesive, regardless of camera position.
theory_units.caution: A composition perfect for a particular camera angle may be very poor when viewed from an opposite angle.

theory_units.title: Integrated Composition and Camera Angles
theory_units.summary: Integrate composition and camera angles so that players and pictorial elements remain properly composed as the camera moves through a sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: Essential for any sequence involving camera or player movement and multiple setups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a consistently strong visual aesthetic throughout the sequence, avoiding jarring compositional shifts.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Composition from Long Shot to Close-up
theory_units.summary: A good long-shot composition will generally work well for closer shots if camera set-ups are not drastically altered, requiring careful lining up during rehearsal.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting a sequence that moves from wide to closer shots of the same subject matter.
theory_units.expected_effect: Preserves the player/background relationship and overall composition across different shot sizes, creating smooth transitions.
theory_units.caution: Drastically altered camera set-ups can change the player/background relationship and undermine composition.

theory_units.title: Continuous Composition through Harmonious Movement
theory_units.summary: Plan player and/or camera movement to work in harmony, continuously composing the scene and revising player/background relationships as action progresses.
theory_units.applies_when: In dynamic scenes with significant movement, where maintaining strong composition throughout is crucial.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the scene remains continuously well-composed, prevents awkward pictorial situations, and allows for smooth transitions into closer shots.
theory_units.caution: An excellent static composition may deteriorate into confusion if movements are unplanned or player/background relationships change drastically.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Distractions from Frame Edges in Closer Shots
theory_units.summary: When moving into side angles or over-the-shoulder close-ups, be vigilant for distracting objects (e.g., lamps, furniture) that may suddenly appear or merge with players' features.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning closer shots, especially those from new angles like side profiles or over-the-shoulder.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains focus on the main action and characters by preventing unintended visual interference.
theory_units.caution: Distracting objects can detract from the main action or create awkward visual mergers with players.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Continuous Composition Vigilance
theory_units.summary: Continuously maintain proper framing for players, pleasing player/background relationships, and well-composed pauses at key positions throughout moving shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout any scene involving movement, to ensure consistent compositional quality.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a polished and professional visual flow, keeping the audience engaged without distractions from compositional errors.
theory_units.caution: Requires constant vigilance to avoid compositional problems.

theory_units.title: Choreographing Movement for Continuous Composition
theory_units.summary: To best achieve continuous composition, first compose players carefully in each key position for optimal pictorial effect, then work out the movements between those key positions.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning complex scenes with significant player movement and multiple important stopping points.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that both static and dynamic moments within a scene are optimally composed, creating a seamless and visually strong sequence.

theory_units.title: Linear Perspective for Depth and Solidity
theory_units.summary: Linear perspective creates the illusion of depth and solidity in a picture through the convergence of parallel lines and diminishing sizes of objects with distance.
theory_units.applies_when: A fundamental principle to enhance the three-dimensional quality of a two-dimensional image.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps viewers judge distance, creating a realistic sense of depth and form.

theory_units.title: Increasing Solidity with Angle-Plus-Angle Shots
theory_units.summary: Choose camera angles that portray the greatest number of planes or facets of a subject, shooting 'angle-plus-angle' to record front, side, and top/bottom for maximum solidity.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the three-dimensional form and physical presence of an object.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a stronger sense of solidity and volume for the subject.

theory_units.title: Using Lens & Angle for Linear Convergence without Distortion
theory_units.summary: Select a short focal length lens (not necessarily wide-angle) and a suitable camera angle to record realistic linear perspective with converging lines that lead the eye into the scene, without distortion.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to enhance depth and guide viewer attention into the far reaches of a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a realistic sense of depth and draws the viewer's eye into the background of the scene, without undesirable distortion.

theory_units.title: Extreme Wide-Angle Lenses for Special Convergence
theory_units.summary: Use extreme wide-angle lenses exclusively for special effects when a greater than normal degree of linear convergence is desired.
theory_units.applies_when: Only when specifically aiming for exaggerated perspective or a distorted visual effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces strong, exaggerated linear convergence.
theory_units.caution: Extreme wide-angle lenses typically introduce distortion and should not be used for realistic perspective unless intended for special effects.

theory_units.title: Audience Involvement through Camera Proximity
theory_units.summary: Achieve the finest modeling of players and setting, and greatest audience involvement, by bringing the camera as close as possible to the subject.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for intimacy, detail, and strong emotional connection with the subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the tactile quality of the visuals and increases the audience's emotional engagement with the scene.

theory_units.title: Overlapping Objects for Spatial Depth
theory_units.summary: Position players, props, and objects to partially overlap, naturally conveying their spatial relationships and distance from the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to clearly establish spatial relationships between multiple objects or figures in a scene, especially when their known size is not obvious.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an immediate and unambiguous sense of spatial depth, clarity on which objects are nearer, and a three-dimensional illusion on a two-dimensional screen.

theory_units.title: Motion Parallax for Dynamic Depth
theory_units.summary: Introduce motion parallax by moving players or the camera to partially cover and uncover other elements, or by moving the camera through foreground objects, to convey position and distance.
theory_units.applies_when: When players or the camera are in motion, and there's an opportunity to reveal or obscure parts of the scene to enhance depth perception.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the viewer's understanding of spatial relationships, creates a dynamic sense of depth, and adds visual interest to movement.

theory_units.title: Angled Movement for Enhanced Depth
theory_units.summary: Stage player or vehicle movement toward or away from the camera, or angle cross-screen movement slightly, to impart a change in image size and convey spatial depth.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever players or vehicles are moving, to maximize the sense of three-dimensional space.
theory_units.expected_effect: A feeling of spatial depth and distance; a more dynamic and less flat portrayal of movement.
theory_units.caution: Avoid movements precisely at right angles to the lens, which flatten the image.

theory_units.title: Avoid Flat Lighting
theory_units.summary: Do not use overall shadowless illumination, as it flattens the field, removes modeling, and prevents separation of figures and objects.
theory_units.applies_when: In any filming situation, indoors or outdoors, where depth and three-dimensionality are desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents flatness of field, ensures figures and objects have texture and separation.
theory_units.caution: Over-all shadowless illumination produces a flatness of field, minus projections and modeling, lacking texture, and preventing separation of figures and objects.

theory_units.title: Utilize Side & Differential Lighting for 3D Modeling
theory_units.summary: Employ side lighting or contrasting planes of light and shade in interior scenes to create shadow areas and impart three-dimensional modeling and a front-to-back quality.
theory_units.applies_when: When lighting figures and settings, especially indoors, to enhance their three-dimensional appearance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Figures and setting appear well-modeled, with depth and a clear front-to-back quality, preventing flatness.

theory_units.title: Aerial Perspective through Background Lighting
theory_units.summary: Enhance aerial perspective outdoors by including lighter, distant backgrounds, or indoors by lighting the background slightly 'hotter' to draw the viewer's eye into the depth of the setting.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming outdoors with distant elements or indoors to create a sense of deep space.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds additional aerial perspective, guiding the viewer's eye into the far reaches of the setting and enhancing depth.

theory_units.title: Backgrounds as Storytelling Aids
theory_units.summary: Integrate backgrounds into the story to contribute activity, authenticity, and realism, choosing camera angles and staging action against backgrounds that clearly convey the specific activity.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever filming on location, especially for non-theatrical or documentary subjects, to enrich the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds greater scope, pictorial interest, and a 'you-are-there' feeling, making the story more believable and informative.
theory_units.caution: Many cameramen ignore or misuse backgrounds, missing opportunities to enhance the story.

theory_units.title: Subtle Background Reinforcement
theory_units.summary: The background should constantly, yet subtly, remind the viewer of the story's location, adding realism without distracting from the main action.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout a film, especially documentary or location-based narratives, to ground the story in its setting.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds realism and context, ensuring the viewer consistently understands the environment the story unfolds in.

theory_units.title: Avoid Nondescript/Distracting Backgrounds
theory_units.summary: Carefully scout indoor locations to avoid backgrounds that are quiet, nondescript, or detract from the story, ensuring they contribute rather than hinder the narrative.
theory_units.applies_when: When choosing staging for interior scenes, or when tempted to use plain settings for convenience after establishing shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains story coherence and viewer engagement, preventing loss of location's true meaning.
theory_units.caution: Staging scenes against nondescript backgrounds deters from the story; filming only establishing long shots then retiring to plain settings loses the purpose of expensive travel to location.

theory_units.title: Isolate Players for Concentrated Focus
theory_units.summary: Isolate players against a simple, nondescript background (like the sky) when action or dialogue demands complete audience concentration without distracting elements.
theory_units.applies_when: When the camera moves closer to a small group or single player, and their action/dialogue is paramount.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience's complete attention is on the players, preventing distractions.

theory_units.title: Background Does Not Distract
theory_units.summary: Ensure the background never steals the show by being more interesting than the main action or dialogue, or by distracting the audience with its make-up, movement, or color.
theory_units.applies_when: In all compositions, but especially as the camera moves closer to the subjects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience focus on the primary subject and narrative, ensuring clear communication of the story.
theory_units.caution: A background that is too interesting will steal the show; it should not intrude on foreground players or action.

theory_units.title: Distinct Foreground-Background Separation
theory_units.summary: Position players and objects to ensure distinct separation from the background, utilizing lighting effects, contrasting tones, or distinct colors to prevent flattening of the picture.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, but particularly important in close-ups where the player's head should stand out from the background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a three-dimensional appearance, ensures figures 'stand out', and avoids merging that flattens the image.
theory_units.caution: A figure or object similarly toned or colored, merging with the background, will flatten the picture. Annoying lines or shapes piercing a player's body/head, or disturbing background elements.

theory_units.title: Foreground Frames for Compositional Aid
theory_units.summary: Utilize foreground pictorial elements (e.g., arches, windows, branches) to partially or completely frame the main subject, containing the action and preventing viewer's eyes from wandering off-screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene benefits from enhanced depth, contained action, or directed viewer focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a pictorial foreground element, contains the action, prevents viewer's eyes from wandering off-screen, and adds depth.
theory_units.caution: Frames should not be composed evenly on all sides unless perfectly symmetrical.

theory_units.title: Lighting Foreground Frames for Depth and Separation
theory_units.summary: Employ back-cross or complete backlighting for frames to edge-light and outline them, separating them from the distant view, adding depth through shadows, and preventing merging caused by flat front light.
theory_units.applies_when: When using foreground frames to enhance their three-dimensional appearance and distinction from the background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds depth, solidity, edge-lights the frame, imparts a luminous/ethereal quality to translucent objects, and creates shadows for depth. Prevents a 'cardboard cut-out' appearance and frame-scene merging.
theory_units.caution: A frame should not be shot in a flat front light, or it will include the same tonal values as the main scene and merge with it.

theory_units.title: Appropriate and Non-Distracting Frames
theory_units.summary: Ensure frames are appropriate to the scene and do not detract from the main subject; avoid elaborate, artificial, or otherwise distracting frames.
theory_units.applies_when: When selecting or creating foreground frames for a shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: The frame serves as an aid without competing for attention, keeping the focus on the main subject.
theory_units.caution: Improper frames are often artificially contrived and can cause trouble if too elaborate or distracting. The subject is the picture; the frame is only a compositional aid.

theory_units.title: Effective Partial Frames with Solid Connection
theory_units.summary: When a full frame isn't present, use a partial frame (e.g., top and one side) to break up empty space, but ensure it shows solid connection and isn't so minimal it teases the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When dealing with large expanses of empty foreground or bald skies, and a full frame is not feasible.
theory_units.expected_effect: Breaks up dull areas, adds compositional interest, and enhances depth without confusing the viewer.
theory_units.caution: A part of a tree branch, or other object, should not just 'hang in space'. Too little of a frame may tease the audience if they cannot deduce what it is.

theory_units.title: Sharp Frame Focus for Clarity
theory_units.summary: Keep foreground frames sharp to avoid distracting the viewer, using split focus or hyperfocal distance to ensure both frame and main object are equally sharp.
theory_units.applies_when: When using foreground frames, especially those occupying a major portion of the picture.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clarity and prevents audience distraction from an out-of-focus foreground.
theory_units.caution: An out-of-focus foreground object, occupying a major portion of the picture, can prove very disturbing. A slightly soft-focus frame is only permissible if underexposed or in silhouette and sufficient depth-of-field is unavailable.

theory_units.title: Adjusting Camera/Lens for Subject-Frame Size Relationship
theory_units.summary: If the main subject appears too small in relation to the frame, move the camera back and employ a longer focal length lens to make the subject appear larger while still recording the full frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing a shot with a foreground frame where the main subject is too small and needs to be emphasized.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a clearer hierarchy, making the main subject more prominent within the framed composition.

theory_units.title: Controlled Frame Movement
theory_units.summary: Avoid wildly moving frames that distract from the main subject. Camera movement is permissible if the frame itself remains static, allowing for smooth pans or dollies into a framed composition.
theory_units.applies_when: When integrating camera or subject movement with a foreground frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains focus on the main subject while allowing for dynamic camera work and effective reveals.
theory_units.caution: Wildly moving frames (e.g., branches in wind) should be avoided because they may detract from the main subject. Panning across a frame with strong verticals close to the camera can cause an annoying 'shipping' effect.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Composition for Abrupt Effects
theory_units.summary: Employ dynamic composition to evoke sudden change in a static setup, introducing forceful pictorial elements (figures, objects, vehicles) abruptly into the frame to surprise or invigorate a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When abrupt or surprising effects are desired, to bring quiet scenes to life, or to recapture audience attention after a calm passage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a startling, vigorous, or dramatically active effect, drawing immediate attention and disrupting complacency.
theory_units.caution: Requires utmost discretion and should be limited to properly-motivated dramatic situations to avoid being jarring or arbitrary.

theory_units.title: Suspenseful Composition through Concealment or Prolongation
theory_units.summary: Utilize composition to hide significant action, create absence, or prolong a reveal, keeping the audience in doubt and building suspense.
theory_units.applies_when: When 'cliff-hanging' suspense is the keynote of a sequence, needing to prolong audience uncertainty.
theory_units.expected_effect: Builds tension and emotional engagement by keeping the audience eager for a reveal or resolution, making them feel the duration of a difficult moment.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful staging and camera work to effectively withhold information without frustrating the viewer.

theory_units.title: Dynamic and Aesthetic Catalog Composition
theory_units.summary: Compose catalog-style shots of objects not as static displays but using patterns, forms, and movement (pan, dolly, zoom) to create aesthetic or emotional impact, convey purpose, or group elements harmoniously.
