theory_units.applies_when: When photographing groups of tools, machines, products, or similar items for industrial, military, or training films.
theory_units.expected_effect: Transforms potentially static shots into engaging compositions, conveying action, purposefulness, or a sense of unity, avoiding clutter.
theory_units.caution: Avoid showing static catalog shots that interrupt the film's flow; equipment should be shown in the course of work.

theory_units.title: Compositional Variety for Viewer Engagement
theory_units.summary: Maintain a unified style while presenting a variety of compositions, camera angles, and image sizes to prevent monotony and sustain viewer interest.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the entire film, but especially when dealing with similar settings or repeated actions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps players and settings from being depicted in a monotonous pattern, adding interest and avoiding viewer disengagement.
theory_units.caution: Avoid similar compositional treatment, staging, player movement, or camera movement across different settings or sequences. Cameramen may slip into a rut on tight schedules.

theory_units.title: Comprehensive 'Compose in Depth' Strategy
theory_units.summary: Proactively create compositions in depth to build a three-dimensional illusion on screen, utilizing a combination of staging, camera angles, lighting, and foreground/background elements to immerse the viewer.
theory_units.applies_when: As a foundational approach to almost all cinematography, whenever striving for a rich, immersive visual experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Viewers feel immersed in the setting, rather than observing from afar; creates a solid, three-dimensional appearance for players, setting, and objects.
theory_units.caution: Avoid restricting depth for ease of lighting or focus. Always think in depth. Avoid flat angles, flat lighting, cross-screen movement, and lined-up, straight-across staging.

theory_units.title: Simplicity as the Core of Good Composition
theory_units.summary: Strive for simplicity in composition, focusing on a single center of interest and economizing elements to ensure immediate viewer recognition and assimilation, preventing clutter and distraction.
theory_units.applies_when: In every compositional decision, from framing to object arrangement, ensuring clarity and impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: A composition that is immediately recognizable and readily assimilated by the audience, who does not have to search for the shot's meaning. Prevents irritation and loss of interest.
theory_units.caution: A complicated or cluttered composition, even if technically correct, will not be as effective. Any element not required for storytelling attracts unwarranted attention and may steal the scene.

theory_units.title: Balance in Composition
theory_units.summary: Understand the differences between formal and informal balance, and apply them strategically to elicit the desired audience response.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing any shot or sequence where the arrangement of elements influences audience perception and emotion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides audience emotions and understanding, ensuring the visual presentation aligns with the script's intent.

theory_units.title: Single Center of Interest
theory_units.summary: Limit each screen composition to a single, clear center of interest to maintain audience focus, unless a disturbed or scattered effect is deliberately intended.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot where a clear focal point is desired, or when intentionally creating a sense of disturbance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience's attention is directed to the intended subject, preventing visual confusion.
theory_units.caution: Avoid multiple centers of interest unless intentionally aiming for a disturbed or scattered effect.

theory_units.title: Lead Room for Moving Subjects
theory_units.summary: Frame moving subjects (players or vehicles) with adequate space in the direction of their movement, known as 'lead room' or 'looking room'.
theory_units.applies_when: Framing any shot that includes a subject in motion or about to move.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides visual comfort for the viewer, anticipates the subject's movement, and enhances the sense of motion and natural flow.

theory_units.title: Pre-planning Camera Angles for Sequences
theory_units.summary: When composing a master scene, consider and plan for all subsequent camera angles required to cover the entire sequence, not just the initial long shot.
theory_units.applies_when: During the planning and blocking phase of any scene that will be covered with multiple shots, starting from a master scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures comprehensive and continuous coverage, facilitates efficient shooting, and maintains visual continuity across edits.
theory_units.caution: Do not solely plan for the master long shot, as this can lead to coverage gaps or continuity problems.

theory_units.title: Composition in Depth for 3D Appearance
theory_units.summary: Arrange elements within the frame to create a sense of depth, giving the screen a three-dimensional appearance.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot, particularly to avoid a flat or two-dimensional image.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances immersion, realism, and visual interest by creating the illusion of space and dimension on a flat screen.

theory_units.title: Using Foreground Frames
theory_units.summary: Employ appropriate foreground elements to frame the main subject, enhancing composition and guiding the viewer's eye.
theory_units.applies_when: Seeking to add depth, direct attention, or improve the aesthetic appeal of a composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds layers of depth, directs focus to the main subject, and makes the composition more dynamic and aesthetically pleasing.
theory_units.caution: Ensure foreground frames are appropriate to the scene and do not distract from the main subject.

theory_units.title: Connecting Backgrounds to Action
theory_units.summary: Integrate backgrounds with the principal action to provide context and meaning, making them an active part of the narrative rather than mere scenery.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot that includes a significant background, especially to enrich the narrative or character's environment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enriches the narrative, adds depth to the scene, and creates a more cohesive and meaningful visual experience.

theory_units.title: Viewer Eye Scan Across Shots
theory_units.summary: Consider how the viewer's eye will naturally move and locate points of interest from one shot to the next when planning shot transitions.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning shot sequences and editing decisions to ensure smooth visual flow and audience comprehension.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and intuitive viewing experience, prevents disorientation, and maintains visual continuity.

theory_units.title: Visual Variety in Composition
theory_units.summary: Regularly change compositional effects within a sequence to maintain audience engagement and prevent visual monotony.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing a series of shots or planning the overall visual style of a scene or sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps the audience interested, prevents visual fatigue, and adds dynamic energy to the storytelling.

theory_units.title: Simplicity in Composition
theory_units.summary: Prioritize clear and simple compositions, avoiding unnecessary frills, gimmicks, or overly complex arrangements.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot, especially when tempted to add decorative or superfluous elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves greater clarity and impact, prevents audience distraction, and makes the main subject stand out.
theory_units.caution: Avoid unnecessary frills, gimmicks, and overly complex arrangements which can confuse or detract from the message.

operations.explanation_template: Rearrange a player's position or adjust camera angle to make them appear taller in a two-shot, enhancing their presence or narrative role without audience detection.
Adjust the camera's frame or object's position to exclude a distracting or unnecessary element (e.g., a lamp corner) from a close-up, improving the overall composition.
Position the camera for a large close-up to move the audience closer to the action, allowing them to view a significant and emphasized portion of the narrative.
Place the camera farther away to utilize a wide shot, enabling the audience to appreciate the magnificent grandeur or vastness of a landscape or setting.
Position the camera higher to look down upon a subject (e.g., a construction project), providing an overview and potentially diminishing its presence.
Place the camera lower to look up at a subject (e.g., the face of a judge), making it appear more imposing, powerful, or significant.
Move the camera alongside a character (e.g., a galloping horseman) to maintain focus on their movement and convey a sense of continuous, dynamic action.
Move the camera into a dramatic scene to heighten story interest and draw the audience deeper into the emotional or narrative core.
Move the camera away from a gruesome or intense setting to create emotional distance for the audience or to de-escalate the visual impact.
Ensure actors never look directly into the camera lens, even inadvertently, to maintain the illusion that the camera is an unseen observer and characters are unaware of its presence.

suggested_change.Shot Sequence: Close-up of character looking off-screen followed by subjective shot

operations.explanation_template: Precede a subjective point-of-view shot with a close-up of the character looking off-screen to explicitly establish that the audience is now seeing through that character's eyes.

Applying {{Image Distortion}}, {{Camera Blur}}, or {{Camera Shake}} to an into-the-lens subjective shot for mentally-unbalanced sequences makes it more effective by visually conveying the character's impaired state.

suggested_change.Actor Instruction: Speak directly into lens at all times

operations.explanation_template: By instructing the interviewee to look {{Actor Eye-line}} at all times and {{Actor Instruction}}, the 'double-look' is prevented, maintaining audience focus and a stronger subjective connection.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Cut or zoom to close-up of interviewee looking into lens

operations.explanation_template: Positioning reporter-interviewee for an {{Shot Composition}} shot and then using {{Camera Movement}} to a close-up of the interviewee looking into the lens can better handle the look-into-lens effect, allowing for a natural transition.

suggested_change.Actor Eye-line: Slightly to the side of the camera

operations.explanation_template: In a POV shot, when an on-screen player looks at the character whose viewpoint is depicted, they should look {{Actor Eye-line}}, preventing them from breaking the objective camera feel by looking directly into the lens.
To establish an objective shot as a Point-of-View shot, precede it with a {{Preceding Shot}}, signaling to the audience that the following shot is from that player's perspective.

When a player points off-screen, they should {{Player Exit Direction}} from the direction pointed, unless a direct relationship between movement and object is narratively significant, to avoid confusing the audience.

suggested_change.Player Movement: Move toward or away from camera

operations.explanation_template: Varying {{Camera Movement}}, {{Player Movement}}, or {{Lens Type}} allows the image size to change during a single shot, enabling seamless transitions between shot types like a long shot graduating into a close-up.

For an Extreme Long Shot, generally use a {{Camera Movement}} with a wide angle. A {{Camera Movement}} should only be employed if it actively increases interest or reveals more of the setting/action as it progresses, rather than a static map-like shot.

suggested_change.Camera Height: High vantage point (platform, building, mountain, air)

operations.explanation_template: Filming Extreme Long Shots from a {{Camera Height}} enhances their impressiveness, conveying the grandeur and scope of the setting.
Employ a {{Shot Type}} to establish all elements in a scene, including characters, their location, and movements, especially when their location is narratively significant.
When considerable player movement is involved, re-establish the scene with a {{Shot Type}} to prevent audience confusion regarding character whereabouts in relation to the setting and other players.
Even for sequences primarily taking place indoors, open with an {{Opening Shot}} to establish location and provide 'air,' preventing the picture from appearing closed-in.
To achieve dominance in a profile two-shot, employ {{Lighting}} or {{Dialogue/Action}} that captures audience attention for one player over the other.

suggested_change.Blocking: Player/camera movement to bring players together

operations.explanation_template: Use {{Blocking}} to naturally and casually bring players together in a two-shot, avoiding a static, 'toe-to-toe' composition unless dramatically intended.

suggested_change.Framing: Slightly overlap frame

operations.explanation_template: For economy and to eliminate background, film inserts {{Filming Timing}} and {{Framing}} for a clean, full-screen close-up.
To maintain visual consistency, ensure that {{Continuity}} in an insert matches those in the preceding shot.

suggested_change.Framing: Loose framing (important elements away from edges)

operations.explanation_template: When filming inserts for wide-screen projection, use {{Framing}} to prevent important text or images from being cropped or made illegible by various theatre screen aspect ratios.
Angle the camera in relation to the subject so that two or more sides (and top/bottom) are viewed, which is the most effective way to record three-dimensional solidity.
Move the camera to one side, or move furniture, vehicles, and props, so that they are seen with as many surfaces as possible, enhancing their solidity and depth.
Shoot a room or setting so that two or more walls are seen, which contributes to the perception of depth and space.
Turn the subject forty-five degrees (three-quarter angling) to the camera so that both the front and side of the face are visible, ensuring a round appearance and full display of the eyes.
Angle the camera so that parallel lines within the scene diminish and converge, preferably towards the right, which helps carry the viewers' eyes into the distance and creates depth.
Angle the camera so that it looks down a street that converges into the distance, effectively using linear perspective to suggest depth.
Film the background at an angle, rather than flat-on, to produce diminishing compositional lines that enhance linear perspective.
Angle the camera in relation to the subject to create strong diagonal patterns (e.g., horsemen, foreground soldiers, guns, swords), which inherently suggests conflict and dynamism.
Consciously adjust the height of the camera in relation to the subject and scene to align with the desired artistic, dramatic, and psychological impact on the audience.
Film objective shots from the eye-level of an average observer (around 5.5 feet high), ensuring vertical lines do not converge and maintain their parallel alignment.
Utilize a level camera when eye-level views are specifically required, or when it's imperative for vertical lines (e.g., walls, buildings) to remain undistorted and parallel to each other.
For technical films depicting tools, machines, or instrument panels, use a flat, level, undistorted view to ensure clarity and accuracy for engineering study.
When moving into a close-up, adjust the camera height to the subject's eye-level, whether they are standing or sitting, to foster an eye-to-eye basis with the audience.

For POV close-ups between players of different heights (e.g., standing/seated, adult/child), angle the camera upward or downward to simulate the opposing player's eye-level, possibly cheating the angle slightly to prevent distortion while maintaining the 'look up/down' effect.

For subjective close-ups where the subject looks directly into the lens, always film from their exact eye-level to maintain a natural, level eye-to-eye relationship with the viewer, preventing an awkward looking up or down.

suggested_change.Subject Feature: Turned-up nose, Flabby jowls, Wide nostrils

operations.explanation_template: To visually correct a turned-up nose, flabby jowls, or wide nostrils, use a slightly higher camera angle, looking down subtly.
To improve a weak chin or make male subjects appear more virile, use a slightly lower camera angle, looking up subtly.
Film a car, train, or other vehicle rushing head-on toward the camera with a level camera angle to create a subjective impression of speed and increasing image size, heightening dramatic impact.

Use a high angle, often an extreme long shot, to film subject matter laid out in a pattern upon the ground (e.g., gardens, race tracks, industrial complexes) or to establish the geography of a setting.

Utilize a high angle to film action occurring in depth, such as a football game or military formation, allowing the camera to shoot across the entire area from front to back and capture the whole scene.
Raise the camera and shoot downward from a high angle to cover a front-to-back area with less difference between near-and-far focus, aiding in keeping the entire picture area in sharp focus.
Position the camera high, employing a wide-angle lens, and reduce the subject's image to lowly insignificance in relation to the setting, to belittle a player or show them beaten down.

suggested_change.Camera Angle: Avoid High Angle (for fast movement toward/away camera)
suggested_change.Filming Speed: Undercrank (if high angle is used and speed is needed)

operations.explanation_template: If a high angle must be used for fast-moving action, consider under-cranking the camera (shooting at less than 24 fps) so that subjects will appear faster when projected, counteracting the slowing effect.
Use a low angle to film religious objects, grand architecture, or important personages (e.g., President, judge) to inspire awe in the audience by making them look up to the subject.

Employ a low angle in a point-of-view shot when one player looks up to another who dominates the story or represents authority (e.g., a degraded character looking up at an opponent or judge), increasing audience identification with the lowly player's plight.

Position the star or dominant character slightly forward of a group and film them from a low angle to make them tower over others, giving them prominence and allowing them to dominate the event. This effect can be intensified if they step forward during a moment of dramatic action or significant dialogue.

Use a low angle for cut-away reaction close-ups to position the subject against the sky or another nondescript background, dropping the horizon out of the frame to remove background identity and facilitate flexible editing.

Employ a low angle, further emphasized by a wide-angle lens, to make people, objects, or structures loom up in the picture, appearing with a broad base and diminishing perspective, thereby increasing their stature and dominance.
When filming an advancing soldier or vehicle, use a low angle to increase its perceived size and cause it to rise higher in the frame as it approaches the camera, enhancing its imposing presence.

suggested_change.Subject Movement: Advancing from bottom of frame toward camera

operations.explanation_template: Film an advancing group of players, an individual, or vehicles from a static low angle as they enter from the bottom of the frame and approach the camera, making them appear to rise up and grow in stature.

Film with an 'angle-plus-angle' setup, combining an angle in relation to the subject (to show front and side) with a tilt (to show top or bottom), to achieve the greatest number of subject facets, finest modeling, and most forceful linear perspective.
Employ subtle angle-plus-angle on every possible type of shot to prevent flatness, introduce diagonals, and enhance plastic modeling in players and objects, making them stand out from the setting.
Use wide-angle lenses to increase the angular effect and record a more forceful perspective, enhancing the three-dimensional impact of angle-plus-angle shots.

For moving vehicles, use a three-quarter low angle with a wide-angle lens, ensuring the horizon is near the bottom frame line, to create an illusion of tremendous speed and power as the subject approaches and grows larger/higher in the frame.
Film a moving column of soldiers, a long line of vehicles, or a train with a three-quarter low angle as they approach the camera, making them appear larger and more dynamic with converging lines.

For frenzied chase scenes, use a trucking shot with the camera tilted slightly upward to make the background (buildings, trees) appear to fall away backward from the players, intensifying the turmoil.

Employ a deliberate Dutch angle to create a visually off-balance, diagonally tilted image, particularly effective when combined with a low camera setup, wide-angle lens, and three-quarter subject angle, to convey instability or violent action.

For a player who has lost equilibrium, is drunk, delirious, or in a high emotional state, use a tilted shot or series of shots (perhaps opposing tilts) to visually represent their irrationality and disorientation.

To convey violence or topsy-turvy effects during a catastrophe (accident, riot, earthquake), use tilted camera angles. This effect is amplified if preceded by calm, static shots that lull the audience into a false sense of security.
In montage sequences depicting passage of time, space, or dynamic documentary action, angle several or all short shots with a Dutch tilt to create a forceful, impressionistic view.
Enhance editorial effects by using opposing left and right Dutch tilts in pairs, possibly combined with player movement in opposite directions, within a montage or chaotic scene.

suggested_change.Camera Tilt (Horizon): Lower left to upper right slant

operations.explanation_template: For traveling players, moving objects, or vehicles advancing toward the camera, slant the horizon from lower left to upper right to suggest ascent and an active, forceful presence.

suggested_change.Camera Tilt (Horizon): Upper left to lower right slant

operations.explanation_template: For traveling players, moving objects, or vehicles retreating from the lens, slant the horizon from upper left to lower right to suggest descent and a weak, static presence.
Moving from a general view to a specific one by progressively decreasing shot size.
Juxtaposing two shots of significantly different sizes to create visual opposition.

suggested_change.Camera Angle Sequence: Low Angle, Eye-Level, High Angle (or reversed)
suggested_change.Subject Relation Angle Sequence: Front Angle, Side Angle, Rear Angle (or reversed)

operations.explanation_template: Changing camera angle progressively in terms of height or relation to the subject.
Employing two shots with camera angles in direct opposition for dramatic effect.
Maintaining similar camera angle and distance across a series of shots for consistency, or using opposing matched angles for back-and-forth sequences.
Making a clear, substantial alteration to both shot size and camera angle to ensure smooth and intentional transitions.
Using an ELS to establish the setting and portray vastness.
Using an MS to introduce players as a group.
Using a CU for individual screen-filling shots or to emphasize a particular action/isolate a player.
Using an ECU for full-screen shots of very small objects or actions.
After establishing, vary medium to close shots, returning to wider shots when players move, new ones enter, or to re-establish the scene.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Repositioned

operations.explanation_template: Between continuous shots, change the camera angle, lens, or both, with repositioning the camera being most effective.
Moving the camera straight towards a centered subject to achieve a magnified 'pop-in' effect.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Move in, around to the side

operations.explanation_template: For closer shots, reposition the camera dynamically and choose an intermediate lens to best portray the player.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Move in and around to the side

operations.explanation_template: Repositioning the camera dynamically to capture interactions between subjects across the screen.
Lowering the camera when moving from a long shot to a close-up to maintain natural eye-level perspective.
Using a wide-angle lens for distant or establishing shots.
Using a normal lens for medium shots.
Using a telephoto or semi-telephoto lens for close-ups or extreme close-ups.
Incorporating foreground elements and dynamic viewpoints to enhance depth and three-dimensionality in exterior shots.
Positioning players to ensure narratively important backgrounds are integrated with their actions, using compositional lines and forms.
Using various angles and closer shots for involvement/identification, or wider shots for detachment.
Applying distorted visual effects or unique camera angles to convey a character's altered mental state directly to the viewer.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Pan, Tilt, Zoom, Dolly (for sudden revelation)

operations.explanation_template: Using specific camera angles and movements to strategically hide or suddenly reveal information, building suspense.
Simplifying camera work to ensure full audience attention remains on inherently dramatic subject matter.

suggested_change.Camera Angle: Low Angle, High Angle, Subjective, Dutch Tilt

operations.explanation_template: Employing a range of dynamic cinematic techniques to invigorate dull material or amplify existing drama.
Dynamically changing angle progression for back-and-forth close-ups or returning to a long shot for re-orientation during player movement or new introductions.
Choosing an angle that ensures maximum legibility for static signs, especially long ones.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Pan or Dolly (lettering R to L)

operations.explanation_template: Executing camera movement over a sign such that text enters from the right and moves left, while maintaining an angled perspective to avoid distortion.

suggested_change.Composition: Printed matter sloped from lower-left to upper-right

operations.explanation_template: Arranging multi-line printed text in the frame with an 'up-hill' slope for natural, comfortable eye movement and reading.
Minimizing camera angle and maintaining equidistant player positioning to reduce distortion when using wide-angle lenses in tight spaces.

Breaking a sequence into additional shots filmed with a normal angle lens avoids the distortion associated with extreme wide-angle lenses, especially for detailed subjects, thus achieving a natural perspective.
Panning the camera with a normal lens covers the desired area without the distortion of a single static wide-angle shot, presenting an undistorted view.
Shooting with a slightly off-level camera can make a tilted object appear level or straighten converging vertical lines on screen, improving visual aesthetics.
Following a series of close-ups with an extreme long shot creates visual surprise and variety, preventing audience tedium by breaking predictable patterns.
Opening a sequence with a close-up instead of a long shot offers a fresh and unpredictable viewpoint, increasing audience engagement.
Scaling images up in one shot and down in the next provides varied image sizes, contributing to visual surprise and maintaining viewer interest.
Changing, switching, or reversing player and/or camera movements avoids repetition and keeps the audience visually surprised and engaged.
Viewing settings from the side or top, instead of always from the front, provides fresh viewpoints and visual variety, sustaining audience interest.

Employing over-the-shoulder and POV angles brings the audience 'into' the picture, allowing them to stand alongside players and view from an 'inside angle', thereby increasing involvement and identification.
Presenting events as if they are occurring 'now' fosters a stronger feeling of audience participation and keeps them interested in the unfolding story, especially beneficial for documentaries.

suggested_change.Narrative Structure: Begin just before ending, then flashback, then return to present

operations.explanation_template: Beginning the narrative just before the ending, then using a flashback to recount the story up to that point, and finally returning to the present for the denouement, can mitigate the disadvantage of the audience knowing the outcome of a flashback and maintain dramatic tension.
Using a dissolve to skip unimportant travel (e.g., walking down a hall, taking an elevator) efficiently shortens screen space and time, maintaining audience focus on essential narrative progression.

suggested_change.Shot Selection: Film only areas of special interest/different terrain

operations.explanation_template: By filming only highlights or distinct terrain types, the audience can be given the impression of seeing an entire journey, effectively shortening the perceived space without losing narrative essence.

Altering the lens focal length can drastically change perspective and the perceived distance between objects or the relationship of players to the background, allowing for manipulation of perceived space.

Overlapping several shots of a short action, like walking down a flight of stairs, can subtly lengthen the perceived space on screen, making the flight appear longer without the audience's explicit awareness.

suggested_change.Camera Angle: All shots from same side of action

operations.explanation_template: Filming all shots from the same side of action ensures that the line of march (e.g., in a parade) moves in a constant, understandable direction, maintaining visual continuity for the audience.
Using multiple cameras provides complete coverage for uncontrollable, one-time events, ensuring all angles are captured, which is crucial when action cannot be repeated.

Using a single camera for the master scene, then repeating specific portions of the action for cut-in shots, allows for precise control over lighting and composition for each individual shot when action is staged and repeatable.
Overlapping action and dialogue for each shot ensures smooth transitions and continuity when inter-cutting between the master scene and closer shots.

Employing multiple cameras to record all angles simultaneously is essential for uncontrollable action or when performers cannot duplicate their performance, guaranteeing complete coverage and perfect matching for editing.
Cutting on action allows for smooth transitions between shots, moving players into or out of closer shots seamlessly while maintaining narrative flow.
Inserting a reaction shot of an opposing player can 'improve' an actor's performance or shift dramatic emphasis if a particular portion of a player's performance is weak.

The 'heart' of an individual closer shot can be cheated if player movement into and out of the master scene matches at the cut points, allowing for creative adjustments without breaking continuity at the edit.

suggested_change.Camera Placement: On same side of action axis

operations.explanation_template: Positioning all cameras on the same side of the action axis ensures consistent screen direction and efficient coverage of uncontrolled action.
Precisely blocking player and camera movements and requiring exact, repeatable performances ensures that closer shots will match the master scene for continuity.
Filming only the required portions of a master scene, based on predetermined editorial needs, saves significant production resources.
Extensive planning, blocking of camera setups/lighting/player movements, and rehearsal ensure that multi-camera staged action can be captured completely in one run-through.
Using long focal-length lenses for cut-in cameras keeps them out of the wide-angle camera's line-of-sight.

suggested_change.Action: Overlap at shot beginning and end

operations.explanation_template: Repeating action from the end of a previous shot at the beginning of the next shot creates interlocking images and assures perfect continuity.
Mentally walking through the entire action before filming helps to properly block player and camera positions and plan shots.
Beginning and ending sequences with long shots, and re-establishing them after major changes, orientates the audience and prevents them from becoming lost.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Move in, lower, and around to side

operations.explanation_template: Starting with a wide, high-angle shot and then progressively moving in, lowering, and circling for medium shots and close-ups draws the audience into the action.
Using long shots for establishment, medium shots for action, and close-ups for emphasis helps achieve good continuity and clear narrative communication.

suggested_change.Action: Repeat entire movement from new angle

operations.explanation_template: Cutting after a completed movement and repeating it at the start of the next shot (from a new angle) provides match-cut options and smoother transitions.
Overlapping all complete movements at the beginning and end of consecutive shots provides the editor with maximum flexibility for match-cutting.

suggested_change.Action: Perform overlapping action precisely the same way

operations.explanation_template: Performing overlapping actions identically across shots ensures perfect match-cuts, making transitions seamless.
Freezing a static subject allows the camera to be repositioned to a new angle without disrupting the perceived flow of action, provided stops are pre-planned.

suggested_change.Error Correction: Stop, switch angles, overlap from pre-mistake action

operations.explanation_template: Stopping on a mistake, switching angles, and overlapping from before the error minimizes retakes and saves earlier footage.

suggested_change.Lighting: Don't disturb long-shot lighting, use separate units for closer shots or mark positions if moved

operations.explanation_template: Preserving long-shot lighting or meticulously marking light positions ensures consistency for re-establishing shots and avoids visible lighting changes between cuts.

suggested_change.Coverage: Film sufficient cut-in and cut-away close-ups

operations.explanation_template: Providing cut-in and cut-away close-ups gives the editor tools to shorten sequences or cover continuity lapses effectively.

suggested_change.Screen Direction: Maintain constant L-R or R-L movement

operations.explanation_template: Ensuring a subject consistently moves in one screen direction (e.g., L-R) throughout a sequence clearly shows progression and prevents audience confusion.

suggested_change.Camera Placement: Shoot interior from same side as exterior

operations.explanation_template: Shooting the interior of a moving vehicle from the same side as the exterior creates a smoother transition and avoids the impression of reversal.

suggested_change.Screen Direction: Predetermine and consistently apply 'comings' and 'goings' directions

operations.explanation_template: Deciding and consistently maintaining specific screen directions for travel to and from locations (e.g., L-R for 'going', R-L for 'returning') orients the audience to the geography.

suggested_change.Screen Direction: Subjects move in opposite screen directions (L-R vs R-L)

operations.explanation_template: Showing two subjects moving in opposite screen directions visually indicates they are approaching each other, building anticipation for a meeting or clash.
Using progressively closer shots and cutting them shorter as action nears a climax excites emotions and deepens audience involvement through accelerating rhythm.

suggested_change.Shot Type: Head-on, Tail-away, Front/Rear Tracking, High/Low Angle (exiting top/bottom)

operations.explanation_template: Utilizing neutral shots allows for intercutting with any directional movement, facilitating smooth transitions between otherwise conflicting screen directions.
Depicting only the front or rear of a moving subject ensures an absolutely neutral screen direction, preventing unintended implications of lateral movement.

suggested_change.Shot Transition: Start neutral, then exit/enter frame to establish new direction; or insert neutral shot as buffer

operations.explanation_template: Using neutral shots that begin centered and then exit/enter frame, or inserting them as buffers, allows for a deliberate and smoother switch in screen direction.

suggested_change.Shot Sequence: Insert neutral shots into constant directional sequences

operations.explanation_template: Interspersing neutral shots into constant directional sequences provides visual variety and depth, breaking monotony.
Head-on shots place the viewer centrally with advancing action, jarring them into increased involvement and impact.

suggested_change.Shot Transition: Insert neutral shot between opposite directional shots

operations.explanation_template: Inserting a neutral shot between two shots moving in opposite directions distracts the audience, allowing for a complete screen direction reversal without an abrupt cut.

suggested_change.Camera Placement: Position all cameras on one side of the action axis

operations.explanation_template: Positioning all cameras on a single side of the imaginary action axis ensures that screen direction remains constant throughout a series of shots, maintaining continuity.

suggested_change.Pre-Production: Map out all subject travel axes before production

operations.explanation_template: Mapping out action axes before production ensures consistent screen direction planning and helps cameramen maintain it, especially when shooting off-the-cuff.

Establish the moving players/vehicle in a {Sequence Step 1.Shot Size} from the original side of the axis. Then move in for a {Sequence Step 2.Shot Size} from the same side. An opposing {Sequence Step 3.Shot Size} from the other side may then be filmed. The camera should then return to a {Sequence Step 4.Shot Size} from the original side of the axis, before filming a final {Sequence Step 5.Shot Size}. This ensures shots moving in the opposite direction are 'sandwiched'.
A {Camera Angle} shot, entering from screen left and exiting screen right, is excellent for {Camera Movement} a moving player or vehicle while maintaining left-to-right screen direction.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Static, Pan, or Static then Pan then Static

operations.explanation_template: A {Camera Angle} shot of a player moving left to right can be {Camera Movement}: static, or static for entrance, pan for a short distance, and hold static for exit screen right.
A {Camera Angle} shot of a player entering left and exiting right maintains screen direction.
A {Camera Angle} shot depicting a player entering frame screen left and walking away from the lens maintains screen direction as they move towards a destination.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Across the action axis on a curve or corner
suggested_change.Subject Exit: Same side of frame (or 'wrong' side relative to initial entrance)

operations.explanation_template: Position the camera {Camera Position}. The subject should {Subject Entrance} the frame according to the established direction, then curve/turn and {Subject Exit}, thus establishing a new screen direction for subsequent cuts.

To switch directional movement through a doorway, film the subject with a {Shot 1.Shot Type} as they exit one room, and then pick them up with a {Shot 2.Shot Type} as they enter the new room, allowing for a {Shot 2.Screen Direction} screen direction.

suggested_change.Cross-screen Shots through door: Maintain camera on same side of action axis

operations.explanation_template: If filming cross-screen shots on opposite sides of a door, keep the camera on the {Cross-screen Shots through door} for a smoother appearance and maintained directional continuity.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Switched to opposite side of action axis from actual established side

operations.explanation_template: When production factors require the subject to move in an opposite physical direction, simultaneously {Subject Movement} the subject's movement and {Camera Position}. This maintains the visual screen direction for the audience.

To ensure 'clean' entrances and exits for editorial flexibility, start the {Camera Start} and {Camera Stop}. Allow the {Subject Action} the frame, rather than cutting as it enters or just before it fully exits.

suggested_change.Entrance Proximity (next shot): Similar proximity (e.g., exit screen left, enter screen right)

operations.explanation_template: If a subject exits {Exit Proximity}, ensure the subsequent shot depicts the subject entering the frame in a {Entrance Proximity (next shot)}. Mismatched entry/exit distances will distract the audience.

suggested_change.Doorway Transition: Match entrance/exit direction and character progression

operations.explanation_template: When cutting through doorways, carefully {Doorway Transition} directional movement and the order of multiple characters. Take detailed notes to prevent mismatches, especially over long shooting intervals.

suggested_change.Sequence: Neutral head-on or tail-away shot -> Reaction Close-up -> New directional action shot
suggested_change.Player Head Movement: Follows implied action in new direction (as if behind camera)

operations.explanation_template: To switch screen direction without showing a physical turn, insert a neutral head-on or tail-away shot, then cut to a {Sequence.Reaction Close-up} where the player's {Player Head Movement}. This distracts the audience and legitimizes the subsequent change to {Sequence.New directional action shot}.

suggested_change.Subject Action: Show person or vehicle physically turning around on screen

operations.explanation_template: The most direct way to reverse screen direction is to {Subject Action} within the frame, visually informing the audience of the change.

suggested_change.Subject Exit: Exit the 'wrong' side of the frame

operations.explanation_template: Use a {Shot Type} where the subject {Subject Exit} to introduce a new series of travel shots moving in the opposite direction. This is more effective than a tail-away shot for this purpose as it provides a clear exit.

suggested_change.Sequence: Cut to interior of vehicle -> Cut to exterior moving shot

operations.explanation_template: For vehicle travel, cut to the {Sequence.Cut to interior of vehicle} and then transition to an {Sequence.Cut to exterior moving shot} moving in the {Exterior Shot Direction}. For multiple interior shots, ensure the final interior shot has players facing the new direction.

To align with conventional map orientation, depict eastbound travel (heading toward the right side of a map) as moving {Screen Direction (Eastbound)}. Depict westbound travel (heading toward the left side of a map) as moving {Screen Direction (Westbound)}. This leverages the audience's subconscious understanding.

For northbound travel (often depicted as 'up' on a map), stage movement {Screen Direction (Northbound)}. For southbound travel ('down'), stage movement {Screen Direction (Southbound)}. This aligns with accepted compositional concepts of up/down movement.

In the initial shot of a long-distance journey, ensure the pilot, captain, or passengers are {Initial Shot Subject Facing}. This preserves the continuity of the action axis and reinforces the map direction.

suggested_change.Camera Setups: All on the same side of the building
suggested_change.Lens Viewpoint: Always in the same general direction

operations.explanation_template: In complex interiors, keep {Camera Setups} so that the {Lens Viewpoint} and the camera never crosses the action axis. This maintains directional consistency for all travel within the building.

suggested_change.Subject Entry/Exit: On side preserving established travel direction

operations.explanation_template: If physical limitations prevent same-side camera setups in interiors, use {Shot Type} shots. Ensure subjects {Subject Entry/Exit} (e.g., L-R for travel towards the front of the building, R-L for travel towards the rear).

suggested_change.Pre-production Step: Thoroughly map out all shots in a sequence, establishing the action axis to favor optimal camera angles, sun angles, and backgrounds.

operations.explanation_template: To avoid overlooking screen direction, {Pre-production Step}. This ensures a definite plan for constant progression and established directions.

suggested_change.Planning Method: For complex sequences, plan backwards from the climax location.

operations.explanation_template: For sequences with many shots, especially when a particular location dictates the screen direction, {Planning Method}. This allows the location to decide the screen direction for the entire sequence.

suggested_change.Camera Angle (Exterior): Approximate same angle as interior setup
suggested_change.Camera Angle (Interior): Approximate same angle as exterior setup

operations.explanation_template: To create a seamless transition, film the exterior and interior shots from {Camera Angle (Exterior)} and {Camera Angle (Interior)} respectively, as if the camera moved through the vehicle. The {Travel Axis} must be maintained for a smooth match-cut.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Within 180-degree arc on one side of axis
suggested_change.Camera Movement: Avoid crossing the axis between cuts

operations.explanation_template: By positioning the camera anywhere within a 180-degree arc on one side of the action axis, and never crossing it between cuts, the audience will perceive consistent screen direction and player positions, preventing visual disorientation.

suggested_change.Actor Gaze Direction: Consistent to the established side of the axis

operations.explanation_template: Ensuring players' looks remain consistent to one side of the action axis across match-cuts prevents misinterpretation of their focus and maintains smooth relational continuity.

suggested_change.Actor Gaze Direction: Same direction on each side of a match-cut

operations.explanation_template: Maintaining the actor's gaze in the same direction across a match-cut ensures seamless transitions and consistent spatial relationships, unless the shift in gaze is explicitly shown within a shot.

suggested_change.Off-screen Actor Position: Proper side of camera relative to action axis

operations.explanation_template: To prevent inadvertent mis-matching of looks in opposing close-ups, especially with flat-on P.O.V. angles, position the off-screen player on the correct side of the camera, ensuring the on-screen player's gaze aligns with the established action axis.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Cross axis to film rear players
suggested_change.Camera Angle: Maintain established action axis angle (new parallel axis)

operations.explanation_template: To film players at the rear of a set, the camera may physically cross the action axis if a new parallel axis is established, ensuring the camera angle maintains the original directional continuity. This is akin to optically crossing the axis with a longer focal length lens.

suggested_change.Actor Gaze Direction: Sweep past lens, just above or below, not into lens
suggested_change.Actor Blocking: Shift focus between subjects on either side

operations.explanation_template: Instruct the actor to sweep their gaze past the camera lens, aiming slightly above or below it (depending on camera height), to smoothly transition their attention between multiple subjects. This creates a new action axis for subsequent shots based on their final look.

suggested_change.Actor Gaze Direction: Slightly above or below the lens, to the side of the camera

operations.explanation_template: To achieve a neutral look when a player is observing something at a different height, instruct them to look slightly above or below the lens, while still maintaining their gaze to the side of the camera to respect the action axis. This helps avoid direct eye contact with the audience or misinterpretations of direction.

suggested_change.Blocking Strategy: Redraw action axis at end of each shot

operations.explanation_template: Redrawing the action axis at the end of each shot, especially when players or camera move, automatically maintains matched looks and screen direction for subsequent shots, but requires careful duplication of player positions to avoid jump-cuts.

To maintain continuity in opposing close-ups, either exclude any object positioned between players from both shots, or reposition it closer to one player so it consistently appears in only one of the close-ups.

suggested_change.Blocking Strategy: Draw axis in direction player is facing/looking relative to work
suggested_change.Camera Position: Within 180-degree arc on one side of this single-player axis

operations.explanation_template: For a single player, define an action axis through them in the direction they are facing or looking relative to their task. Position all cameras within a 180-degree arc on one side of this axis to maintain consistent screen direction across cuts.

suggested_change.Camera Angle: Over opposite shoulder of dominant hand

operations.explanation_template: When filming a right-handed player performing an action (e.g., signing), shoot over their *left* shoulder to clearly show the action of their right hand. Conversely, for a left-handed player, shoot over their right shoulder to avoid obscuring the action.

suggested_change.Camera Position: On one side, shooting toward centerline

operations.explanation_template: To achieve direct opposing looks for a speaker and audience, draw the action axis down the center aisle (or a centerline) and position the camera consistently on one side, shooting toward this line. This simplifies establishing opposing looks for all shots.

suggested_change.Blocking Strategy: Draw axis across audience (parallel to seats)
suggested_change.Camera Position: Anywhere within triangle formed by speaker and audience row

operations.explanation_template: For more visual variety and freedom, draw the action axis across a row of audience seats. Position the camera within the 'triangle' formed by the speaker and this audience row, allowing the speaker to sweep their look and audience members to look left or right, which are then inter-cut for opposing looks.

suggested_change.Editing Technique: Final audience shot opposes next speaker shot

operations.explanation_template: When editing speaker and audience shots, inter-cut the speaker's gaze with an audience member's look in the opposite direction. If multiple audience close-ups follow, ensure the final audience shot opposes the subsequent speaker shot for smoother continuity.

suggested_change.Camera Position: One side of centerline axis
suggested_change.Subject: Speaker

operations.explanation_template: Positions the camera to frame the speaker looking toward screen left, establishing one side of the opposing look.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Opposite side of centerline axis (relative to audience)
suggested_change.Subject: Audience

operations.explanation_template: Positions the camera to frame the audience looking toward screen right, opposing the speaker's look.

suggested_change.Camera Position: On the same side of the centerline axis as the speaker, but framing audience

operations.explanation_template: Captures the audience from the speaker's side of the axis, maintaining the opposing look to the speaker for overall scene context.

suggested_change.Camera Position: May optically cross axis

operations.explanation_template: Allows for close-ups of individuals in the audience while maintaining continuity, even if it involves an optical axis crossing.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Parallel to audience rows
suggested_change.Subject: Speaker

operations.explanation_template: Frames the speaker who can naturally look left and right to engage the audience on both sides.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Left side of theater (relative to stage)
suggested_change.Subject: Audience (Left Side)

operations.explanation_template: Frames the left-side audience looking right, creating an opposing look to the speaker (when the speaker looks left).

suggested_change.Camera Position: Right side of theater (relative to stage)
suggested_change.Subject: Audience (Right Side)

operations.explanation_template: Frames the right-side audience looking left, creating an opposing look to the speaker (when the speaker looks right).

suggested_change.Camera Position: Rear of theater

operations.explanation_template: Provides a neutral shot from the rear, often for scene establishment or to break up a sequence of opposing looks.
Ensures audience members on the left side appear to look towards the right, consistent with facing a speaker on stage.
Ensures audience members on the right side appear to look towards the left, consistent with facing a speaker on stage.

suggested_change.Subject Action: Speaker turns look from one audience member to another
suggested_change.Action Axis: New axis established between speaker and current focus

operations.explanation_template: Defines a new action axis when the speaker's focus shifts, allowing for new two-shots to be framed correctly for each interaction.
Breaks up the back-and-forth cutting, providing visual variety and flexibility for character looks without disorienting the viewer.
Allows a speaker to change their gaze direction within a neutral shot without breaking continuity for subsequent opposing shots.
Creates a neutral treatment for a long shot, suitable for general establishment without strong directional bias.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Same side of centerline axis

operations.explanation_template: Creates an opposing effect while maintaining the axis rule, ensuring subjects face each other visually.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Opposite sides of centerline axis for stage and audience long shots

operations.explanation_template: Explicitly warns against this setup as it causes speaker and audience to face the same direction, breaking natural interaction and continuity.
Best for clear, straightforward interactions between a speaker and audience, such as in a classroom setting.
Allows for more dynamic camera work and visual interest, especially when the speaker engages a wider audience.

suggested_change.Axis Type: Combination of Centerline and Parallel Axis

operations.explanation_template: Combines benefits of both for complex or lengthy sequences, providing flexibility without sacrificing clarity.

suggested_change.Look Direction: Opposing looks between stage and audience

operations.explanation_template: Eliminates the need to maintain opposing looks between performers and audience when they do not directly interact, simplifying filming.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Remain on one side of centerline axis

operations.explanation_template: Ensures consistent screen direction for opposing looks, critical for maintaining viewer orientation.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Neutral (head-on)

operations.explanation_template: Allows for neutral shots that do not violate the action axis rule, often used for establishment or transitions.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Cross centerline axis in consecutive shots

operations.explanation_template: Crossing the axis makes characters appear to look in the same direction, breaking continuity and confusing the viewer.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Anywhere

operations.explanation_template: Leverages the fixed nature of an auditorium to allow camera freedom when cuts are spaced out, minimizing disorientation.

suggested_change.Subject Position: Dominant player on one side of screen
suggested_change.Supporting Players Position: Two supporting players on opposite side of screen (as a unit)

operations.explanation_template: Creates a clear visual separation and opposing looks, simplifying the scene's spatial dynamics.
Establishes clear opposing looks between the dominant player and the supporting unit.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Same side of action axis (drawn through two nearest players)

operations.explanation_template: Maintains continuity for close-ups within this three-shot setup by adhering to the established action axis.

suggested_change.Subject Action: Dominant player looks at or acts towards a specific supporting player
suggested_change.Action Axis: New axis formed between these two players

operations.explanation_template: A clear gaze or action from the dominant player establishes a new axis, justifying camera repositioning for subsequent shots.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Between the two players forming the new axis

operations.explanation_template: Allows for a close-up of the dominant player that aligns with the newly established axis, maintaining a smooth visual flow.

suggested_change.Screen Direction: Dominant player's look/action directed screen right (towards far player)

operations.explanation_template: Ensures a smooth cut from a side angle to an in-between rear angle, preserving the dominant player's look and directional continuity.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Remain on same side of original axis

operations.explanation_template: Prevents confusion when the action establishing a new axis is not strong enough to warrant a full camera repositioning, maintaining established spatial relations.
Establishes a foundational single axis for the three spread-apart players, simplifying their spatial organization.

suggested_change.Camera Position: May optically cross axis

operations.explanation_template: Allows for close-ups of the background player while maintaining the overall continuity of the scene.

suggested_change.Condition: As players relate to each other

operations.explanation_template: Handles dynamic interactions by breaking the three-shot into a series of two-shots, each with its own implied axis, for clarity.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Cross the action axis

operations.explanation_template: Crossing the axis will cause players to transpose screen positions, creating viewer confusion and breaking continuity.

suggested_change.Subject Grouping: Treat two close players as a single unit
suggested_change.Camera Position: Film from same side of axis

operations.explanation_template: Simplifies the spatial relationship and ensures consistent screen direction when two players act as one unit.
Reinforces their unity and clear spatial relationship with the opposing player, maintaining visual consistency.

suggested_change.Look Direction: Opposing look to current relating player

operations.explanation_template: Ensures proper directional continuity for each active two-player interaction, adapting to shifting focus.

suggested_change.Action Axis: New axis created with each two-shot interaction

operations.explanation_template: Dynamically adjusts the action axis as player interactions and gazes shift, maintaining accurate spatial relationships.

suggested_change.Scene Establishment: Clearly establish overall scene of players around table

operations.explanation_template: Orients the audience to the layout of the scene and positions of characters before moving to closer shots.
Ensures correct opposing looks in close-ups based on who is interacting, preventing confusion about who is speaking to whom.

suggested_change.Camera Movement: Move around table for individual close-ups
suggested_change.Action Axis: New axis created by on-screen player's look towards off-screen player

operations.explanation_template: The gaze of the active player towards an off-screen player defines a new axis, justifying camera repositioning for their close-up and maintaining continuity.

suggested_change.Subject Action: Player switches look to another player
suggested_change.Look Direction: Maintain opposing looks for each interaction

operations.explanation_template: Ensures that as a player shifts their attention, the visual continuity of opposing looks is preserved, keeping the viewer oriented.

suggested_change.Editing Pattern: Three-shot followed by two-shots that transpose middle player's screen position

operations.explanation_template: This pattern causes viewer confusion by making a character abruptly shift screen position, breaking spatial continuity.
Preferred methods to avoid screen position shifts and maintain clear continuity when cutting from a three-shot to closer views.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Turned around

operations.explanation_template: Simulates a reverse shot by physically repositioning both subject and camera while maintaining their relative orientation, bypassing physical limitations.
Ensures the viewer perceives the cheated shot as a direct reverse, consistent with the initial setup's spatial logic.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Remain on same side of new action axis
suggested_change.Player Look: Remain on same side of new action axis

operations.explanation_template: Crucial for maintaining screen direction and continuity despite the physical 'cheat' in player and camera placement.
Necessary if the cheated background will appear in other scenes and needs to be consistent, preventing visual discontinuity.

suggested_change.Production: Film production scenes with matching/opposing looks/angles

operations.explanation_template: Ensures all elements (stock and newly filmed) align correctly for continuity, creating a seamless visual flow.

suggested_change.Technique: Perform mental pan from reference shot's look to new shot's subject
suggested_change.Outcome: Determines correct opposing look and camera angle

operations.explanation_template: A cognitive trick to quickly and accurately determine the necessary screen direction and camera angle for matching shots, maintaining spatial consistency.
Ensures the character's gaze direction is consistent with the implied off-screen action, creating a believable reaction.

suggested_change.Object Movement: Take-off or landing of plane (or similar movement)

operations.explanation_template: Critical for matching continuity of motion between shots, especially when combining new footage with stock footage.
Maintains logical orientation for a pilot within a moving vehicle, enhancing realism and viewer understanding.

suggested_change.Expected Effect: May transpose players; introduces new backgrounds; viewer confusion

operations.explanation_template: Highlights the potential negative consequences of unmanaged reverse shots, such as disorienting the viewer with sudden spatial shifts.

suggested_change.Outcome: Eliminates matching/editorial problems in reverse shots

operations.explanation_template: The action axis is the fundamental key to successfully executing reverse shots, ensuring spatial consistency and preventing editorial errors.

suggested_change.Shot Type: Opposing OTS/POV close-ups; Head-on/tail-away travel shots

operations.explanation_template: These specific types of reverse shots, when adhering to the action axis, maintain consistent player looks and subject travel direction despite opposite angles.

suggested_change.Setting Type: Fixed seating (theaters, vehicles); Distinct front/back (churches, courtrooms)

operations.explanation_template: The fixed nature of the setting or clear front/back distinction clarifies camera movement for the viewer, minimizing confusion during reverses.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Stay on same side of centerline axis (whenever possible)

operations.explanation_template: Even with freedom, maintaining the axis side improves directional consistency and viewer orientation.

suggested_change.Alternative Shot Type: Shoot toward front/back from same side of axis

operations.explanation_template: These options provide clear views while maintaining axis consistency or offering a neutral bridge.

suggested_change.Condition: Crossing the axis for opposite looks

operations.explanation_template: A neutral shot can bridge a problematic axis crossing, preventing viewer disorientation caused by sudden directional changes.
Distinctive features help orient the viewer during reverse shots by providing clear visual landmarks.
Such rooms will confuse the viewer during a reverse shot due to a lack of orienting visual information and similar backgrounds.
Provides the audience with crucial spatial context, allowing them to understand the room's layout and interpret reverse shots correctly.

suggested_change.Subject Movement: Exits right, enters left (in reverse shot)

operations.explanation_template: Ensures logical screen direction for characters crossing a space with reverse shots, preventing confusing spatial jumps.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Film from same side of action axis
suggested_change.Effect: Show progression for constant travel direction

operations.explanation_template: Essential for maintaining consistent directional movement and the viewer's sense of progression in a travel sequence.

suggested_change.Subject Action: Fixed group looks off-screen at entering player
suggested_change.Action Axis: New axis created between group and entering player

operations.explanation_template: The group's collective gaze establishes the new axis for the interaction, guiding subsequent camera placement.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Behind fixed group (opposite side of room)
suggested_change.Condition: Remain on same side of new axis

operations.explanation_template: Allows for a reverse shot of the entering player while respecting the newly formed action axis, maintaining consistent eye-lines.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Reverse angle
suggested_change.Subject Position: Entering player framed between two other players
suggested_change.Subject Movement: Entering player walks toward group's look

operations.explanation_template: Creates a visually cohesive and spatially logical shot of an entering character, integrating them into the group's established focus.

suggested_change.Camera Action: Reverse camera to show what player sees

operations.explanation_template: The character's gaze justifies and guides the camera's reversal to their perspective, making the transition clear and motivated.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Same side of axis

operations.explanation_template: Ensures opposing looks are maintained in the reverse POV shot if an interaction is implied, preserving continuity of the relationship.
Directly addresses the primary source of confusion in reverse shots, which can disorient the viewer and break immersion.

suggested_change.Scene Establishment: Establish scene type (e.g., church, bus) or distinctive feature in overall view

operations.explanation_template: Provides crucial orienting information to the audience, helping them understand the space and interpret reverse shots correctly.

suggested_change.Editing: Match on each side of straight cut

operations.explanation_template: Fundamental for achieving seamless continuous action, ensuring no jarring jumps in movement or spatial relationships.
Ensures characters enter and exit logically within the established screen space, maintaining viewer orientation.

suggested_change.Look Direction: Properly matching looks for all players (on/off-screen)

operations.explanation_template: Crucial for maintaining character relationships and spatial awareness in detail shots, even for off-screen characters.

suggested_change.Condition: Player or camera movement changes original axis within a shot

operations.explanation_template: Updates the continuity guideline for the next shot, ensuring accurate spatial relationships are maintained despite internal shot changes.

suggested_change.Outcome: Camera and subjects free to roam/look without wrong directional look

operations.explanation_template: The axis acts as a guiding principle, allowing for creative freedom in movement and blocking without sacrificing spatial continuity.

suggested_change.Editing: Must be same on each side of match-cut

operations.explanation_template: The fundamental rule for maintaining continuity across match-cuts, ensuring no abrupt shifts that confuse the viewer.

suggested_change.Pre-Production/On-set: Note movement/look at beginning and end of each shot
suggested_change.Action Axis: Redraw if differs from start-of-shot axis

operations.explanation_template: A practical step to ensure the action axis is correctly tracked and updated for subsequent shots, maintaining continuity throughout a sequence.

suggested_change.Action: Players change direction/looks/positions, cross axis; Camera pans/dollies, crosses axis

operations.explanation_template: Emphasizes the freedom of movement and dynamic changes that can occur within a single continuous take.

suggested_change.Action: Players change direction/looks/positions; Camera crosses axis

operations.explanation_template: This is the core rule for maintaining spatial continuity across match-cuts; such changes will disorient the viewer.

suggested_change.Rule Application: Strict match-cut continuity rules DO NOT APPLY

operations.explanation_template: These transitions signal a deliberate break in continuous action, allowing for changes in continuity without confusing the audience.

suggested_change.Rule Application: Strict match-cut continuity rules DO NOT APPLY

operations.explanation_template: Jumping locations also signals a break in continuous spatial action, making strict match-cut rules unnecessary.

suggested_change.Rule Application: Strict match-cut continuity rules DO NOT APPLY

operations.explanation_template: The combination of axis treatments inherently offers more flexibility, reducing the strictness of continuous match-cut rules.
Essential for maintaining the flow of action and viewer orientation in sequences that cut between different subjects or locations.

suggested_change.Camera Position: Remain on same side of moving/static players/vehicles

operations.explanation_template: The fundamental method for maintaining established movement or look continuity, ensuring logical progression across cuts.

suggested_change.Subject: Place name at entry, newspaper with date

operations.explanation_template: Uses specific visual elements to efficiently convey critical scene information like time and location to the audience.
Introduces a new narrative unit or major section from darkness, providing a clear visual cue for a beginning.
Concludes a narrative unit by fading to black, providing a sense of closure or finality.

suggested_change.Narrative Context: Passage of time (same locale) or switch to new setting

operations.explanation_template: Serves as a clear marker for temporal or spatial shifts, helping the audience understand breaks in continuity.
Overuse can break narrative immersion and make the story feel disjointed rather than fluid.
Softly indicates a temporal or spatial shift, allowing for a gradual rather than abrupt change in scene.
Smooths over cuts that might otherwise be jarring, enhancing the visual flow and reducing viewer disorientation.
Adjusts the pace of the transition to fit the scene's emotional or narrative rhythm, supporting the storytelling.

suggested_change.Visual Element: Similar form, motion, or content between scenes

operations.explanation_template: Uses visual parallelism to create a fluid and meaningful transition, often reinforcing narrative themes or ideas.

suggested_change.Matched Dissolve: Too tricky, draws attention from narrative, images don't stem from story

operations.explanation_template: Matched dissolves should serve the story subtly; if they become too distracting or unmotivated, they detract from the narrative.
Visually communicates an altered perception or a shift to a non-linear narrative, immersing the audience in the character's subjective experience.
Combines audio and visual elements to enhance the effect of an altered state, creating a more immersive and impactful experience.
Standard practice for clearly indicating non-linear time, preventing viewer confusion about temporal shifts.

suggested_change.Transition: Omit return dissolve, use straight cut

operations.explanation_template: Allows for creative departures from the standard bracketing when appropriate, such as to startle the viewer from a dream or hallucination.
Visually communicates an arrest of time between scenes, creating a contemplative or impactful pause.
Creates a unique artistic visual, blurring the line between photography and art for a highly aesthetic transition.
A multi-step transition that visually represents an event becoming a published news story, often with a sense of formality or historical distance.

suggested_change.Effect: One scene pushes another off screen

operations.explanation_template: The basic function of a wipe, providing a clear and often dynamic visual demarcation between scenes.
More stylized options for wipes, offering a distinct visual aesthetic for scene transitions.
Wipes can feel mechanical and anachronistic in modern dramatic films, signaling their typical use in trailers, advertising, and commercials.

suggested_change.Editing Technique: Montage (series of short scenes via cuts, dissolves, or wipes)
suggested_change.Purpose: Condense time or space, depict complex events efficiently

operations.explanation_template: A powerful tool for narrative compression, accelerating pace and conveying lengthy events without showing every detail.
Employing a metronome for precise action beats and ensuring similar or contrasting subject/camera movement contributes to the overall tempo and impact of the montage.
Similar camera or subject movements throughout montage shots create a fluid and cohesive sequence for effective results.
Contrasting camera or subject movements throughout montage shots can create visual dynamism or thematic tension for effective results.
Isolating the character in a close-up at the end of the first scene helps mask the upcoming location change and maintains focus on the monologue.
Picking up the next scene with a close-up re-establishes focus on the character in the new setting before revealing the wider locale.
Cutting or pulling back after the close-up reveals the new locale, completing the transition smoothly after re-establishing the character.
Ensures continuous movement across cuts, making the edit invisible and providing flexibility for cutting on action.
Provides detail or shifts focus, effectively covering a jump-cut or shortening a sequence.
Distracts the audience from a problematic edit in the main action, improving visual continuity.
Shifts focus to a character's response, allowing an action edit to be hidden and saving a sequence with jump-cuts.
Alternating between different events or perspectives allows the editor to match and blend actions that occur across separate segments, creating a seamless flow.
By interspersing footage of different events, the director can prevent monotony and inject new energy into the narrative whenever attention might wane.

Alternating between advancing opposing forces, while progressively speeding up the cuts and tightening the shots, creates a palpable sense of escalating conflict and draws the audience into the imminent climax.
By cutting between two events that directly influence each other, the editor keeps the audience invested in both outcomes, knowing that one's progress affects the other.

suggested_change.Shot Size: Close-ups for critical details (e.g., ticking bomb)

operations.explanation_template: Cutting back and forth between, for example, a search and the object of danger (like a ticking bomb close-up), constantly reminds the audience of the stakes and accelerates their anxiety towards the climax.
By showing different subjects in an alternating sequence, the director prompts the audience to notice their similarities or differences, fostering comparative understanding.
By presenting contrasting subjects in an alternating fashion, the director makes the differences immediately apparent and impactful for the audience.

suggested_change.Editing Pattern: Alternate between simultaneous events in different spaces

operations.explanation_template: Alternating between different locations where simultaneous events are progressing allows the audience to follow multiple threads of the story and grasp their real-time interconnection.

suggested_change.Editing Pattern: Alternate between present events and past/future events

operations.explanation_template: By interweaving scenes from different time periods, the director can highlight thematic connections, show evolution, or underscore continuity/change over time.
A longer, wider initial shot allows the audience ample time to understand the setting and subjects before rapid cuts introduce other parallel events.

suggested_change.Information Disclosure: Immediate and clear identification of event, characters, location.

operations.explanation_template: Clear visual and/or audio cues quickly establish the context of each new cross-cut, ensuring the audience remains clear about the unfolding events.

suggested_change.Editing Pattern: Parallel editing of two or more events

operations.explanation_template: Parallel editing allows a documentary to explore complex relationships or thematic connections by presenting multiple strands of information concurrently, making the presentation more engaging.

suggested_change.Cut Point: During a player's movement (e.g., opening a door, sitting, walking)

operations.explanation_template: By cutting precisely when a subject is in motion, the visual momentum carries across the edit, making the cut less perceptible and maintaining flow.

suggested_change.Filming Technique: Shoot moving action to completion, then repeat end portion for overlap in subsequent shot

operations.explanation_template: Providing extra footage before and after the critical action point in consecutive shots gives the editor a 'buffer' to precisely align the movement for a smooth match cut.
Cutting from a longer shot of movement to a close-up allows the editor to skip or repeat portions of the movement in the wider shot, thereby adjusting the perceived time without a jump-cut.

suggested_change.Blocking: Player moves into the close-up frame from off-screen or from a wider shot position.

operations.explanation_template: By having the player move into the close-up, the editor can cut the preceding scene shorter, seamlessly transitioning to the player in the closer shot without the audience perceiving a missing part of the movement.

suggested_change.Camera Operation: Start camera before actor enters frame, stop after actor leaves frame.

operations.explanation_template: Filming extra frames at the beginning and end of a player's movement into or out of a shot provides the editor with flexibility to hide the cut, ensuring a 'clean' transition.

suggested_change.Match: Action across straight cuts, exposure, lighting, color, technicalities.

operations.explanation_template: Meticulous matching of all visual and technical elements between shots ensures that the audience perceives a seamless and continuous reality, rather than noticing disruptive inconsistencies.

suggested_change.Pre-production: Careful planning of camera angles and action at cut points.
